Introduction — The Proliferation Paradox

## 1.1 Prologue

### The Flood and the Swarm

On Saturday, October 7, 2023, at 6:29 in the morning, the barrier fell. Rockets rose over the western Negev. Behind them came the men. Thousands of fighters crossed the fence at 119 points, the vanguard from the Nukhba, Hamas’s elite assault force.[^fn1] They came on motorcycles, in pickups, on powered paragliders, and on foot. Their first targets were not the kibbutzim. Their first targets belonged to the army.

The Nukhba teams knew where the Gaza Division kept its nerve centers. They struck the division headquarters at Re’im. They struck the company outposts along the fence. They struck the observation posts that watched the wire. Within the first hour they killed commanders in their beds and cut the cables that carried the orders. The division that guarded the border lost the ability to see and the ability to speak.[^fn2]

Hamas named the operation the Al-Aqsa Flood.[^fn3] The method was the swarm. A swarm does not seek one decisive blow. It seeks to arrive everywhere at once, to split the defender’s attention, to drown the system in simultaneous emergencies.[^fn4] Hamas had studied the seam between the army and the home front. It tore that seam open. By eight in the morning, gunmen moved through more than twenty communities, through a music festival near Re’im, and north along the roads toward Sderot, toward Ashkelon, toward the center of the country.

The failure ran deeper than the morning. In the hours before the attack the army had read movement on the Gaza side and had raised a quiet alert. It left the festival in place. It left the thin line along the fence.[^fn5] One premise had hardened into doctrine. Hamas was deterred. Hamas was contained. Hamas would not dare.[^fn6] When the wire gave way, the doctrine gave way with it, and the conscripts on the line met numbers no one had told them to expect.

The confusion did not lift when the firing started. For hours no echelon held a clear picture of an invasion at more than a hundred points at once. Forces that reached the kibbutzim sometimes pulled back after the first contact rather than press into the fight. In one kibbutz, units fought through the same lanes without knowing the others were inside.[^fn7] The army’s own inquiries, published in the months that followed, would record the breakdown in detail. I begin with the collapse because the collapse is the frame for everything that follows. This book is the story of a small set of military units that Israel built across ninety years. On the morning those units mattered most, the system built to direct them did not function. There was no command. There was no plan. There was the country, and the men and women who had once worn its uniform.

### The Second Wave

The chain of command had broken. What stopped the invasion was a second wave that no order summoned. Off-duty soldiers heard the news and drove south. Reservists pulled rifles from closets and looked for a ride. Police officers, intelligence operatives, and retired commanders converged on the envelope, the belt of communities around Gaza, in private cars and civilian clothes, without papers and without instructions. They formed teams from strangers. They shared a map over a phone. They drove toward the sound of the guns.

I have built a dataset of the security personnel who died in the fighting of October 7 and 8, 369 names in all. The collection, the coding, and the findings sit in an appendix at the end of the book. Two patterns belong here. The dead fell in two waves. The men who were already in place when the attack began were young and most of them conscript, and they died early, where the attack found them. The men who reached the fighting after it started were older, more professional, more often reserve and officer, and they died later, after the time it takes to wake, to understand, to arm, to drive, and to arrive.[^fn8] The gap between the two waves is the time the second one needed to assemble itself out of private living rooms. No staff planned that mobilization. The country performed it on its own.

The special-operations share is the second pattern. Of the 369 who fell, sixty came from special operations units, close to one in six.[^fn9] Special operators are a sliver of the Israeli order of battle, a fraction of a percent of the men under arms. Among the security dead of the first forty-eight hours they were one in six, and among the volunteers who drove to the fight on their own the share ran higher still. The ratio is a proxy, and what it measures is speed and mass. Operators died in those numbers because they reached the worst places first and in strength, while the system that should have deployed them stayed silent. Most did not fall because someone sent them. Most sent themselves.

Here I want to be exact about the claim. I do not argue that the special units saved the country alone. Conscripts died at their posts and bought time with their lives. Members of the kibbutz response squads fought and fell at their own gates. I argue something narrower. When the formal system failed, the capacity to respond lived inside individuals, and it was densest in a few small units. The people who carried the most of it were the ones those units had trained. They reached the battle as men. Only later, in the kibbutz lanes and the burning fields, did they re-form into units.

I follow three of them through the day. The Yamam, the police counterterror unit. Shaldag, the air force’s commando unit. Sayeret Matkal, the general staff’s reconnaissance unit. Each fought a different war that morning. Together they show one thing: a force that functioned without its head because the head had been built into the hands.

### The Morning: Three Roads South

The first call reached the Yamam at 6:45, sixteen minutes after the barrier fell.[^fn10] The standby team did not wait for the picture to clear. It left for Sderot at once, and the rest of the unit followed, some from the base, most from home in private cars.[^fn11] At 7:26, still riding in a civilian vehicle, the lead fighters met dozens of gunmen near the Big shopping center on the edge of Sderot.[^fn12] The attackers carried anti-tank missiles, machine guns, grenades, and charges. The fighters carried what they had brought from home. The clash began before the army arrived and before the air force flew.[^fn13]

Through the morning the war ran along the roads. The junctions north of the kibbutzim were the chokepoints, the places where gunmen funneled toward Route 4 and the cities past it. The Yamam fed its teams to those junctions to hold them and to keep the attackers off the highway. “We understood that if the terrorists keep going north, they reach Ashdod, Ashkelon, and the center of the country,” a senior officer of the unit said. “We are the last force that will stop them.”[^fn14] The fighting at the junctions had no pause and no shape, and several Yamam fighters fell around Sha’ar HaNegev in the first hours.[^fn15]

The Yamam moved as a unit. Most of the second wave did not. A Maglan major, off duty when the sirens began, drove toward the envelope alone. In a Sderot street he found two girls hiding and handed them his car keys. He went on by himself, swept the nearby moshav of Yakhini, killed two gunmen, and took rounds in the hand and the abdomen before he stopped.[^fn16] He is one figure in a flood of them, the off-duty and the discharged, the ones who pointed themselves south with whatever weapon they owned.

Far to the north, the Shaldag commander woke at his home in a moshav and started south within minutes, calling his officers from the road. “Bring everyone, there is a war,” he told them, and the unit answered, from the training platoon’s youngest fighters to its oldest reservists.[^fn17] One of the oldest answered on his own. Master Sergeant Ido Rosental, known as Krido, was forty-five, the oldest and most experienced fighter in Shaldag. He had enlisted in the unit in 1996 and had served in it for more than twenty-five years.[^fn18] He was off duty that Saturday. He made his own way to the unit and flew south with the others. No order placed him on that helicopter.

Sayeret Matkal moved the same way. Its fighters learned of the attack through messages and word of mouth, gathered at the unit, and split toward the envelope in whatever transport they could find.[^fn19] The most secret unit in the army assembled that morning the way the reservists did, by private decision, one fighter telling the next.

### Midday: Be’eri and Alumim

The fastest route ran through the air. A little before nine, on the chief of staff’s order, a helicopter set a Shaldag team down beside Kibbutz Be’eri.[^fn20] At 9:03, thirteen fighters entered the kibbutz.[^fn21] For hours they were the only organized military force inside it. The army’s later inquiry counted some 340 attackers in Be’eri at the height of the morning, against a handful of armed defenders.[^fn22] Shaldag lost a fighter at the breach and pulled back toward the gate, a decision the inquiry would judge a grave error, and the kibbutz held on its own people, the members of the response squad and a retired general among them, some firing to their last rounds.[^fn23] No single commander directed that battle. The inquiry recorded the confusion that followed: forces that withdrew without pressing the enemy, and units that fought in the same kibbutz without knowing the others were there.[^fn24] I note the failures because they are part of the same story. The system was not slow that morning. For hours it was absent.

Rosental’s helicopter came down near Kibbutz Alumim, a few kilometers north. The fighting there was its own massacre, in the foreign workers’ quarters and along the fence. Rosental fell in it.[^fn25] Alumim drew the second wave from every direction. By one account some 350 fighters passed through the area that day, most of them assigned nowhere near it, crossing on their own toward Be’eri and the other kibbutzim.[^fn26] Two brothers from Be’er Sheva who drove down to fight fell at Alumim. A combat engineer captain fell there. So did a sergeant from the police special patrol, whose body Hamas carried into Gaza.[^fn27] They came from a city, from an engineering unit, from a police unit, from an air force commando unit, and they died in the same few fields, because each of them had decided, alone, to go.

I dwell on Rosental because his life holds the argument of this book in one span. He had given the unit more than half his life. In his civilian years he was an artist. He photographed the margins of Israeli society: children selling packs of gum at a Jerusalem junction, the crews of the ships he guarded at sea, a desert lake going dry.[^fn28] He left a wife and three children.[^fn29] He was not a young conscript caught on the line. He was a forty-five-year-old man who had built a life outside the army and who, on the morning the country broke open, drove to a helicopter without being called. The capability that filled the vacuum that day was made of people like him. It had taken twenty-five years to build inside this one man, and it left with him at Alumim.

While Shaldag fought in the south of the envelope, the Yamam turned to rescue. At the Nahal Oz base, women soldiers of the field-observation unit had sealed themselves in the operations room while gunmen tried to burn them out.[^fn30] A Yamam team broke in, killed the attackers in the room, and pulled the survivors clear.[^fn31] A few kilometers away, at Kfar Aza, a team of the engineering commando reached the home of the Idan family. They pulled two small children, Amalia and Michael, past the body of their father, the photographer Roi Idan. The six-year-old told the fighters that gunmen had carried off her baby sister, Avigail.[^fn32] In the same kibbutz, three undercover fighters of the Border Police worked house to house in civilian clothes and unarmored cars, on scavenged ammunition, recognizing gunmen in stolen army uniforms by their weapons and their movement. One ran down to twenty-nine rounds. He recorded a goodbye message to his fiancée, then deleted it and told himself he would not die that day.[^fn33]

Sayeret Matkal spent the late morning fighting toward Be’eri. Route 232, the road in, was an ambush line. A team broke through the gunmen on it and reached the kibbutz before eleven, where it linked up with the Shaldag fighters at the entrance.[^fn34]

### Afternoon: The Turn at Re’im

At Be’eri the two units fought into the kibbutz in the close work of clearing houses one by one. Sayeret Matkal carried its own dead out of the Karm neighborhood. Sergeant Naveh Lax was twenty-one, from Lod. He had joined the fight with his friends in the unit and reached Be’eri in the first hours. His commander later told the family that Lax went back into the kibbutz to bring him out.[^fn35] He fell charging the gunmen. His deputy unit commander said he saved the lives of residents in the act of dying.[^fn36] By late afternoon a division commander reached Be’eri and imposed the first order on the sectors. The clearing settled into a method that would run the rest of the day and into the next.[^fn37]

The turn of the day came at Re’im. The base that fell at dawn, the Gaza Division headquarters whose silence had opened the morning, was still in Hamas hands in the afternoon. The Shaldag commander led the assault to take it back.[^fn38] His fighters landed near the base and pushed in under fire. Half the assaulting element went down, evacuated under fire by helicopter.[^fn39] A platoon from Sayeret Matkal joined the clearing, and attack helicopters fired inside the perimeter to break the defenders.[^fn40] At 6:30 in the evening the commander told the division commander that the base was clear.[^fn41] The headquarters that fell at dawn returned to Israeli hands at dusk. Somewhere between those two moments the defenders stopped only holding and began to take ground back.

### Night and the Second Day

Night did not end the fighting. In Sderot the police station had become a fortress for the attackers, and the battle for it ran close to a full day. Twenty-five gunmen held the building and more held the ground outside.[^fn42] The Yamam rescued officers trapped inside and could not reach the wounded on the roof, because the stairwell offered no safe path up.[^fn43] One of the officers called for a fire-brigade crane. The crane rose against the building under fire and set fighters on the roof, and snipers killed the guards.[^fn44] An officer and two fighters of the unit died at the station. When the last living man and the last body had come out, the unit commander and the district commander brought the building down on the gunmen still inside it.[^fn45]

The last fight of the day was the one no plan had imagined. In Ofakim, a town well behind the border, five gunmen had taken the home of Rachel and David Edri, a couple in their sixties.[^fn46] The Yamam treated it as what it was, a hostage barricade, and worked it for hours. Rachel worked it from the inside. She kept the gunmen in coffee and conversation while her son, a police officer, passed the layout of the house to the team outside.[^fn47] After many hours the assault took minutes, and the couple walked out alive.[^fn48] Far to the southwest, a regional counterterror team that had driven north against the tide breached the gate of Kibbutz Holit, where a sniper killed one of its fighters. Inside, the team reached a family that answered the door with a password, the words Hakuna Matata, and pulled them out.[^fn49]

The second day belonged to Be’eri, the longest fight of all. The Yamam reinforced the kibbutz with half a company and went house to house.[^fn50] “We break into the first house, kill the terrorists, move to the next, and do it again,” the unit commander said. “Yamam fighters are killed as we fight, some are wounded and evacuated, the doctors patch them up, and they come back.”[^fn51] Sayeret Matkal fought in the same lanes. The division commander counted more than a dozen units in the clearing, and he measured the work in one line. “To take a hundred and eight terrorists out of a kibbutz is not a conquest mission,” he said. “It is a slaughter mission.”[^fn52] The last gunman in Be’eri died on Monday.[^fn53]

The cost is the measure. By the count it released eight days later, the Yamam killed about 200 gunmen on the first day, most of them at point-blank range.[^fn54] Nine of its fighters fell and thirty-five suffered wounds, and the wounded who could stand came back from the hospital to the fight.[^fn55] Set the nine against the unit’s history. Since its founding in 1974, the Yamam had lost sixteen men in all its operations together. On one Saturday it lost nine.[^fn56] It still could not reach every emergency, and it never reached the festival at Re’im. “If we had another hundred or two hundred fighters we could have sent them,” the commander said. “The blanket was short.”[^fn57]

The other ledgers read the same way. Shaldag lost five fighters, two of them officers, and fifteen suffered wounds, on a day without precedent in the unit’s history.[^fn58] Its oldest fighter was among the five. Sayeret Matkal, the most secret of the three, does not narrate its days, and most of its October 7 stays behind the classification line. The open record places it at Be’eri and at Re’im through the units that fought beside it, and press accounts of the fallen record two of its company commanders among the dead of the war’s first stretch.[^fn59] I flag the gap rather than fill it. Duvdevan, the undercover unit of the commando brigade, lost seven fighters in the envelope.[^fn60] The Shin Bet lost ten of its people.[^fn61] These are not all the units, and these are not all the stories. None of these men received an order to fly into Be’eri, to storm Re’im, or to charge a column of gunmen between two kibbutzim. They went because the country was open and they were trained to close it.

The units in this book did not fight on October 7 the way the book will describe them. The book describes institutions: their doctrines, their lineages, the entrepreneurs who built them, the wars that shaped them. On October 7 the institutions could not assemble. The headquarters was dark, the orders did not come, and the men reached the battle one car at a time. They fought first as individuals. They became units again only after the first hours, when enough of them found each other to form a team.

This is the paradox I want the reader to carry into the chapters ahead. A country can lose its command and keep its capability, if the capability has been built into enough of its people. Hold two of the day’s dead side by side. A sergeant of twenty-one from Lod, who drove to Be’eri with his friends and went back into the kibbutz to carry out his commander. A master sergeant of forty-five, an artist and a father of three, who had given the unit half his life and flew to Alumim without being called. Neither received an order. Both went. The sixty special operators among the 369 dead measure how deep Israel had laid that capability, and what it cost on the day the system failed.[^fn62]

That depth is the subject of this book. How does a small state build, across ninety years, a body of human capital so dense that it can fight without a head? I answer the long way, through the lives of the men who made these units and the wars that made the men. The story starts long before Gaza, in the dust of the Arab Revolt and the night patrols of a heavy, restless commander named Yitzhak Sadeh. It runs through the British commandos and the Palmach, through the reprisal raids and Unit 101, through the reconnaissance patrols and the hostage rescues that made the Israeli units famous. It begins here, on the first day, with the units fighting as men.

### The Puzzle

In the months after the 1973 war, the Israeli army dissolved the two units that had carried its small wars since 1967. Sayeret Charuv, the reconnaissance commando of Central Command, had fought the pursuit campaign against Palestinian guerrillas in the Jordan Valley. Sayeret Egoz, its counterpart in Northern Command, had fought the same kind of war along the Lebanese and Syrian frontiers. Between the wars, the two units saw more sustained combat than almost any formation in the army, and their ranks became a school for the next generation of field commanders. The General Staff had decided to disband them before the war. The war only delayed the sentence. When it ended, the army carried the decision out and folded their men into the battered armored brigades.[^fn63]

In the same years the army was building. A reserve commando platoon took shape inside an existing unit. An airborne rescue unit stood up. The first of a new family of missile units formed. The army was burying special units and founding them at the same time.

This was not a single season's confusion. Over the decades that followed the pattern held. The army founded units in response to crises or new needs, and the units lived precarious lives. Some died in infancy for want of a champion. Others it dissolved and then, years later, raised again under the same name and number. To found a special unit in this army was a common act. To keep one alive was not.[^fn64]

Meanwhile, across the IDF the number of formations that called themselves special kept climbing. In the end almost every branch acquired one. The artillery, the air-defense arm, the combat-intelligence corps, and the engineers each came to field a unit of its own, and several fielded more than one.[^fn65]

Here is the puzzle this book sets out to solve. At the level of the branch, special operations forces proliferate. At the level of the unit, they often perish. The two facts pull against each other, and the explanation that comes first to mind does not reconcile them. If these units exist just to meet operational need, they should appear when the need is sharp and fade when it dulls. They have done the opposite. They have died while the threat that justified them was still in the field, and they have multiplied after that threat receded. Need alone cannot account for a population of units that grows when the danger falls and thins when it rises.

I argue that the answer is institutional, not operational. These units rise, die, and multiply for reasons that have more to do with the politics of the security establishment than with the missions in front of it. A unit is founded when a shock cracks the institution open and a determined officer, protected by a patron, builds something new that closes the gap. A unit dies when no such officer stays to defend it, or when a larger unit wants its soldiers. And units multiply across the branches because an elite formation confers prestige on the corps that holds it. The spread of these units comes to track the standing they confer, not the threat they were built to meet. Over the years, the mechanism reinforced itself. Veterans of the elite units rose to the head of the army and into political office. Patronage, once the gift of a rare protector, became a property of the leadership itself.

That is the argument in miniature. The section that follows sets out the framework in full, as a general account that should travel beyond any single country. The rest of the book then tests it against a century of one national case, in which the founding, the dying, and the multiplying can all be watched at close range.

## 1.2 Conceptualizing Special Operations Forces

Special operations forces are hard to define, and the difficulty is old. Not long ago, conventional armies held irregular soldiers in low regard. Irregular and specialized tactics are as old as war. Dedicated special operations forces are not. Their formalization belongs to the twentieth century. Yet the conditions that produced them are permanent. Almost every major war exposes the gaps between the two sides: numbers, skill, knowledge of the ground, and technology.[^fn66]

Those gaps pushed armies toward irregular methods. A weaker side could offset a stronger one by fighting outside the conventional script. Commanders relied on clandestine intelligence and reconnaissance to reduce their uncertainty. In hard moments they turned to irregular fighters for missions the regular formations could not carry out. These fighters outflanked enemy columns, sabotaged armories, cut supply lines, and broke enemy morale. The tactics were old, and they worked. They were also suspect. Many officers saw them as a denial of military virtue, and tied them to rebels, bandits, and mercenaries. The professional mainstream kept its distance.[^fn67]

The Industrial Revolution changed the calculation. War grew more complex and more fluid, and armies began to weigh what irregular operations were worth. The shift was uneven. Armies of new nation-states, the United States among them, carried the memory of militia and frontier war, and took to irregular tactics with less resistance. The colonial powers of Europe were warier. Their commanders read such methods as a threat to imperial order and resisted building them into institutions. The pressure of modern war wore that resistance down. Integration became first necessary, then unavoidable. By the middle of the twentieth century these forces were everywhere. We still lack a settled idea of what they are.

Most accounts describe these forces by what they do. The instinct is fair, but it does not yield a definition. Few concepts in the study of war are as unsettled. The confusion is not new. In 1944, four years after the first commando units formed, a philologist at Columbia University tried to fix the meaning of the word and admitted he could not:

“At the present time, we may conclude, the word Commando is not very clearly defined… To some people (including, apparently, those in Great Britain who deal officially with such matters), it means a unit of command in the British Special Service Forces; to others, it means an individual soldier who is a member of one of these units. Indeed, there are those for whom, somewhat illogically, it means both of these things.”[^fn68]

The trouble runs deeper than one stubborn word. The major definitions do not refine one another. They locate the essence of the thing in different places. Alliance doctrine locates it in the institution: forces specially designated, organized, trained, and equipped, using techniques that conventional forces do not.[^fn69] Strategists locate it in the mode of fighting: regular soldiers trained to fight by irregular means.[^fn70] Others locate it in the operators, in the caliber and the scarcity of the people who fill the ranks.[^fn71] These are not three versions of one idea. They are three claims about where the essence sits: in the institution, in the method, or in the people.

The vocabulary will not settle either. Commando entered English from the Boer wars as the name of a militia, a Dutch word for a command. Only in the Second World War did it harden into a battalion-sized unit for combined operations.[^fn72] The same tasks appear across allied armies under different national titles, and the label tracks administrative habit more than any difference in the thing itself. The dominant term proves the point. SOF is a bureaucratic coinage. It spread after 1987, when the United States and Britain gathered their nonconventional forces under unified commands. The Americans could not reuse special forces, which had named the Army’s Green Berets since 1952, so their new headquarters became the United States Special Operations Command. The academic vocabulary followed the administrative one.[^fn73]

A category whose name and core keep moving is telling us something. No single trait runs through every case. The definitions share overlapping traits with no common center, the pattern philosophers call a family resemblance.[^fn74] The disagreement is not noise around a stable concept. It is evidence. The basis each writer chooses tracks the institutional problem in front of them. Where a state has built a formal command, membership turns on designation, on which units the institution claims as its own. Where the pressing question is who can fight a new kind of war, the operator moves to the center. The definition shifts with the institutional problem it is asked to solve.

So I define the category by its function and let the rest vary. A special operations force, in this book, is a military or paramilitary unit marked first by a distinctive role and function. Its defining capacity is to undertake missions that fall outside, or beyond the reliable reach of, conventional forces. It carries, second, at least one of three substitutable markers. The first marker is a distinctive organization, visible in selection, training, and equipment. The second is the distinctive operator, in the caliber and the scarcity of the personnel. The third is a distinctive designation inside the military institution. The functional core stays fixed. The markers trade places, and which one a force leans on tracks the threat it faces and the strategic culture it carries.

## 1.3 Theoretical Framework: SOF, Critical Junctures, Entrepreneurs, and the Proliferation Paradox

### Armies as sticky institutions

Start with the thing to be changed. Armies are large bureaucracies built for stability. They standardize, they routinize, they reward conformity, and they punish deviation. A force that must move tens of thousands of people in coordinated violence cannot run on improvisation, and the habits that make it reliable also make it slow to change. Conservatism is not a flaw layered atop the institution. It is the institution working as designed.[^intro-2]

The mechanism has a name. Path dependence is the process by which an early commitment locks an organization onto a course and raises the cost of leaving it with every year invested. Weapons systems absorb sunk costs. Doctrine hardens into assumption. Careers accumulate around the dominant platform, and the officers who rose with it become a constituency for keeping it. Each year on the path yields increasing returns to staying on it, and the price of switching climbs out of reach. A branch that has poured a generation of money and prestige into a dominant weapon will not welcome a unit whose founding premise is that the weapon has reached its limit.[^intro-3]

Recent work adds a sharper point. Stability in a military is not only inertia. It is a choice. A force that changed its doctrine every time the environment shifted would never master anything, and a measure of deliberate conservatism is the necessary complement to innovation, not its opposite. This matters for the argument that follows. The resistance a new unit meets is not stupidity or sloth. It is the institution defending a good it has reason to protect. Most of the time, the gatekeepers win, and the path holds.[^intro-4]

### The critical juncture

If institutions are sticky, change needs a special kind of moment. The historical-institutional literature calls it a critical juncture: a brief period when the usual stabilizers fail and choices that were unthinkable a year earlier become possible. War is the clearest case. The collapse of a front, the loss of a capability, the exposure of a doctrine as bankrupt, each loosens the structure for a time and admits options the peacetime army would have refused.[^intro-5]

The literature separates two things that the word crisis tends to blur, and the distinction earns its keep. A permissive condition loosens the structure and opens the window. A productive condition fills the window with a particular outcome. The two are not the same, and neither produces an institution on its own. The war is the permissive condition. It pries the window open and silences the gatekeepers. The entrepreneur is the productive condition. He decides what passes through. A shock without an entrepreneur yields recrimination and reorganization. An entrepreneur without a shock yields a proposal that dies in a drawer. Together they yield a unit.[^intro-6]

### Why militaries change

Why do organizations built for stability adopt change at all? Four decades of scholarship on military innovation have circled that question, and the answers sort into six schools. The oldest locates the engine outside the armed service. Military organizations are conservative bureaucracies that drift toward stagnation, and innovation arrives when civilian leaders, alarmed by an external threat, impose it from above, often through maverick officers who bypass institutional resistance. A second school finds the engine in the rivalry between services. When a new threat or technology creates a mission that no service owns, the services compete for it, each betting that the winner takes the budgets and the prestige. A third school looks inside a single service and argues that change begins when respected senior officers formulate a new theory of victory and protect it by opening promotion paths for the mid-level officers who adopt it.[^intro-7]

A fourth school turns to culture. The organizational and strategic culture of a service defines what it believes about war, which threats it sees, which weapons and doctrines it treats as legitimate, and which solutions it treats as legitimate; solutions that violate the culture meet resistance until leaders run a planned campaign of cultural change. A fifth school inverts the direction of causation. Soldiers and field commanders, learning under fire, improvise methods that spread sideways between units before the senior command notices and adopts them. The sixth borrows from economics. Adoption at the top settles nothing because implementation depends on mid-level agents who can drag their feet or sabotage the change, and leaders must monitor, enforce, and reward to push the innovation through.[^intro-8]

Later work abandoned the search for one cause and treats innovation as layered: pressure from above, rivalry between services, coalition-building within them, and feedback from the field. I draw on this work. I also part from it on one point. Each school asks why the military changes. No one asks why the change so often takes the shape of a unit, or why those units live the lives they live. Rivalry and threat explain the pressure to innovate. They do not explain which units get built, which die young, and which multiply. [^intro-9]

The reason is that the pressure never stops. A state locked in a long conflict lives inside a permanent contest in which each side responds to or adapts to the other's last move. I treat that contest as a necessary condition and not a sufficient one. It is the constant background of military life, and a constant cannot explain why an army builds a deep-reconnaissance unit in one decade and lets a counter-infiltration unit die in the next. For that we need a theory of the institution, not a theory of the struggle.

### The entrepreneur

The agent who fills the window has a name in two literatures that the military-innovation field rarely reads together. The first studies institutional entrepreneurs, the actors who change the rules of an organized field. It defines them by behavior, not by motive. An institutional entrepreneur meets two tests: he initiates a change that breaks with the existing order, and he takes an active part in carrying it out. The test asks what the person did, not what the person felt, and it lets the analyst select cases on a stated, repeatable basis rather than by hindsight. The same criterion draws a line that the argument needs. An ordinary commander runs an existing unit well. An entrepreneur brings a unit into being, or remakes one, against the resistance of the surrounding institution. Many capable officers are not entrepreneurs, and the distinction is not a judgment of quality. It is a judgment of what the officer changed.[^intro-10]

The second literature study on entrepreneurship within government, where there are no market rewards for a good bet. Here, the entrepreneur works without the discipline and without the prize that the private sector supplies. He pursues public value, builds the political authorization that lets him act, and assembles the operational capacity to deliver, and he holds the three together or fails. He shows innovativeness, proactiveness, and a tolerance for risk in a setting that punishes all three. The window he needs opens when three streams converge: a recognized problem, a ready solution, and a politician willing to back it. The crisis of a lost battle joins the failure of the old method to a stock of unorthodox ideas and a leadership desperate to show initiative, and the policy window opens.[^intro-11]

The behavior has a structural signature. Inside any organization, two kinds of strategic behavior run side by side. One stays within the existing strategy and aims at goals the institution already recognizes. The other pushes initiatives from below that break the official line. The officer who wants the top of the pyramid adopts the first, because the second alienates the rival branches whose votes he will need. The entrepreneur keeps the second and pays for it. This is the first prediction the empirical chapters can test: the men who build these units rarely reach the highest ranks.[^intro-12]

The work itself splits into two, and the split matters more than it looks. One part is design. Someone has to solve the technical problem, build the thing, and learn what works by trial and error against a live enemy. The other part is politics. Someone has to neutralize the resistance, gather the resources, and frame the novelty so that the gatekeepers can accept it. The two tasks demand different talents and rarely sit in one person. Founding a unit is therefore an act of distributed agency, a small coalition rather than a lone visionary, and the histories that credit a single founder often hide a partner who did the other half of the job.[^intro-13]

The motive is the last piece, and it runs against the careerist reading. The force that carries an entrepreneur through years of bureaucratic resistance is internal. It looks more like an artist's attachment to a vision than a manager's pursuit of reward, and it explains why these officers persist even when persistence costs them. Selection and socialization in elite units also leave durable marks on the people who pass through them. The organizational term is imprinting: conditions present at a formative moment stamp dispositions that outlast the moment, including resilience, self-discipline, and a high tolerance for ambiguity. The evidence for imprinting runs at the level of the individual, not the unit, and I use it that way: as a claim about the people the units produce rather than about the units themselves.[^intro-14]

### The patron and the immune system

The entrepreneur cannot work alone; here, the second figure enters. Every established organization runs what one literature calls a corporate immune system, a set of reflexes that detect a novel internal initiative and move to kill it before it can compete for resources or attention. A new unit, unorthodox by definition, triggers those reflexes at once. The regular officer corps distrusts the irregular, resents the drain of talent and prestige, and treats the founder as a loose element who threatens the chain of command.[^intro-15]

The defense against the immune system is a patron. The literature on special operations returns to this point: elite units almost always encounter fierce resistance from the conventional establishment, and they survive only under the protection of a sponsor high enough to override that resistance. The patron grants the initiative its first legitimacy, routes resources to it through informal channels, and shields the young unit while it is small and easy to kill. Political leaders are drawn to these fighting elites, and they take the units under their wing in part to bypass the caution of the senior command. The protection is real, and it is also a liability, because a project that depends on one patron is exposed the moment the patron moves on. [^intro-16]

The same bureaucracy that resists is also, for a time, permissive. Its ultimate stakeholders, the taxpayers, cannot monitor how the money moves, and the resulting slack gives a protected officer room to build something unorthodox out of sight. That room is where the new unit takes shape. But the window does not stay open. To survive the first reorganization, a unit must cross a threshold of institutionalization: a defined mission, a selection-and-training pipeline, a written doctrine, and a constituency with a stake in its continuation. A unit that crosses the threshold becomes part of the furniture and is hard to remove. A unit that does not remain a personal project; personal projects die when the person leaves.[^intro-17]

Crossing the threshold is network work, and it has little to do with battlefield performance. The survival of a unit turns on its ability to win a bureaucratic contest in the corridors, not a firefight in the field. The entrepreneur builds ties that do different jobs. He needs allies senior enough to override resistance, collaborators whose standing lends the unit legitimacy in its first fragile season, partners in research and procurement who let the unit serve as a testing ground for new equipment, and, over the longer run, alums placed in decision-making seats who protect the budget and the missions after the founders are gone. The decisive resource is position in the bureaucratic network. The unit that builds the network survives. The unit that fights well but stands alone does not.[^intro-18]

### The unit is an engine of diffusion

A unit that survives does more than persist. It changes the force around it. Elite units are small, flexible, and built on human capital rather than heavy platforms, and that makes them cheap places to experiment. They can test a new method against a real enemy, fix what fails at speed, and hand the proven version to the wider force. The argument that elite units function as testing grounds for the larger army is old, and it captures a real mechanism: the unit absorbs the risk of the first trial, and the institution harvests the result.[^intro-19]

The recent history of Western forces shows the mechanism at work. A special-operations task force in Iraq and Afghanistan turned itself from a body built to find and strike targets into one built to exploit and analyze them, fusing intelligence and operations into a single cycle, and the model it proved out spread into the conventional force as the fusion cell. What began as a tactical fix inside one elite organization became a structural change across a much larger one. The transformation ran on networks and on the industrial reorganization of the special-operations enterprise, and it shows how a method born at the edge migrates to the center.[^intro-20]

What spreads, and how fast, follows three things. It follows how well the innovation works in the field, what it costs the receiving organization to absorb, and how far it fits that organization's existing values and routines—the better the fit and the lower the cost, the faster the spread. Inside a single military, the spread also follows prestige as much as utility. A low-status branch that acquires an elite unit improves its image and its recruiting, and rival branches answer by raising elite units of their own. Proliferation tracks the standing the units confer, not the threat they were built to meet, and it continues after the threat recedes. This is the paradox the book is built to explain: at the level of the branch, the units multiply, while at the level of the individual unit, they often die. [^intro-21]

A model that has taken root in one state can also cross to others, and the crossing has a logic of its own. It travels along three paths. It moves through training ties, when one army instructs another and exports its assumptions along with its methods. It moves through personnel networks as veterans leave the service, carrying the model into foreign armies, private firms, and advisory roles. It moves through doctrinal transfer, when the written principles of one force are read, translated, and adopted by another. The diffusion is not even. A model is adopted in which the receiving state faces conditions similar to those that produced it, and it is rejected when the structural fit is poor. The framework that explains why a unit is founded at home begins, in this way, to explain why the pattern is copied abroad in some places and not in others.[^intro-22]

### The origins, and the loop back

The pattern is older than the units this book follows. The intellectual roots reach back before the Second World War. The assault detachments of the First World War, the Italian shock troops formed in 1917, and the German infiltration units that a junior officer built from the bottom up, taught armies that a small body of selected men with the right tactics could break a stalemate that mass could not. Between the wars, the clandestine-penetration units of the German intelligence service carried the idea further, training picked soldiers in foreign languages and enemy uniforms for sabotage and seizure operations behind the lines. The operational vocabulary of special operations existed before the war that made it famous.[^intro-23]

The wartime foundings followed the model this review has drawn. The Special Air Service began in the Western Desert as the proposal of a junior officer with contempt for the staff, pushed against the resistance of a fixed command and carried by the protection of a patron willing to gamble on a small, mobile, lethal raiding force in the enemy's rear. The unit concentrated capability out of proportion to its size, and it shifted the shape of the force from a hierarchy toward a network. Then the war ended and the unit died with the others, only to return in the Cold War under a new lineage. The death and the revival are the clearest evidence in the record that mission alone did not keep these units alive. If need had governed, the units should have appeared when the threat was sharp and faded when it dulled. They did the opposite.[^intro-24]

Even the category resists definition, and the disagreement is itself a piece of evidence. Alliance doctrine defines a special-operations force by its institution: forces with a special designation, organization, training, and equipment, employing methods that regular forces do not. A strategist answers that they are regular soldiers trained to fight in an irregular way. An analyst points instead to the people and their rare qualities, and a more recent literature locates the defining trait in the unit's privileged institutional position and its direct access to political and intelligence power centers. These are not refinements of one definition. They place the essence of the thing in different locations, in the institution, in the way of fighting, in the fighters, and in the unit's place in the structure of power. A category that states define into existence again and again, each time in the image of the problem before them, is not a fixed tool waiting to be used. It is an institutional product, and it calls for a theory of institutions.[^intro-25]

### What the literatures miss

Set side by side, these literatures explain the parts and miss the whole. The institutional literature explains why armies resist. The critical-junctures literature explains when they yield. The innovation field explains the pressure to change. The entrepreneurship literatures explain who drives the change and how. The diffusion literature explains how a model travels. None explains the population of units itself: why some are founded, why many die in infancy, and why the survivors multiply across services and borders long after their reason for being has passed.

I argue that the missing account is institutional, not operational. A unit is founded when a shock opens a window and an entrepreneur, shielded by a patron, builds something new that closes a capability gap. A unit dies when no such officer remains to defend it, or when a larger unit covets its soldiers, or when the patron moves on before the unit has crossed the threshold of institutionalization. Units multiply across the branches because an elite formation confers prestige on the branch that holds one, and proliferation chases the standing the units grant rather than the threat they were built to meet. Over time the mechanism reinforces itself, as the veterans of elite units rise to command and to political office, and the patronage that was once the gift of a rare protector becomes a trait of the leadership itself. The model then crosses borders along the paths of training, personnel, and doctrine, and settles where local conditions match the ones that produced it.

The chapters that follow test this framework against a century of one national case. I choose that case not because it is exceptional but because it is legible, a place where the moving parts stay visible: the competition stays constant, the entrepreneurs can be named, and the foundings, the deaths, and the proliferation can all be watched inside a single institutional world. The framework is general. The case is where it can be seen working.

## 1.4 Why Israel as the Central Case

I choose Israel not because it is exceptional but because it is legible. The framework set out above is general, and a general framework has to be tested somewhere. To test it I need a case in which its moving parts are visible. I need a place where the pressure that opens junctures stays constant. I need units that can be traced from founding to death, and builders who can be named and watched. Israel offers all three in unusual measure. I read the Israeli case not as the subject of a general theory but as the place where the theory can be seen working.

The competition the framework treats as a background condition is, in Israel, an extreme. A small state in a permanent, multi-front conflict has lived for a century inside the adaptive contest the framework describes, and it has lived there at an intensity few states have matched. This makes Israel a hard test in the strict sense. Where the pressure is constant and severe, the institutional mechanism operates in high relief. If critical junctures, entrepreneurs, and the prestige cascade explain the rise of special operations forces anywhere, they should explain it here. If the framework cannot account for the case where its conditions are most concentrated, it is in trouble.[^fn118]

The case also supplies the variation a test requires. A national setting that produced only foundings would let me describe the mechanism but never test its range. Israel produced all three of the outcomes the framework predicts, inside a single institutional world. It founded units at moments of contingency. It let units die when the entrepreneur or the patron was missing and the threshold went uncrossed. And it spread elite units across its branches long after the threats that justified them had passed. Within one polity the constants hold roughly fixed, the political culture, the conscription system, the strategic predicament, while the outcomes vary. That is the design that lets the case do more than illustrate.[^fn119]

A test of this kind stands or falls on evidence about sequence: who proposed what, who protected it, what opened the window, and when. For most special operations communities that evidence stays locked away. Israel's has not. Over the past decade and a half that has changed. The state archives have opened at a quickening pace. The operators retired young and wrote with candor. The broadcasters and private projects put thousands of hours of contemporaneous footage and interviews within reach. The result is that the Israeli case can be process-traced at a resolution that few others allow, and the entrepreneurs and their patrons can be identified rather than inferred.[^fn120] I say more about these sources in the next section.

The obvious danger of a concentrated case is that it is idiosyncratic. What looks like a general mechanism might be a product of Israeli political culture, or of the particular relationship between this army and this society, and might not travel at all. I guard against that conclusion in two ways. The first is comparison. I set the Israeli case against a small number of others. I choose them for variation on the conditions the framework names, so the mechanism is not confirmed only where it was found. The second guard is the diffusion evidence itself. The Israeli template has been adopted abroad, through training, through personnel, and through doctrine, and a mechanism that crosses borders is not the property of one nation. The spread of the model is, in this sense, part of the test and not only part of the story.[^fn121]

I want to state the generalizing claim and not soften it, because the rest of the book rests on it. The concepts the framework uses do not belong to Israel. Institutional lock-in, the external shock, the entrepreneur and the patron, the prestige cascade across the branches, the slow layering between the junctures, none of these is an Israeli artifact. Israel is where they become visible, not where they are confined. I dwell on the Israeli case because it shows the mechanism in full view, and I bring in the comparison and the diffusion to show that the mechanism is general. The chapters that follow move through the Israeli century in order. At each step I ask the same two questions. What does the case reveal about the mechanism? And what would the mechanism predict for cases beyond it?

## 1.5 Methodology and Sources: The Comparative Design

(This segment precedes the existing "Sources, Method, and the Outsider's Position," the edited draft of which stands as the body of §1.4.)

The Israeli case is the core of the book, but a single case cannot establish that a mechanism is general. One country can show how the mechanism works; it cannot show that the mechanism is not a local accident. So I pair the in-depth case with a structured, focused comparison. I examine a small set of other special-operations communities through the same questions and against the same variables. The comparison is built to test the framework, not to decorate it.[^fn122]

I do not choose the comparison cases at random, and I do not choose them to represent a population. I choose them for variation on the conditions the framework names. Three conditions matter most. They are the intensity and constancy of the adaptive competition a state faces; whether it has identifiable entrepreneurs and patrons to shield them; and the institutional setting in which proliferation takes hold or does not. Cases that share some of these conditions and differ on others let me see whether the outcome turns on the variables the framework says it should.[^fn123]

Some of the comparison cases are also recipients of the Israeli model, and that is deliberate. It lets one design do two jobs. Where the framework's conditions recur, I can ask whether the mechanism recurs with them. Where the Israeli template has been adopted, I can ask whether it took root because the local conditions fit. The same comparison thus tests the general claim and the diffusion claim at once.[^fn124]

The comparison rests on four cases, named and justified in chapter 13. I withhold the names here and give the selection criteria instead, so the choice reads as principled rather than convenient. Each case is chosen for its value on the three conditions above. At least two are chosen because the Israeli model reached them, so that adoption and non-adoption can both be observed.[^fn125]

A focused comparison of this kind buys depth at the price of breadth. It is not a large-sample test, and it does not estimate how often the mechanism operates across all militaries. Its claims are about how the mechanism works, not about how common it is. I take that trade on purpose. The questions this book asks, about sequence, about agency, and about contingency, are answered by tracing processes within a few cases, not by counting many.[^fn126] The sources that make such tracing possible, and the position from which I read them, are the subject of the rest of this section.

## 1.5 Sources, Method, and the Outsider’s Position

I have no ties to Israel’s special operations community. I have served, like every Israeli of my generation, in the IDF; my own service was in the medical corps during the First Gulf War, and what I know about Sayeret Matkal, Shaldag, or Shayetet 13, I know as an outsider. I have not requested access to classified material. I have not interviewed serving officers. I do not draw on documents that were leaked or shared outside official channels.

I try, throughout, to keep two commitments to the reader. The first is to minimal jargon. The study of armies carries a heavy vocabulary, military and academic alike, and I translate it into plain language wherever plain language will carry the meaning. The second is to neutral expression on a subject that provokes strong feeling. The study of the IDF, in particular, is rarely read at a temperature of zero, and I have made an effort to describe rather than to celebrate or to condemn.

The book draws on the large and increasingly accessible body of public sources that the IDF, the Israeli press, the Israeli academy, and a generation of retired operators have generated over the past three decades. These sources range across several kinds, and they overlap.

The base layer is declassified archival material from the IDF and Defense Establishment Archive, the Haganah Historical Archive, the Yad Tabenkin archive of the kibbutz movement, the Israel State Archives, and, for the British connection, the National Archives at Kew, including the SOE files released since the 1990s. The Israeli archival regime is uneven. Some units are well documented; others are nearly opaque. It is improving year over year, and the pace of declassification accelerated after 2010.

Running alongside the archives is the contemporaneous Hebrew-language press. The Israeli press has covered the IDF, including the SOF community with  intensity. Two state-licensed military periodicals, Bamahane (the IDF weekly) and Maarachot (the journal of the IDF’s publishing house), have been publishing on these units since the 1950s. The civilian Hebrew-language press, much of it now accessible through the Hebrew Press Historical Archive at the National Library, has reported on operations and personalities since the 1920s. The depth of the press archive is one of the most distinctive features of the Israeli case.

Then come the memoirs, biographies, and authorized unit histories. Israeli operators retire young, write often, and candidly. The book-length unit history, often written by a journalist working with a former unit commander, is another. These sources have to be read carefully. They overstate successes, understate failures, and reflect the institutional politics of the moment in which they were written. They are also voluminous, increasingly available in digital form, and increasingly cross-checkable against one another.

A newer layer is the video and audio archives. Israel’s Ministry of Defense, the State Archives, the National Library of Israel, the IDF Spokesperson’s Unit, and several private archival projects have, in the past decade, uploaded thousands of hours of contemporaneous footage and operator interviews to publicly accessible platforms. Operator interviews recorded shortly after the events in question, often with reconstructed maps, have become an unusually rich source. I have transcribed and coded several thousand hours of this material for the project.

Television has added a category of its own: the investigative-journalism programs, especially Uvda (Fact) and its peers on Channel 13 and on the public broadcaster Kan. These programs have, over the past twenty years, produced a body of footage and interview material that, by the standards of comparative SOF studies, is exceptional.

Beneath all of it sits the secondary scholarly literature in Hebrew and English, including the multi-volume works of Yoav Gelber on the Jewish Brigade and on the Israeli intelligence services, Zehava Ostfeld on the founding of the IDF, Uri Milstein on Unit 101 and the paratroopers and Sayeret Shaked, Mike Eldar on the naval commandos and on Sayeret Shaked, Moshe Zonder and Avner Shur on Sayeret Matkal and Avraham Arnan, Raphael Marcus on Israeli military innovation and adaptation under fire, the most recent monograph that directly addresses the adaptation framework applied to the IDF, and the journalism of Ronen Bergman, Yossi Melman, Amos Harel, and others.[^fn127]

A relational database that I have built specifically for this project sits underneath the book. It tracks units, operations, individuals, dates, locations, equipment, casualties, and source citations. The full database, with source links and quotations under fair-use standards, is hosted as a dynamic online appendix and is open to corrections, additions, and challenges from readers. I take the view that the study of clandestine institutions from outside benefits from radical methodological transparency, and the appendix is the form that transparency takes.[^fn128]

The methodological hazards are real. Official accounts overstate successes. Memoirs reconstruct memory under the pressure of self-presentation. Some sources are intentionally deceptive. Deception, after all, is one of the crafts that several of the units I cover have specifically professionalized. I cannot guarantee that every detail in the book is correct. I can guarantee that every claim is sourced, that every contradictory account I encountered is flagged in the notes, and that the analytical argument does not rest on any single source that, if removed, would collapse the case.

The comparative material on the SAS, the OSS, Delta Force, and the other non-Israeli units draws on the published historiography in English, supplemented by the National Archives files at Kew. I have read this literature carefully but I have not done original archival work in the British or American collections beyond what was necessary to verify points of comparison. The book’s contribution to the SAS literature is interpretive rather than archival.

## 1.6 Plan of the Book

The book moves through a century in order. It is built around four critical junctures. Each juncture anchors a chapter at the heart of the book. The chapters between them trace what the junctures set in motion: the units that survived, the units that died, and the elite formations that spread across the branches in the quiet years.

The second chapter sets the stage. It lays out the traditions of irregular warfare that the first founders drew on. The first juncture opens in 1936, in the third chapter, with the entrepreneur who built the first Jewish special units. The fourth chapter follows the long shadow of that founding through the 1950s. It lingers on the early units that failed, because the failures show the mechanism as well as the successes do.

The second juncture, in 1960, is the fifth chapter. It traces the deep-reconnaissance template and the unit that came to sit at the apex of the community. The third juncture, in 1974, is the sixth. There a near-defeat is answered with precision strike and with the move of ground operators into the air arm. The seventh chapter steps back from the junctures. It follows the proliferation across the branches and compares the lifecycles of the units that lived and the units that did not.

The middle chapters test the architecture. The eighth sets the community against the war of 2006 and finds the 1974 design ill-matched to the fight it met. The ninth shows why a clear diagnosis did not produce a deep reform. The tenth follows two slower changes: the consolidation of the commando units under one command, and the long campaign waged between the wars.

The fourth juncture opens on 7 October 2023, in the eleventh chapter. The twelfth follows the special operations forces through the multi-front war that came after. The thirteenth turns outward, to the diffusion of the model beyond Israel. That is the test of how far the framework reaches. The fourteenth returns to the paradox and the four junctures. It asks what the case teaches about the rise of these forces across the world since 1945.

At every step I hold to the two questions the framework poses. What does the case reveal about the mechanism? And what would the mechanism predict for the cases that lie beyond it?

# Chapter 1 — Watchmen and Settlers

*Jewish Armed Self-Defense in Palestine, 1878–1920*

## 1.1 The Night Watch at Petah Tikva, late 1880s

There was, in the first weeks of every spring in the orange groves east of Jaffa, a stretch of approximately five hours between midnight and the first appearance of light over the Judean foothills during which one young man, or two, or at most three, were the only people responsible for the physical survival of one of the eight Jewish agricultural settlements that, in the late 1880s, made up the entire institutional reach of the Zionist project in Ottoman Palestine.

He carried a rifle if one had been issued to him — Mauser, in most cases, surplus from one of the European armies, acquired by the settlement committee through one of the European Jewish philanthropic networks that had begun, by the mid-1880s, to extend their financial reach into the Yishuv. He carried a lantern. He walked the perimeter of the cultivated fields the settlement had cleared in the previous decade, listening for the sound of a knife in a citrus branch, the snort of a tethered animal that had detected movement, the careful step of an intruder who had crossed the unfenced boundary between the Jewish-cultivated land and the Arab-cultivated land that, in 1888 as in every preceding year of the settlement’s history, ran a hundred meters away from the houses themselves. The settlement was Petah Tikva — the Gate of Hope, in literal Hebrew, named for a verse in the Book of Hosea that the founders had taken as their charter — and the watcher, on any given night, was one of the small group of young men whom the settlement’s committee had appointed to the task of guarding what the settlement, as a corporate entity, had been built to defend.[1]

The watcher was almost certainly a young man and almost certainly Jewish. This was a recent state of affairs. Through most of the 1880s, the agricultural settlements of the First Aliyah had relied for their nighttime perimeter security on local Arab guards — natur in Arabic, shomer in Hebrew — hired by the settlement committees from the surrounding Palestinian villages and paid in cash or in kind from the settlement’s communal accounts. The arrangement had practical advantages. The Arab guards knew the terrain. They knew the local family networks within which most night-time incidents — the theft of livestock or crops, the petty assault on a settler caught moving between the settlement and the nearby town — could be defused before they became serious. They knew which of the local clans were inclined to violence and which were inclined to negotiation. The arrangement also had, in the political vocabulary of the late-nineteenth-century Yishuv, a defect that would become increasingly intolerable as the settlement project matured. The Zionist project’s foundational claim was that the Jewish people would, by returning to their ancient land, transform themselves into a normal nation that defended itself rather than relying on the protection of others — and the practice of hiring Arab guards to defend Jewish settlements at night was, by every available reading, the institutional embarrassment that contradicted that claim every twenty-four hours.[^ch1-2]

The transition from Arab guards to Jewish guards was the first institutional question the Yishuv had to answer about its own military organization, and it was a question the Yishuv would still be answering, in different forms and across different decades, for the next seventy years. The watcher at Petah Tikva in 1888 was, in his own night-by-night practice, the first answer the Yishuv produced. He was the institutional figure with whom the long story this book traces begins.

## 1.2 The Yishuv in 1878 — Settlement, Security, and the Absence of State

To understand what the watcher at Petah Tikva was watching, the reader needs to understand what Palestine, in the closing decades of the nineteenth century, was — and was not.[^ch1-3]

It was a province of the Ottoman Empire. The territory that would, in 1922, become Mandatory Palestine was, before the First World War, administratively divided across the Mutasarrifate of Jerusalem (a special administrative unit reporting directly to Constantinople, comprising the southern half of the country) and the vilayets of Beirut and Damascus (which together comprised the northern half). The Ottoman state, by the 1880s, was a declining imperial power whose grip on its peripheral provinces had been weakened by a half-century of European intervention, internal reform programs, and recurring fiscal crisis. The state’s military and police presence in Palestine, outside Jerusalem and the few coastal cities, was thin. The administration of justice in the rural areas, where the agricultural settlements were located, was largely a matter of negotiation between the local Ottoman kaymakam (district governor), the local Arab notable families whose clan networks held the de facto authority over the surrounding villages, and whatever external European consul — French, British, Russian, Austrian — could be brought to bear in defense of any non-Ottoman subject whose interests had been compromised. The European capitulations — the eighteenth-century treaties that gave foreign powers the right to extraterritorial protection of their nationals in Ottoman territory — were the legal infrastructure on which a great deal of the early Zionist project rested, because they meant that the Jewish settlers, most of whom retained their Russian, German, Austrian, or French citizenship in the early years, could appeal beyond the Ottoman administration to their respective consulates when local disputes turned violent.[^ch1-4]

It was a country with a population of approximately four hundred and fifty thousand people in 1878, of whom approximately twenty-five thousand were Jewish — almost all of them concentrated in the Four Holy Cities of Jerusalem, Hebron, Safed, and Tiberias, supported by the halukkah, the system of charitable remittances from the Jewish communities of Europe and the Ottoman Empire that funded the religious-study communities of the pre-Zionist Yishuv ha-Yashan (the Old Yishuv). The Jewish population was not, in 1878, an agricultural population. It did not own significant tracts of cultivable land. It did not, with rare exceptions, work the soil. The communities of the Four Holy Cities lived in religious study and prayer, in the small commercial activity that the cities sustained, and on the European charitable remittances. The institutional infrastructure of an agricultural Jewish presence in Palestine — land purchases, settlement committees, agricultural schools, irrigation works, marketing cooperatives — did not yet exist.[^ch1-5]

It was a country in which violence, when it occurred between communities, was governed by an unspoken but well-understood code that the local Arab population had worked out over the preceding centuries of Ottoman rule. The code was customary, not statutory; it was enforced through the clan structures and the inter-clan negotiating mechanisms (the sulha tradition of reconciliation, the fasl system of clan compensation for injury or death) rather than through the Ottoman criminal courts. It was a code that, on the whole, kept the level of inter-community violence low — there had not been a major massacre of the Jewish communities of Palestine since the riots of 1834 against the Jews of Safed, and the smaller incidents that occurred regularly were generally resolved through inter-communal negotiation rather than through escalation. The code, however, depended on the assumption that newcomers would learn it and abide by its conventions. The Zionist settlers of the First Aliyah, who began arriving in late 1881 and who founded their first agricultural settlements in 1882, did not know the code; they had to learn it, and they had to learn it under conditions that the existing Jewish-Arab equilibrium of the country was not well equipped to manage.[^ch1-6]

The proximate trigger for the First Aliyah was the wave of anti-Jewish violence that swept the western provinces of the Russian Empire in 1881–1882, in the aftermath of Tsar Alexander II’s assassination in March 1881. The pogroms, the May Laws of 1882 that restricted Jewish settlement within the Russian Empire, and the broader collapse of the maskilic hope that Russian Jewry’s integration into the Russian state was politically possible, produced a wave of Jewish emigration that, in its overwhelming majority, went to the United States. A small fraction — perhaps twenty-five thousand individuals across the decade between 1882 and 1891 — went, instead, to Palestine. They came from western Russia, from Romania, from Galicia. They came with savings that ranged from modest to substantial, with political and religious commitments that ranged from secular socialist to traditional Orthodox, and with agricultural experience that ranged from nearly none to none at all. They settled, by 1888, in approximately fifteen agricultural moshavot — Petah Tikva (refounded in 1883 after an earlier 1878 attempt had failed), Rishon LeZion (1882), Zikhron Ya’akov (1882), Rosh Pinna (1882), Yesud HaMa’ala (1883), Rehovot (1890), and the others — that, taken together, constituted the institutional novelty in Palestine that the local Arab and Ottoman populations had not previously encountered.[^ch1-7]

The novelty was a Jewish population that, for the first time in the modern history of the country, wanted to own and work agricultural land in its own name, using its own labor, on its own terms. The institutional consequences would consume the next seventy years.

## 1.3 The First Defenders — Settlement Militias, 1878–1907

The story of armed Jewish self-defense in Palestine begins, by every account I have been able to consult, with the spring of 1886 and an incident on the outskirts of Petah Tikva that the Petah Tikva settlement archive has preserved in unusual detail.[^ch1-8]

The protagonist was a young man named Yehuda Raab, who had taken the Hebrew family name Ben-Ezer — son of help, in literal Hebrew — and who was, in March 1886, twenty-one years old. He had been born in Hungary, brought to Palestine by his family as a child in 1875, and had grown up in the small agricultural project on which his father had been a founding member: the 1878 attempt at Petah Tikva, which had collapsed within two years due to malaria and to a dispute with the local Arab village of Mlabes whose lands the settlement had nominally been founded on, and the 1883 refounding of the same settlement on slightly different ground a few kilometers away. Ben-Ezer had grown up working the citrus and almond fields that the settlement was beginning to cultivate. He had absorbed, in his late teens, the practical Arabic that the settlement’s everyday business with the surrounding villages required. He had also absorbed, from the same daily contact, a clear understanding of the structural problem the settlement faced: the orange groves and almond orchards that were the settlement’s economic base were physically interleaved with the cultivated lands of the surrounding Palestinian villages, and the boundary between the two was, in 1886, neither fenced, nor marked, nor formally surveyed.[^ch1-9]

The incident of March 1886 began when a herd of livestock from one of the neighboring villages — by the standard reconstruction, the village of Yahudia — crossed the unmarked boundary into Petah Tikva’s almond orchards and began grazing on the settlement’s crops. Ben-Ezer, with two of his colleagues — Yehoshua Stampfer and Sander Haddad — confronted the shepherds, impounded the herd, and announced their intention to drive the herd to the Ottoman kaymakam in Jaffa to lodge a formal complaint and recover damages. The three young men left Petah Tikva for Jaffa on the morning of Monday, 29 March 1886, with the impounded herd.[^ch1-10]

What followed, in the hours after they left, has become the founding atrocity in the institutional memory of Petah Tikva’s defense organization. Residents of the neighboring villages, alerted by the morning’s events and aware that the settlement’s three principal young men had departed for the city, mobilized for an attack. By midday, a group of approximately fifty armed villagers had reached Petah Tikva’s outskirts. They fired on the settlement’s houses, where the women, the elderly, and the children had taken cover. They entered the orchard outbuildings. In the course of the assault they beat to death Rachel Haddad Halevi, the mother of Sander Haddad — the first violent Jewish fatality in the institutional record of Yishuv self-defense in the modern Zionist period — and they seized a smaller herd of Jewish-owned livestock as compensation for the herd Ben-Ezer had impounded. By the time Ben-Ezer and his colleagues returned from Jaffa that evening, the attack had ended; the attackers had withdrawn; the dead had been counted; and the institutional question had been posed in terms that the settlement, and every other settlement that learned about the events of 29 March, would not be able to ignore.[^ch1-11]

The question was straightforward and the settlement’s answer was, in retrospect, equally straightforward. The settlement could not afford to outsource its physical security to the surrounding Arab villages whose internal political dynamics it could not control. It had to organize its own defense, and that defense had to be organized in a way that placed the obligation on the settlement’s own young men rather than on hired outsiders. In the weeks that followed the March 1886 attack, Ben-Ezer, Stampfer, and several others organized what the settlement archive describes as a mishmar — a watch — that rotated nightly across a roster of approximately a dozen young settler men, each carrying a rifle or a club, each responsible for a specific sector of the settlement’s perimeter, each reporting to a settlement committee that the mishmar itself reported to. The institution was informal. It carried no name beyond the generic Hebrew word for guard duty. It paid its participants nothing beyond a small allowance for nights spent on watch. But it was, in the institutional history I am tracing, the first piece of organized Jewish armed self-defense in Palestine in the modern Zionist period — and the model it established would be replicated, with local variations, across the agricultural settlements of the next two decades.[^ch1-12]

The replication was, by 1900, complete. Rishon LeZion had its own mishmar. So did Rehovot. So did Zikhron Ya’akov. So did the smaller settlements of the Galilee and the coastal plain.
