The land border between Vichy-controlled territory and British-controlled Palestine became, overnight, a potential invasion corridor for the German army then advancing through the Balkans. By the spring of 1941, with the German conquest of Greece and Crete and the consolidation of pro-Axis political forces in Iraq, the strategic situation in the eastern Mediterranean had deteriorated to the point at which a German invasion of Palestine appeared, to the British military command in the region, a serious operational possibility.[^ch2-73]

The British response, in the small space available to it, included an unusual concession to the Yishuv. The Special Operations Executive — the British clandestine warfare agency, founded in July 1940 by Churchill’s directive, charged with sabotage operations, support to resistance movements, and the conduct of irregular warfare in territories the Germans had occupied or might soon occupy — opened a Cairo station with operational responsibility for the eastern Mediterranean. The Cairo station, against the formal preferences of the British Colonial Office and the British military command in Palestine, established direct relations with the Haganah’s leadership and proposed a joint clandestine operation against Vichy assets in Lebanon. The Yishuv would supply the men and the local knowledge. The SOE would supply the training, the transport, and the operational guidance.[^ch2-74]

Golomb went to Sadeh.

The reconstituted offensive arm — the new force that would absorb the inheritance of the FOSH, the SNS, and the Russian Civil War partisan tradition — was formally established at a meeting at Kibbutz Mishmar Ha-Emek in mid-May 1941. The name selected for the new arm was Plugot Mahatz — Strike Companies — abbreviated, in the Hebrew acronym that would carry through the next seven years and into the institutional memory of every subsequent Israeli special operations unit, as Palmach. Sadeh was named commander. The first standing companies were drawn, again, from the operational core of the former FOSH and SNS. The training was modeled, in part, on the SOE methodology that the British were preparing to teach. The doctrine was Sadeh’s.[^ch2-75]

The Palmach’s first operation followed within seventy-two hours. On the night of Sunday, the eighteenth of May 1941, twenty-three young men, accompanied by a British SOE observer, sailed aboard the British patrol ship Sea Lion from Haifa to the port city of Tripoli in northern Lebanon, where their mission — Operation Boatswain, in the British operational nomenclature — was to sabotage the Vichy oil refineries at Tripoli to disrupt the supply of fuel to any German forces that might enter the region. The operation failed. The boat disappeared in Lebanese coastal waters on the night of the eighteenth of May. None of the twenty-three Palmach operators, and none of the SOE observer, were ever recovered. The names of the men of Operation Boatswain — including Zvi Spektor, one of the original FOSH operators of 1937 — would become, in the institutional memory of the Palmach, the founding casualties of the new arm.[76]

The Palmach survived the failure. The British SOE continued the collaboration. The Palmach’s companies were trained, equipped, and stationed across the Yishuv’s agricultural settlements through 1941 and 1942 in an arrangement — known as the kibbutz hachshara — under which Palmach members spent half their time in agricultural work in the host kibbutz and half their time in military training, with the kibbutz absorbing the cost of housing and food. The arrangement, which Sadeh had personally negotiated with the kibbutz movement, produced two things that mattered for the next decade. It produced an operational reserve of trained men who could be mobilized from across the country within hours. And it embedded the Palmach into the social and political center of the Labor-Zionist kibbutz movement to a degree that no other Yishuv military body had ever been embedded.[^ch2-77]

Sadeh commanded the Palmach until 1945, when, at the age of fifty-five, he handed off the command to his closest protégé, Yigal Allon, and took up a senior staff role in the Haganah’s general command. Through 1945 and 1946 and 1947 the Palmach grew, operated against the late-Mandate British administration in support of illegal Jewish immigration and against Arab paramilitary forces along the borders, and prepared — under Sadeh’s continued senior supervision — for the war that the Yishuv’s leadership knew was coming.[^ch2-78]

## 1.12 The Last Four Years

The war came on the night of the thirtieth of November 1947, the day after the United Nations General Assembly voted in favor of the partition of Palestine into a Jewish state and an Arab state. The fighting opened with attacks by Arab paramilitary forces on Jewish road convoys, Jewish settlements, and the Jewish neighborhoods of mixed cities. It continued, in escalating intensity, through the winter and spring of 1948. On the fifteenth of May 1948, the day after David Ben-Gurion declared the establishment of the State of Israel in Tel Aviv, the regular armies of Egypt, Transjordan, Syria, Lebanon, and Iraq invaded the new state.[^ch2-79]

Sadeh’s role in the 1948 war was operational and consequential. He commanded the 8th Armored Brigade — the new IDF’s first armored formation, hastily assembled in the summer of 1948 from a combination of Palmach veterans, recent immigrants from the displaced-persons camps of Europe, and the limited inventory of armored vehicles the new state had been able to acquire. He led the brigade in the southern campaign of the autumn of 1948 — Operation Yoav, Operation Lot, and the breakthrough into the Negev that culminated in the capture of Beersheba on the twenty-first of October 1948. By the end of the southern campaign he was, by the operational record, one of the two or three most decorated field commanders of the new army.[^ch2-80]

He was also, by November 1948, on the wrong side of an institutional struggle whose outcome would determine the next phase of his life.

The struggle had not begun in November 1948. It had begun in the spring of 1947, during the six-week intensive self-tutorial that Ben-Gurion conducted in his Tel Aviv apartment as he prepared to assume the security portfolio that the recently concluded Twenty-Second Zionist Congress had assigned him. Across late March and April 1947, in his apartment at 17 Keren Kayemet Boulevard, Ben-Gurion debriefed dozens of Haganah commanders on the state of the organization. The notebooks he filled during what he called his “self-seminar” — the black notebooks for which he would later be remembered — recorded his judgments on the senior figures of the Haganah’s command. Of Sadeh, he recorded the assessment of Moshe Carmel, then commander of the Haganah’s Northern District: “the acting chief of staff, Yitzhak Sadeh — he is not an organizational man but a man of action.” Ben-Gurion did not dispute the framing. Two months later, in the memorandum he circulated to the Haganah leadership on 18 June 1947, he announced that the current senior leadership, including Sadeh, would be replaced. Yaakov Dori, who had served as chief of staff until 1945, would be brought back to the position. The institutional logic that would, eighteen months later, produce the dissolution of the Palmach general staff was already in place. Ben-Gurion was, in the late summer of 1948, finishing the work he had begun in the spring of 1947.[^ch2-80a]

Years later, in a 1966 conversation with the historian Mordechai Naor, Ben-Gurion would describe the doctrinal incompatibility that had stood behind the institutional decision. “Imagine,” he told Naor, “that one of the senior commanders told me: ‘A platoon must not have a machine gun — it will be a burden when it has to hide in the mountains or orchards.’ They compared themselves to partisans in Russia and didn’t notice that we faced a war against regular armies.” The “they” was the Palmach generation that Sadeh had built. The “we” was the conventional army that Ben-Gurion was preparing for in 1947 and that he would create in 1948. The institutional question that had stood between Sadeh and Ben-Gurion since the early 1940s — partisan-style irregular force versus conventional regular army — would be answered, after Sadeh’s removal, in Ben-Gurion’s favor.[^ch2-80b]

The struggle was with David Ben-Gurion. Ben-Gurion’s view, by the late summer of 1948, was that the new state required a conventional, professional, hierarchical military that was politically subordinate to the elected civilian government and institutionally independent of the labor-Zionist political movements out of which the Yishuv’s pre-state military bodies had emerged. The Palmach, in his view, was both unacceptably political — its officer corps was overwhelmingly affiliated with the kibbutz movement and with the parties to the left of Ben-Gurion’s Mapai — and unacceptably autonomous, with its own general staff, its own command structure, and its own institutional culture. The Haganah’s general staff he had already folded into the new IDF’s general staff. The Palmach’s general staff, in his view, had to be dissolved as well.[^ch2-81]

On the seventh of November 1948, Ben-Gurion issued the order. The Palmach general staff was dissolved. Its officers were either folded into the new IDF’s regular command structure or — in the cases of those whose political affiliations or institutional loyalties made absorption impossible — quietly retired. Sadeh, who had presided over the founding of the Palmach seven years earlier and who had remained, even after handing the command to Allon, the institutional figure under whose general supervision the Palmach operated, was placed in the second category. He completed his command of the 8th Brigade through the end of major hostilities, and was then, in stages between the spring of 1949 and the autumn of 1950, eased out of active service.[^ch2-82]

He spent the last four years of his life in Tel Aviv. He wrote. He published The Notebook Is Open: First Episode, the autobiographical volume that he had been planning for two decades, in 1951; the second volume, on which he had been working in the spring of 1952, was never completed. He lectured at the Hebrew University and at small adult-education programs in the kibbutzim. He maintained the personal friendships he had built across the labor-Zionist intellectual world over thirty years. He was, by the recollections of the writers who saw him in those years, neither bitter nor reconciled — simply, in the manner of a man who had completed the work that he had been able to do, finished. The cancer was diagnosed in the autumn of 1951. He kept the news from all but his closest friends. He died on the twentieth of August 1952.[83]

The funeral procession that, in the opening pages of this chapter, moved from Ha-Sharon Hospital to the Histadrut headquarters and on to the cemetery at Givat Brenner was the institutional acknowledgment of what Sadeh had built. What Galili said at the graveside was the simpler version of the larger thing: that Yitzhak Sadeh had set the Yishuv on its trajectory of irregular warfare, that he had introduced the future commanders of the army to the principles of military reconnaissance, that he had taught them how to fight while hating war. The analytical language for saying more than that — for placing Sadeh inside the longer arc of national military adaptation, for naming the institutional conditions under which the FOSH had been able to exist — would not be available for another fifty years, and was not, at the graveside, what was wanted.

The cemetery at Givat Brenner closed behind the cortege as the last light of the August afternoon left the kibbutz fields. Yigal Allon walked back to the car that had brought him. Moshe Dayan walked beside him. They had carried the casket together from Beit Ha-Bima five hours earlier; they had walked behind it through the procession of the Palmach veterans; they had stood through the eulogies. Neither said much on the drive back to Tel Aviv. They had been Sadeh’s protégés for fifteen years. They were now the senior figures in the army he had helped build.

But the army they had inherited was new, and the world it had been built inside was changing. The doctrinal materials that Sadeh had assembled in his sixty-two years — the Russian Civil War partisan tradition, the British irregular tradition that Wingate and the Special Night Squads had transmitted, the maritime tradecraft of the POM, the operational logic of the Palmach companies — had been put together in the conditions of the late Mandate and the 1948 war. The conditions of the early 1950s were going to be different. The chapter that follows leaves Givat Brenner and August 1952, and opens eleven years earlier, in the western desert outside Cairo, in the operational architecture that the British Special Operations Executive and a small number of unconventional British officers were beginning to construct, in the summer of 1941, against the German and Italian forces then advancing along the North African coast.

# Chapter 3 — The Desert

*The British Special Operations Tradition, the Yishuv as Junior Partner, and the Doctrinal Cross-Pollination of the Second World War*

## 3.1 The Western Desert, July 1941

Sometime in the first days of July 1941, an officer of the Scots Guards named David Stirling — twenty-five years old, the eldest son of a Scottish baronet, on convalescent leave from a parachute experiment that had gone badly wrong in the desert south of Mersa Matruh three weeks earlier — got out of a hospital bed at the Scottish General Hospital in Alexandria, retrieved his crutches, and made his way by stages to Cairo. He went, by his own subsequent account and by the account that the American journalist Virginia Cowles would publish under his name in 1958, with the specific intention of presenting an operational proposal to the senior officers of the British Middle East Command at their headquarters in Garden City. The proposal was a small one. It concerned a new kind of unit. The unit would be drawn from the dispersed remnants of a recently dissolved Commando formation that had spent the preceding six months attempting, with diminishing success and rising casualties, to conduct amphibious raids against the German and Italian forces along the Libyan coast.[1]

The Layforce of which Stirling had been a member — a brigade of three Commando battalions, named after their commander, Colonel Robert Laycock, that had been sent from Britain to the Middle East in February 1941 — had been dissolved at the beginning of the summer for reasons that Stirling, in the corridors of Middle East HQ on the morning of his crutches walk, was not in a position to dispute. The Royal Navy could no longer spare the destroyers and landing craft on which the Commandos' amphibious raids depended. The German air pressure over the eastern Mediterranean had become severe. The Crete campaign of late May and early June 1941 had absorbed Layforce in a hopeless defensive battle and had reduced its operational strength by a third in two weeks of rearguard fighting. By the time Stirling was on his feet again, the brigade that had brought him to the Middle East no longer existed.[^ch3-2]

What Stirling proposed instead, on the morning of his unauthorized visit to Middle East HQ — by his account he was spotted at the main entrance by a guard from whom he had previously fled, abandoned his crutches in order to evade pursuit, and gained the office of the deputy chief of staff, Major-General Neil Ritchie, by an interior route the regular bureaucracy of the headquarters had not been designed to monitor — was that the dispersed Layforce veterans should not be folded back into the conventional infantry units from which they had been drawn six months earlier. They should instead be re-formed, in much smaller numbers and under deliberately irregular command arrangements, as a special unit whose principal operational method would be the airborne and overland insertion of small parties of operators deep behind the German lines for the destruction of aircraft, supply dumps, and communication infrastructure. The cost, Stirling argued, would be small. The potential return — measured in German aircraft destroyed on the ground rather than in the air, in supply convoys disrupted at depth rather than at the front — would be disproportionate to the investment. Ritchie, who had been in the deputy chief of staff's chair for less than a fortnight and was looking for a reason to push back against the conventional preferences of the staff he had inherited from his predecessor, agreed. The unit Stirling described would be named, by a coincidence of clandestine bureaucracy that the next sections of this chapter will trace, L Detachment, Special Air Service Brigade.[^ch3-3]

Stirling's proposal of July 1941 is the founding scene of the British SAS — the unit that, more than any other single Second World War formation, would supply the operational template, the institutional self-understanding, and the cultural genealogy of the post-war national special operations forces that the rest of this book traces. The proposal was also one of two events of that summer, two thousand kilometers apart, that mattered for the larger argument the book is constructing. The other event was unfolding in the Jezreel Valley of Mandatory Palestine, where Yitzhak Sadeh, two months earlier, had begun to assemble the first standing companies of the Palmach — the strike force that, as the previous chapter has described, he had been authorized to establish on the night of the fifteenth of May 1941 in the kibbutz dining hall at Mishmar Ha-Emek. The two events were institutionally unrelated. Stirling did not know that the Palmach existed. Sadeh did not know that Stirling existed. The British Middle East Command in Cairo and the Special Operations Executive's Cairo station, between them, were aware of both formations and were quietly arranging for the operational collaboration between them that the next four years would deepen and that the Yishuv's military leadership would, in retrospect, recognize as the formative external influence on the Palmach's doctrine.[^ch3-4]

The simultaneity is the chapter's organizing thesis. In the summer of 1941, under the operational pressure of a German military advance that had run from Norway to the gates of Alexandria in a little under fifteen months, the British Empire and the Jewish national project in Palestine — institutionally separated, politically antagonistic on the question of the post-war future of the Mandate, operationally aligned for the duration of the war against the common Nazi enemy — were independently constructing the same kind of military instrument. The instrument was the small, deliberately unconventional, intellectually heterodox special operations unit. The unit was, on the British side, the SAS that Stirling had just proposed and the Long Range Desert Group that Ralph Bagnold had founded a year earlier and the Special Boat Section that Roger Courtney had pushed into existence in 1940 and the No. 51 Middle East Commando that Henry Cator had recruited from Palestinian Jewish and Arab volunteers in the autumn of 1940. The unit was, on the Yishuv side, the Palmach that Sadeh was building and, within the Palmach, the Mistarvim platoons that would shortly assume the identity-deception operational role that the Brandenburgers, on the German side, had pioneered four years earlier under Theodor von Hippel. The two emerging traditions — the British and the Yishuv — were neither parallel nor identical. They overlapped at specific operational and personnel junctures that this chapter will trace. They diverged in others. They drew, in important measure, on the same European inheritance of irregular warfare doctrine that the previous chapter has identified — the von Lettow-Vorbeck Schutztruppe tradition, the Russian Civil War partisan tradition, the British colonial small-wars tradition that Wingate had carried into the Special Night Squads of 1938. They produced, by the war's end, two distinct national SOF traditions that would, in the post-war decades, follow institutional trajectories so different that the family resemblance between them would be visible only to historians who took the trouble to look for it.[^ch3-5]

This chapter takes the trouble. It opens with the German doctrinal challenge that produced the British emergency response. It traces, across the second half of 1940 and the first half of 1941, the improvisational founding of the British SOF ecosystem — the Commandos, the Special Operations Executive, the Special Boat Section, the Long Range Patrol. It moves, with the British command, from London to Cairo, where the Middle East theater became, between the autumn of 1940 and the autumn of 1942, the principal laboratory in which the new units were tested. It returns, in its final third, to the Yishuv — to the small Jewish auxiliary units that the British Middle East Command and the SOE recruited from the Mandate's Jewish population in those years, to Sadeh's Palmach and to the operational and doctrinal channels through which the British SOF tradition reached the Yishuv's emerging strike force. The chapter closes with the post-war dissolutions of October 1945, when the British military establishment, in the institutional reflex that the rest of this book will trace as the recurring fate of national SOF traditions in peacetime, dissolved the units it had built and let the doctrinal inheritance pass into the keeping of the few officers and operators who would, in the next round of wars, reassemble it.

The chronology of the chapter therefore runs from the summer of 1940 through the autumn of 1945 — from Dunkirk to demobilization. It is bracketed by Sadeh's institutional position on either side: the Palmach he founded in May 1941 will be operating, under his direct supervision, throughout the chapter's middle section, and will be operating, under Allon's command after Sadeh's 1945 hand-off, in the chapter's closing pages. The Palmach is not, however, the chapter's principal subject. Its principal subject is the British SOF tradition that the Palmach formed alongside, drew on, and would carry, in its institutional memory, into the IDF that succeeded it. The Palmach is the chapter's anchor. The British SOF tradition is the chapter's argument.[^ch3-6]

## 3.2 The German Doctrinal Challenge

To understand the speed at which the British military established the operational architecture that Stirling, in July 1941, was attempting to expand, the chapter has to step back, briefly, to the German military innovations of the inter-war period that the British response was constructed against. The German innovations were several, and they were not the principal source of the British SOF tradition that emerged after 1940 — that tradition drew, as the previous section has indicated, on a deeper inheritance of British colonial small-wars practice and on the irregular operational traditions that Wingate and Clarke had carried into the late-Mandate Palestine of the Arab Revolt. But the German innovations supplied the operational problem. The British SOF tradition was, in 1940 and 1941, the empire's emergency answer to a German military system that, in the eighteen months between the invasion of Poland in September 1939 and the German operations in the Balkans in April 1941, had run rings around every conventional European army that had stood against it.[^ch3-7]

Three of those German innovations matter for the argument this book is constructing. The first was the Panzergrenadier concept — the mechanized infantry doctrine that the German army had developed in the late 1930s as a complement to the armored formations of the Panzer divisions. The Panzergrenadiers solved the operational problem that the introduction of armor had created for the conventional infantry of the European armies: a foot soldier could not keep up with a tank. Mounted on half-tracks and all-terrain vehicles, the Panzergrenadier infantry advanced with the tanks rather than behind them, cleared obstacles, conducted close-range battlefield reconnaissance, and engaged the anti-tank and anti-aircraft weapons of the defending forces while the armored elements pressed forward against the enemy's main lines. The combined arms warfare of the German blitzkrieg of 1939–1941 — the operational pattern that overran Poland in five weeks, France in six weeks, and the Balkans in a fortnight — depended on the Panzergrenadier doctrine as much as it depended on the Panzers themselves. The doctrine was, in the eighteen months that followed the fall of France, the canonical example of what the conventional European armies had been overmatched by.[^ch3-8]

The second German innovation that mattered for the British response was the Fallschirmjäger — the airborne paratroop arm of the Luftwaffe that Hermann Göring had been authorized to establish, on Hitler's direct instruction, as part of the German pre-war combined arms preparation. The Fallschirmjäger had been an idea before they had been a unit. Soviet airborne demonstrations in the early 1930s, which German liaison officers had observed during the period of cooperation between the Reichswehr and the Red Army, had suggested that paratroops could be inserted behind enemy lines to seize bridges, airfields, and headquarters facilities ahead of the main land advance. The Wehrmacht did not require the Fallschirmjäger in the rapid Polish campaign of September 1939. But on the ninth of April 1940, in the opening hours of Operation Weserübung — the German invasion of Denmark and Norway — Fallschirmjäger paratroops jumped onto and seized two airfields in Aalborg, demonstrating the operational utility of vertical envelopment in a way that no European army had previously witnessed. A month later, on the tenth of May 1940, eighty Fallschirmjäger landed in gliders on the roof of Fort Eben-Emael — the Belgian fortress that had been considered, in the inter-war planning of the French and Belgian general staffs, the strongest fortified position on the European continent — broke through the casemates with hollow charges, and forced its surrender within hours. The Eben-Emael operation opened the German invasion of the Low Countries. The Fallschirmjäger jump on Crete in May 1941 — the operational climax of the Balkan campaign that had absorbed Layforce in its rearguard defensive battle — confirmed, in costlier and more ambiguous terms, that the airborne arm was a permanent feature of the new operational order.[^ch3-9]

The third German innovation, and the one that mattered most for the operational genealogy this chapter is reconstructing, was the Brandenburger unit of the Abwehr — the German military intelligence service. The Brandenburgers were the German army's clandestine special operations force. Their founder was Theodor von Hippel, the officer whom the previous chapter has identified as Paul von Lettow-Vorbeck's other inter-war disciple — the second figure, alongside Yerachmiel Lukacher, who had carried the East African Schutztruppe doctrine into a national military institution that did not yet exist. Where Lukacher had carried von Lettow-Vorbeck's doctrine into the Gdud Ha-Avoda's secret military school at Tel Yosef in 1924 and from there, by personnel transmission, into the FOSH and the Palmach of the late 1930s and early 1940s, von Hippel had carried the same doctrinal inheritance into the Bau- und Lehr-Kompanie zur besonderen Verwendung 800 — the Construction and Training Company for Special Employment, Number 800 — that the Abwehr had authorized him to establish on the eve of the war. The unit's principal innovation was the operational use of identity deception. Brandenburgers spoke the languages of the territories they operated in, wore the uniforms of the local armies or police forces, and were inserted ahead of the main German advance to seize strategic targets — bridges, telegraph stations, headquarters facilities — under the cover of being recognized as friendly local personnel. They had performed, in this role, in Poland in September 1939, in the Low Countries in May 1940, in Yugoslavia in April 1941, and in the opening hours of the German invasion of the Soviet Union in June 1941. The technique was effective and the operational record was substantial. It was also a deliberate violation of the laws of armed conflict — a violation that, on the German side, the Brandenburgers' commanders had calculated would be answered, by the affected powers, with reprisal and refusal of quarter, and that the Brandenburgers' operators accepted, when captured, on those terms.[^ch3-10]

The Brandenburger model was, for the operational genealogy this book is constructing, the German doctrinal answer that the British and Yishuv special operations communities would, in 1941 and 1942, attempt to construct an answer to. The Yishuv's answer would be the Mistarvim — the platoons of Arabic-speaking Jewish operators, drawn from the Mizrahi and Sephardi Jewish communities of Palestine and from the immigrants from Arab countries who had arrived in the Yishuv in the late 1930s and early 1940s, who would, by 1944, constitute one of the principal arms of the Palmach's Seventh Company. The British answer would be Captain Herbert Cecil Buck's Special Interrogation Group — the small unit of German-speaking Jewish operators, drawn from the German Platoon of the Palmach and from the German-Jewish refugees of the Auxiliary Military Pioneer Corps, that Buck would assemble at Marsa Matruh in early 1942 and that would carry out, in May and June 1942, the disastrous raid on the Luftwaffe airfields at Martuba and Derna that the closing section of this chapter will reconstruct. The Brandenburger model would also be answered, on the Soviet side, by the OMSBON brigades of the NKVD that operated behind German lines from 1942 onward, and on the American side, by the OSS Operational Groups that the United States would deploy in occupied Europe from 1943. Five national special operations traditions — German, British, Yishuv, Soviet, American — were, by the closing years of the war, drawing on a single tactical inheritance that the Brandenburgers had pioneered and that von Hippel had carried from his apprenticeship under von Lettow-Vorbeck in inter-war Germany.[^ch3-11]

The German doctrinal challenge, in other words, was not a single innovation but a system. Panzergrenadier mechanized infantry. Fallschirmjäger airborne envelopment. Brandenburger identity-deception operations. Each of the three innovations corresponded, in the operational architecture of the Wehrmacht and the Luftwaffe and the Abwehr, to a specific operational problem that the conventional European armies of the 1930s had not solved. Each was a deliberate departure from the dominant inter-war doctrinal orthodoxy of trench-and-position warfare. And each was, by the spring of 1941, deployed at operational scale across the European, North African, and Balkan theaters in a combined system that the British military establishment had been unable to defeat by conventional means. What the British emergency response of the summer of 1940 would attempt was, in essence, the construction of an institutional answer to each of the three German innovations, plus a fourth element — the maritime sabotage and coastal raiding capability that the Royal Navy's diminishing strength in the eastern Mediterranean had created an operational vacuum for. The Commandos, the SOE, the SBS, the Long Range Patrol, the Middle East Commandos, and the SAS, in different combinations and across different theaters, were the British answers to the German system. The Palmach, the Mistarvim platoons, the German Platoon, the SOE Syrian Scheme operators, and the Buck SIG were, on the Yishuv side, the parallel and partly cooperative answers that the Palestine Jewish community produced through its operational collaboration with the British Middle East Command and the SOE Cairo station.[^ch3-12]

The next section of the chapter takes up the British half of that story. It begins where the chronology of the British emergency response begins — on the evening of the fourth of June 1940, in the closing days of Operation Dynamo, when Winston Churchill, having watched the last of the British Expeditionary Force lifted off the beaches of Dunkirk in the destroyers and trawlers and pleasure boats that the Royal Navy and the civilian flotilla had improvised, rose in the House of Commons and delivered the speech that would, within forty-eight hours, supply the political authorization for the British SOF tradition that the rest of this chapter is about.[^ch3-13]

## 3.3 Britain's Emergency Improvisation, June–December 1940

The chronology of the British SOF tradition begins, by every standard institutional reckoning, on the night of the fourth of June 1940 — when Winston Churchill, three weeks into his prime ministership, addressed the House of Commons on the conclusion of Operation Dynamo. By the morning of the fifth, 338,000 British and French soldiers had been brought home from the beaches of Dunkirk. The British Expeditionary Force had been evacuated; it had not been destroyed; the immediate continental disaster had been averted. But the equipment of the BEF — tanks, artillery, transport, communications — had been left on the French coast. The army that returned to Britain in the first days of June 1940 was a body of trained men without the tools of a modern army to fight with, and it returned to a country that, by Churchill's calculation, would have to defend itself against a German invasion attempt within sixty days. Operation Sea Lion — the German invasion of Britain — was, in the assessment of the British general staff in early June 1940, the principal operational problem the United Kingdom was about to face.[^ch3-14]

Churchill's speech of the fourth of June was the political answer to that assessment. "We shall go on to the end," the most famous passage of the speech ran. "We shall fight in France, we shall fight on the seas and oceans, we shall fight with growing confidence and growing strength in the air, we shall defend our Island, whatever the cost may be, we shall fight on the beaches, we shall fight on the landing grounds, we shall fight in the fields and in the streets, we shall fight in the hills; we shall never surrender." The speech is conventionally remembered as a morale-restoration exercise — the rhetorical apparatus by which the new prime minister rallied a defeated army and a frightened civilian population for the defensive battle that lay ahead. It was also, in the institutional history this chapter is reconstructing, an operational directive. Two of the senior officers at the War Office who heard it — General Sir John Dill, the Chief of the Imperial General Staff, and his military assistant Lieutenant-Colonel Dudley Clarke, whom the previous chapter has introduced as Wingate's parallel on the British staff in Mandate Palestine of 1937–1938 — took Churchill's words as the political opening that the operational concept they had been quietly drafting required.[^ch3-15]

Clarke had been thinking about small-unit raiding operations for at least two months before the Dunkirk evacuation. The thinking had its origins in his own service history. He had observed the operational pattern of the Spanish guerrilla campaign against Napoleon's army during the Peninsular War of 1807–1814, on which he had read extensively in the inter-war period. He had covered, as a journalist for the Morning Post in 1924, the Berber Rif War in Spanish Morocco, where Abd el-Krim's irregular forces had pinned down a Spanish colonial army of more than 100,000 men through three years of guerrilla operations in the Atlas Mountains. He had served, in Palestine in 1936–1938, on Wavell's and Dill's staffs as a junior intelligence officer during the Arab Revolt and had watched the British Army's conventional infantry operations against the Arab partisan parties produce, at extraordinary expense in manpower and money, an institutionally embarrassing operational result. The Boer commando model of 1900–1902, on which Clarke's own reading on the Peninsular War rested, suggested to him that a small, well-led, locally adapted irregular force could produce strategic effects out of proportion to its size — provided the political conditions were created within which such a force could operate without the regular military bureaucracy disowning it.[^ch3-16]

The political conditions, in Clarke's reading of Churchill's evening of the fourth of June, were now in place. On the morning of the fifth, Clarke drafted a one-page memorandum and presented it to Dill in the chief of staff's office at the War Office. The memorandum proposed the formation of small army units of approximately fifty men each — drawn from existing army formations, trained for amphibious raiding, equipped lightly, and tasked with conducting nuisance operations against the German-held coast of Western Europe. The units would be named, after the Boer model that Clarke explicitly invoked in the memorandum, Commandos. The proposal anticipated the inevitable objections from the conventional infantry establishment by stipulating that the new units would be formed without diversion of resources from the Home Guard. The first commitment Clarke needed, he wrote in the memorandum, was the prime minister's political authorization. Dill liked the idea. He passed the memorandum to Churchill on the same day.[^ch3-17]

Churchill, who had read in detail in the inter-war period on irregular warfare and who had, by temperament and by his own brief and ill-fated experience as an officer in the South African War of 1899–1902, an instinctive sympathy for the operational style Clarke was proposing, authorized the Commandos forty-eight hours later. On the sixth of June 1940, in a personal minute to his chief military assistant, General Lionel Hastings Ismay, Churchill set out the political mandate that Clarke would operate under: "Enterprises must be prepared, with specially-trained troops of the hunter class, who can develop a reign of terror down these coasts, first of all on the 'butcher and bolt' policy." The phrase that Churchill chose — "butcher and bolt" — was the British colonial military's nineteenth-century shorthand for the punitive raiding operations that the regular army had conducted on the North-West Frontier of India against the Pashtun tribal groups of the Khyber Pass. The phrase placed Churchill's authorization, by deliberate rhetorical reach, in the long British imperial tradition of small-scale punitive operations. The institutional vehicle would be new. The operational style would not be.[^ch3-18]

With Dill's backing and Churchill's authorization in hand, Clarke established, on the seventh of June 1940, a new section within the Military Operations Directorate of the War Office. The section was designated MO9. Its principal task was the formation of the first Commando units. Clarke's first hire was Major-General Otto Lund, who came in as deputy director of military operations and supplied the bureaucratic cover under which MO9 would operate. Clarke's other early hires included David Niven — the British actor who had returned from Hollywood at the outbreak of war and had requested combat duty — and a small cadre of younger officers whom Clarke selected on the basis of unconventional intelligence and physical fitness rather than seniority. The first volunteers were drawn from the Army's Independent Companies, the small ad hoc units that had been raised earlier in 1940 for operations in Norway; from the Royal Marines; and from the regular infantry regiments whose commanding officers were willing, in the summer of 1940, to release men they regarded as marginal to the new units.[^ch3-19]

The first Commando operation followed within three weeks of MO9's establishment. Operation Collar, the new units' inaugural raid, took place on the night of the twenty-fourth to twenty-fifth of June 1940. A small Commando party landed on the French coast in Pas-de-Calais, conducted a brief reconnaissance, killed two German sentries, and withdrew. The operation did not achieve its formal reconnaissance objectives. Its sole British casualty was Clarke himself, who had insisted on joining the raid as an observer and had been wounded by a German rifle round at close range. The operation's principal effect, from the British command's perspective, was as cinema. Film crews had been embedded with the raiding party; the footage of small parties of British soldiers in blacked-up faces emerging onto a French beach was released to the cinema newsreels of the United Kingdom in early July; the footage made the Commandos famous in a country whose civilian population was, in those weeks, in the depths of the post-Dunkirk political crisis and was in need of evidence that the war was not being conducted entirely defensively. By the end of July 1940, the number of volunteers for the Commandos exceeded the units' personnel ceilings by an order of magnitude. By the autumn, the screening process for new entrants had been formalized; selection had become competitive; a training depot had been established in the highlands of Scotland under the direction of Colonel Charles Vaughan; and the operational pattern of the British Commandos as a permanent feature of the British military landscape had been institutionally consolidated.[^ch3-20]

The Commando initiative was not, however, the only British SOF institution that the summer of 1940 produced. A month after Clarke's MO9 had been authorized, on the sixteenth of July 1940, Churchill issued the directive that established the Special Operations Executive — the new clandestine warfare agency, formally housed within the Ministry of Economic Warfare under the Labour minister Hugh Dalton, that was charged, in the prime minister's instruction, with the mandate "to coordinate all action, by way of subversion and sabotage, against the enemy." The SOE was institutionally distinct from the Commandos. Its operational mandate was different — clandestine sabotage and resistance support, rather than amphibious raiding. Its personnel were drawn from a different recruitment pool — refugee European nationals, multilingual British civilians, intelligence specialists rather than infantry officers. Its institutional culture, by the end of 1940, was already in tension with the parallel intelligence apparatus of the Secret Intelligence Service, whose senior officers regarded the new agency as an institutional rival rather than a complementary tool. But the SOE, like the Commandos, was a product of the same political-strategic moment — the post-Dunkirk improvisation, the willingness of the new Churchill government to fund and to politically protect the unconventional operational instruments that the conventional establishment regarded with skepticism, the recognition that the immediate operational problem facing the United Kingdom could not be solved by conventional means alone.[^ch3-21]

The third British SOF institution of the summer of 1940 was the Special Boat Section — the small-boat raiding unit that emerged, more by accident than by design, from the persistence of one of the early Commando volunteers. The volunteer was Captain Roger Courtney of the King's Royal Rifle Corps. Courtney was thirty-seven years old in 1940, an English public-school boy who had spent the inter-war period as a big-game hunter in East Africa and as a sergeant in the British police in Mandate Palestine during the Arab Revolt. He had become, in the course of his African years, an accomplished amateur canoeist; he had once paddled a folding canvas canoe — a folboat — down the length of the Nile. When he volunteered for the Commandos in June 1940, he proposed to the senior staff that the new units should incorporate folboats for close-in reconnaissance and clandestine sabotage of moored shipping. The Royal Navy, in the persons of Admirals Roger Keyes and Theodore Hallett, was skeptical. Courtney did not accept the skepticism. Late one night in July 1940, he paddled a folboat alongside the moored HMS Glengyle, climbed silently aboard, removed the cover of one of the ship's main armaments, and paddled back to shore without being detected by the Royal Navy watch. Dripping water, he entered the hotel where the senior officers were meeting and presented the gun cover as evidence. A second clandestine boarding, this time conducted under official observation, confirmed the result. By the autumn of 1940, Courtney had been promoted to captain and authorized to raise the No. 1 Special Boat Section — a twelve-man unit, initially attached to the Commandos, that became the institutional ancestor of the post-war British SBS.[^ch3-22]

The fourth British SOF institution of the summer of 1940 was geographically distant from London and operationally different from the other three. It emerged in the Western Desert, in the headquarters of the Commander-in-Chief Middle East at Cairo, where Major Ralph Bagnold — the Royal Signals officer whose inter-war expertise in desert reconnaissance had been built up across two decades of private exploration of the Libyan Desert — approached General Sir Archibald Wavell in the first days of July 1940 with a proposal. The proposal concerned the geographic problem the Middle East Command was about to confront. With Italy's declaration of war on the tenth of June 1940 and Mussolini's deployment of his colonial army into Libya for an advance on the Suez Canal, the British defensive position in Egypt depended on the small Western Desert Force's ability to monitor and to disrupt Italian operations across an area of half a million square miles of largely impassable terrain. Bagnold proposed that the Middle East Command authorize a small, motorized reconnaissance and raiding unit that would penetrate the Italian rear areas by overland desert routes, using vehicles that Bagnold himself had modified across the inter-war period for sand-dune operation, and that would report back on Italian movements while conducting low-level harassment of supply convoys and outposts. Wavell, who had been familiar with Bagnold's work since their parallel service in Palestine in 1937–1938, approved the proposal on the third of July 1940. The unit was established under the designation No. 1 Long Range Patrol Unit. Bagnold's friends in the Middle East would later refer to it, more accurately, as the Long Range Desert Group.[^ch3-23]

By the end of the summer of 1940 — three months after Dunkirk — the British military had stood up the Commandos, the SOE, the SBS, and the LRP. Four new institutional vehicles, each authorized at the political level, each operating outside the conventional command structures of the army and the navy, each tasked with a different operational problem, each in active development. None of the four had yet produced operational effects on a scale that the conventional military establishment regarded as significant. All four were, by the standards of the established service institutions, under-resourced, institutionally insecure, and politically vulnerable. But all four existed. They had been authorized. They had been staffed. They had been allowed to begin to develop the operational doctrine and the personnel ecology that, by the middle of 1942, would make them the most institutionally productive component of the British Empire's military response to the war.[^ch3-24]

The institutional centrifuge that the summer of 1940 had set in motion in London would, by the end of the year, move east. In November 1940, the British army established the Special Service Brigade — the institutional umbrella under which the expanding Commando units were grouped into five battalions. The same month, the No. 51 Middle East Commando was raised at the British base at Geneifa, near the Bitter Lake in the Canal Zone, under the command of Lieutenant-Colonel Henry Cator. The new commando was the first of three British units to be drawn substantially from the Jewish and Arab volunteers of the Auxiliary Military Pioneer Corps — the British army labor formation that, since the outbreak of war, had absorbed the Mandate's foreign-national volunteers, including the Yishuv's Jewish manpower that the Mandate authorities considered suitable for labor service but politically problematic for combat employment. The 51 Middle East Commando's 360 volunteers, drawn primarily from the Yishuv, would constitute one of the principal Yishuv–British operational interfaces of the early war, and would, after the unit's disbandment in 1941, supply the personnel from which Buck's Special Interrogation Group would later be assembled. On the eighteenth of December 1940, Wavell formally requested that Clarke be transferred from London to Cairo to take charge of the Middle East Command's strategic deception apparatus. Clarke arrived in Cairo on the same day. His official designation was as the regional director of MI9, the British escape-and-evasion organization; his actual remit was the establishment of what would, four months later, become the dedicated military deception organization known as 'A' Force. Clarke would remain in Cairo for the remainder of the war.[^ch3-25]

By the end of 1940, the British SOF ecosystem had migrated, in personnel and institutional weight, from the offices of MO9 at the War Office in London to the Middle East Command's headquarters in Cairo. The reasons for the migration were operational: the principal theater of British ground operations against the Axis was Wavell's Western Desert Force; the principal opportunity for the kind of small-unit raiding and reconnaissance that the new institutions were designed for was in the Libyan Desert; the principal command authority willing to protect the unconventional units against the conventional staff was Wavell himself, whose Palestine staff in 1937–1938 had included both Wingate and Clarke and who had carried, into the Middle East Command, an institutional appetite for irregular operations that the conventional army establishment did not share. Cairo, in the first months of 1941, became the laboratory in which the British SOF tradition would be elaborated and in which the Yishuv's parallel operational instruments would, by accident and by deliberate British policy, be drawn into operational collaboration with the British units. The next section of this chapter takes up that story.[^ch3-26]

## 3.4 Cairo as Laboratory, December 1940 – June 1941

When Dudley Clarke stepped off the Imperial Airways flying boat at Rod-el-Farag on the morning of the eighteenth of December 1940, the city he entered was already, by the institutional standards of the wartime British Empire, one of the densest concentrations of unconventional military thinking anywhere outside London. Wavell's General Headquarters Middle East occupied a block of converted apartment buildings in Garden City, on the eastern bank of the Nile, between the British Embassy and the Qasr al-Aini Hospital. Bagnold's Long Range Patrol — by that point renamed the Long Range Desert Group and operating out of a forward base at Siwa Oasis, four hundred miles to the west — kept a small Cairo cell in the same Garden City building. The Special Operations Executive's Cairo station, established in October 1940 under the direction of George Pollock, had taken over a converted villa at Rustum Buildings, in the residential quarter immediately south of the British Embassy. The Inter-Services Liaison Department — the cover designation under which the Secret Intelligence Service operated in the Middle East theater — was housed in a wing of the same Garden City complex as GHQ itself. The Security Intelligence Middle East organization, charged with counter-intelligence operations against German and Italian agents in the Levant, occupied a third floor of the Grey Pillars building. The Cairo of December 1940 was a city in which a captain of the Royal Tank Regiment could walk, in the course of a single morning, from a desk at GHQ to a meeting at SOE Cairo to a luncheon with an LRDG officer on home leave to a coded message from a Haganah liaison in Jerusalem — and could do so, much of the time, without leaving the same six city blocks.[27]

Clarke's official designation in the Cairo establishment of the winter of 1940–1941 was as the regional director of MI9 — the British military intelligence organization responsible for evading and escaping Allied personnel behind enemy lines. The designation was institutional cover. Clarke's actual remit, conveyed to him directly by Wavell on the afternoon of his arrival, was to construct, from the institutional materials Wavell could allocate, a dedicated military deception organization for the Middle East theater. The new organization — which would, in March 1941, be formally designated 'A' Force and would operate, for the remainder of the war, as the principal coordinator of British strategic deception in the Mediterranean and the Indian Ocean — would have three operational tasks. It would mislead the Italian and German intelligence services about British troop strengths in Egypt and Palestine. It would conceal the timing and direction of British offensive operations. It would, where possible, create in the minds of the German and Italian field commanders false beliefs about British operational capabilities that would induce those commanders to disperse their forces against threats that did not exist. Wavell, who had served alongside Allenby's intelligence staff in Palestine during the closing campaigns of the First World War and had observed the operational effects of Richard Meinertzhagen's deception efforts at Beersheba in October 1917, regarded strategic deception as a permanent feature of modern operations rather than an occasional supplement to them. He gave Clarke a free hand.[^ch3-28]

Clarke's first major operation, in the first weeks of January 1941, would, by an institutional coincidence the rest of this chapter is built around, supply the name that David Stirling — operating in another office in the same Garden City complex six months later — would take for his new unit. The operation was the fabrication of the British 1st Special Air Service Brigade. The brigade did not exist. Clarke had invented it. The strategic problem the invention was designed to address was the Italian command's growing concern, in the late autumn of 1940, that the British were about to insert a substantial airborne force into Italian-held Cyrenaica to coincide with the ground offensive of General Richard O'Connor's Western Desert Force. The Italians had no reliable means of detecting an airborne insertion until it occurred. The British, in operational reality, possessed neither the transport aircraft nor the trained airborne personnel that an insertion of the kind the Italians feared would have required. Clarke's solution was to create the brigade on paper. He fabricated unit documents — operational orders, equipment schedules, casualty returns from training exercises that had not occurred — and arranged for selected fragments of the documentation to be planted, through controlled channels, where Italian intelligence would find them. He arranged for wooden dummy parachutists, painted in green and brown and rigged with cut-down parachute harnesses, to be dropped at low altitude over Italian-observed terrain along the Cyrenaican frontier. He planted, in the wreckage of the dummy drops, fragments of British uniform and broken pieces of British parachute equipment that Italian intelligence would, on examination, identify as authentic. He arranged for British personnel in selected Cairo bars known to be frequented by Italian agents to speak openly, in the kind of indiscretion that careful operational security would have forbidden, about transfers to the 1st Special Air Service Brigade and the brigade's training program at a facility outside Heliopolis that did not exist. The deception worked. By the spring of 1941, Italian and German intelligence had accepted the brigade as an operational reality. Internal Axis intelligence assessments from this period — recovered after the war and analyzed in the official British histories of strategic deception — show the fictional brigade entering the Italian and German order-of-battle estimates and remaining there, in steadily revised form, through the autumn of 1942.[^ch3-29]

The fictional 1st SAS Brigade was, in the institutional history of the British SOF tradition, the bureaucratic envelope into which Stirling's L Detachment would, in July 1941, be inserted. The story of how Clarke and Stirling — neighbors in the corridors of GHQ Middle East in the summer of 1941 — arranged the naming will be told in the next section of this chapter. What concerns the present section is the institutional ecology in which the arrangement became possible. By March 1941, the Cairo establishment had acquired a recognizable shape. 'A' Force occupied a wing of Grey Pillars. The SOE Cairo station, expanded under Pollock's direction to absorb the volume of clandestine operations against the Italian rear in Cyrenaica and the Vichy French positions in Syria and Lebanon, employed perhaps two hundred officers and civilian specialists by the spring. The LRDG had grown to three patrols of forty men each, operating across an area of roughly one million square miles. The Commando establishment in the Middle East — the three Layforce battalions that had been sent out from Britain in February 1941, plus the Middle East Commandos that Cator had raised at Geneifa — totaled around 2,000 men by April. And the SOE's parallel apparatus for clandestine operations against Vichy Syria — known as the Syrian Scheme, and run from a converted hotel at Mishmar Ha-Yam on the Carmel coast under the direction of Maurice Oldfield and Tony Simonds — was already, by the spring of 1941, in active negotiation with the Yishuv's military leadership for the training of Jewish operators who could be inserted, in Arab cover, into the Vichy French and German-aligned positions in the northern Levant. The Cairo SOF laboratory of the early months of 1941 was not, in other words, a laboratory in which British officers were experimenting in isolation. It was a laboratory in which the British improvisation of the previous summer was being scaled up, institutionalized, and — at the operational margins — extended to draw on the manpower and the operational knowledge of the Yishuv's existing self-defense apparatus.[^ch3-30]

The clearest institutional expression of that extension, in the autumn and winter of 1940–1941, was the No. 51 Middle East Commando. Henry Cator, the Norfolk landowner and inter-war Levant traveler whose Arabic and Persian fluency had been acquired across two decades of independent residence in Tehran, Aleppo, and Baghdad, had been appointed by Wavell in October 1940 to raise a new Commando battalion at the British base at Geneifa, near the Bitter Lake in the Suez Canal Zone. The recruitment instruction Wavell gave Cator was explicit: the new battalion was to be drawn principally from the Yishuv Jewish and Palestinian Arab volunteers of the Auxiliary Military Pioneer Corps, the British army labor formation that had, since the outbreak of the war in September 1939, absorbed the Mandate's volunteer manpower whom the Mandate authorities had been unwilling to enroll for combat service. Cator's recruitment teams went directly into the AMPC depots at Sarafand and Rafa in October and November 1940. They interviewed approximately 1,400 volunteers. They selected 360. The selected men — roughly 280 of them Yishuv Jews, with a smaller component of perhaps 80 Palestinian Arabs — were brought to Geneifa in late November and trained through the winter of 1940–1941 in amphibious raiding, demolitions, small-unit infantry tactics, and the desert reconnaissance methods that Bagnold's LRDG had developed.[^ch3-31]

The No. 51 Middle East Commando's operational record was modest. The unit deployed in early 1941 to Eritrea, where it conducted amphibious operations against Italian coastal positions during the East African campaign. It transferred subsequently to Ethiopia, where it operated alongside Wingate's Gideon Force in the closing weeks of the Italian collapse in the Horn. It was withdrawn to Egypt in October 1941 and was formally disbanded in November of the same year, its veterans dispersed back to the AMPC, to the conventional Yishuv units that were by then being raised under the Palestine Regiment designation, or, in a small but consequential number of cases, to the new specialized units — Buck's Special Interrogation Group, the SOE Syrian Scheme operator pool — that the Cairo establishment was assembling for the operations of 1942 and beyond. The 51 Commando's operational achievements were not the unit's principal institutional significance. Its principal significance, in the history this chapter is reconstructing, was that it had demonstrated to the British Middle East Command, on the operational evidence of a year's deployment, that Yishuv manpower could be raised, trained, and committed at battalion scale within the British SOF establishment. That demonstration would, in the spring and summer of 1942, supply the institutional precedent on which the SOE's larger Yishuv operations of the middle war years would be built.[32]

The parallel and operationally larger demonstration of the same principle, in the same winter of 1940–1941, was Orde Wingate's Gideon Force. The previous chapter has reconstructed Wingate's Palestine service of 1937–1938 and the Special Night Squads through which Wingate had, in collaboration with the Haganah's Yitzhak Sadeh and the FOSH cadres Sadeh had trained, conducted the British counter-insurgency operations against the Arab Revolt's mobile partisan parties. Wingate's Palestine appointment had ended in 1939 with his removal from the Mandate, on the recommendation of the Palestine intelligence staff, on the grounds that his open identification with the Zionist national project had become operationally compromising. He had returned to Britain. He had spent the early months of the war in a War Office position that had not utilized his unconventional operational expertise. And then, in the autumn of 1940 — by Wavell's personal request to Dill — he had been flown to Khartoum to take command of an irregular operation that Wavell wished to insert into Italian-occupied Ethiopia in support of the Emperor Haile Selassie's restoration to his throne.[^ch3-33]

Gideon Force — the formation Wingate assembled in Khartoum between November 1940 and January 1941 — was an institutional hybrid that bore the unmistakable imprint of Wingate's Palestine experience. It consisted, at its full operational strength in the spring of 1941, of approximately 1,700 men. Eight hundred of those men were drawn from the Sudan Defence Force's Frontier Battalion — disciplined Sudanese troops, British-officered, who would supply the conventional infantry backbone of the formation. Eight hundred were drawn from the Ethiopian regular forces that the British had been reconstituting from exile cadres in the Sudan since the spring of 1940 — soldiers of the Emperor's restored army, fighting under Ethiopian command. The remaining cadre — perhaps a hundred British and Empire officers and specialist personnel, including the South African operations officer Donald Lush, the Canadian engineer Wilfred Thesiger (later the celebrated Arabian traveler), and the Sandhurst-trained Charles Boustead who would command the Frontier Battalion contingent — supplied the operational planning, the communications, and the leadership cadre that bound the heterogeneous force together. The operational model Wingate adopted was a direct adaptation of the Special Night Squads pattern. Small mixed units, drawing local manpower around a British officer core, operating by stealth at night against an enemy that held the conventional positions by day, coordinating with the Ethiopian Patriot guerrilla bands — the Arbegnoch — that by the early months of 1941 numbered perhaps 25,000 fighters across the Ethiopian highlands. Between January and May 1941, Gideon Force, operating in coordination with the conventional British advance from the Sudan and from Kenya, played a disproportionate role in the collapse of Italian East Africa. Italian forces of approximately 40,000 men — twenty-five times Gideon Force's strength — were tied down in operations against Wingate's force across an area the size of metropolitan France. On the fifth of May 1941, Haile Selassie reentered Addis Ababa with Wingate at his side as Gideon Force's commander and his nominal military escort. The political consequences of the operation belonged to the Ethiopian restoration. The operational consequences belonged to the British SOF tradition that the rest of this chapter is reconstructing.[^ch3-34]

The Yishuv consequences of Gideon Force were institutional rather than operational. No Yishuv personnel served in the Ethiopian operation in any documented capacity. But the news of Wingate's command of the operation reached the Yishuv through the Haganah's contacts in the British Middle East Command by the early weeks of 1941. The man whom the Yishuv had known, in 1937 and 1938, as the British officer who had trained the FOSH cadres in the operational practice of night raiding and who had, almost alone among the British staff of the period, identified the Yishuv's military self-organization as an asset to be developed rather than a threat to be contained, was now commanding what was, in operational terms, the most successful British irregular formation of the early war. The political significance of Wingate's renewed visibility, in the Yishuv's strategic assessment of British intentions, was substantial. The institutional significance, in the operational evolution of the Palmach that Sadeh would begin to constitute four months after Wingate's entry into Addis Ababa, was deeper. The operational pattern Wingate had used in Ethiopia — small mixed force, local manpower around a small leadership cadre, night operations, coordination with indigenous resistance — was the same pattern Sadeh had absorbed from Wingate in 1938. Sadeh would, in the operational doctrine he established for the Palmach in May 1941 at Mishmar Ha-Emek, draw on the same pattern. The Ethiopian operation was, in the Yishuv's military leadership's reading of it through the spring of 1941, the empirical confirmation that the operational doctrine the FOSH had absorbed three years earlier remained viable at scale under modern combat conditions.[^ch3-35]

The Cairo establishment that received Wingate back from Ethiopia in June 1941 was, in the assessment of every senior officer who had been present at GHQ Middle East through the preceding nine months, an institutional formation in which unconventional operations had been mainstreamed to a degree that no other British theater command had reached. Wavell's personal authority had been the political condition for the mainstreaming. The German operational pressure had been the operational condition. The Italian collapse in East Africa in the spring of 1941 had been the early empirical evidence that the new units could produce strategic effects. The unrelenting succession of operational defeats in Greece (April), Crete (May), and the failed British offensives in the Western Desert (Operation Brevity in May, Operation Battleaxe in June) had supplied the institutional pressure under which the conventional staff had been forced to concede operational space to the unconventional units they did not, in the abstract, approve of. By the time David Stirling — recovering from his parachute accident at the Scottish General Hospital in Alexandria through the second half of June and the first days of July 1941 — was preparing the proposal he would carry, on crutches, into Ritchie's office, the Cairo establishment had become a laboratory whose institutional architecture would accept his proposal on terms that the British military establishment of any other theater, in any other moment of the war, would not have.[^ch3-36]

## 3.5 Stirling's L Detachment and the Real SAS, July 1941 – January 1943

The story of how David Stirling reached Ritchie's office on the morning of his unauthorized visit to GHQ Middle East in July 1941 — the story §3.1 of this chapter has already told — concludes, in every standard SAS history, with Ritchie's authorization of L Detachment, Special Air Service Brigade. The naming was not accidental. Ritchie's authorization, granted on the morning of Stirling's first visit to the deputy chief of staff's office, was confirmed in writing the following day by the chief of staff, Lieutenant-General Sir Arthur Smith, on the condition — proposed by Smith and not by Stirling — that the new unit be administratively absorbed within the cover designation of Clarke's fictional 1st Special Air Service Brigade. The administrative arrangement had operational consequences that neither Stirling nor Smith, in the days of the original authorization, fully appreciated. By assigning Stirling's L Detachment to the order-of-battle slot that Clarke's fictional brigade occupied in the Italian and German intelligence assessments, the British command was, in effect, providing the new unit with prefabricated deception cover. The Axis intelligence services already believed the 1st SAS Brigade existed. When Stirling's small unit — sixty men at the establishment's authorization, growing to approximately two hundred by the early months of 1942 — began to produce operational effects in the western desert, the Axis services would attribute those effects to the brigade-sized formation they had been tracking in their order-of-battle estimates since the spring of 1941. The actual unit would, in the operational reality the next eighteen months would build, gradually accrete the institutional substance that the fictional unit had only pretended to possess. The institutional history of the British SAS is, in important measure, the history of the fictional brigade becoming the real one.[^ch3-37]

By the end of August 1941, Stirling had established L Detachment's training camp at Kabrit — a site on the western shore of the Bitter Lake, about ninety miles east of Cairo, on the road between Suez and Ismailia. The camp's initial establishment was conducted, characteristically, by raid. Stirling's officers, on his instruction, conducted a series of nighttime appropriations of tents, cots, mess equipment, and training materiel from a neighboring New Zealand brigade's depot. The New Zealanders, who had not been informed that the appropriations were taking place, awakened on successive mornings to find the contested equipment in use at the SAS camp. The matter was resolved, after several weeks of inter-formation tension, by a personal intervention from Ritchie. Stirling's six initial officers — recruited in the weeks following Ritchie's authorization — were chosen on a recruitment principle that was, by the standards of the British army of 1941, deliberately unconventional. Stirling did not interview candidates for educational background or for parade-ground bearing. He interviewed for intellectual heterodoxy, physical fitness, and willingness to operate under conditions of acute personal risk and prolonged operational isolation. The officers he selected included John Steel "Jock" Lewes, a Welsh Guards officer who had been Oxford's rowing blue in 1936 and who had been Stirling's parachute experimentation partner in the unauthorized jump from the Avro Anson that had ended in Stirling's June 1941 injury; Robert Blair "Paddy" Mayne, a Royal Ulster Rifles officer who had been an Irish rugby international before the war and whom Stirling had recruited from a military prison cell where Mayne was awaiting a court-martial verdict for striking his commanding officer; William "Bill" Fraser, a Gordon Highlanders officer of more conventional background but exceptional personal courage; and a small further cadre. The non-commissioned ranks — initially around sixty men — were recruited from the dispersed Layforce veterans whom the dissolution of the Commando brigade had left without operational employment. Training at Kabrit through September and October 1941 was conducted on the same principle as recruitment: deliberately unorthodox, oriented toward independent small-team operation under conditions of physical extremity, with parachute training conducted from improvised platforms — the campers built a wooden tower of approximately eighteen feet, from which trainees jumped onto the desert sand to simulate landing impact — before any actual parachute training equipment had been delivered to the camp. Two trainees were killed in the improvised parachute exercises. Stirling, on his own subsequent account, regarded the deaths as the operational cost of the training method and did not modify the method to reduce the cost.[^ch3-38]

L Detachment's first operational deployment, in the autumn of 1941, was timed to coincide with the opening of Operation Crusader — the British offensive of November 1941 against Rommel's positions in eastern Cyrenaica that General Sir Alan Cunningham, who had commanded the British forces in the East African campaign, had been given to plan and command. The SAS task was straightforward in concept and, as the operation unfolded, catastrophic in execution. On the night of the sixteenth to seventeenth of November 1941 — twelve hours before Cunningham's armored columns were to cross the wire of the Egypt-Libya frontier — five Bristol Bombay transport aircraft were to insert fifty-five SAS operators by parachute behind German lines at a location approximately eighty miles east of Tobruk. The operators were to attack, on foot from their landing zones, the German Luftwaffe airfields at Gazala and Timimi, where the principal Messerschmitt Bf 109 fighters of the German close air support force were dispersed. The destruction of the aircraft on the ground would, in the operational concept, remove the principal aerial obstacle to Cunningham's armored advance during the first forty-eight hours of Crusader. Stirling himself, in characteristic disregard of the operational principle that commanders should not personally insert with their first operations, jumped with the operation as commander of one of the five sticks. The weather on the night of the drop was the worst the western desert had experienced in living memory. A storm with surface winds of approximately forty-five knots — winds that exceeded by a substantial margin the design tolerance of the parachutes the operation depended on — broke over the drop zones approximately twenty minutes before the lead aircraft made its first pass. Operators were scattered, after deployment, across an area of perhaps two hundred square miles. Many landed in the storm at velocities that the British parachute equipment of 1941 had not been engineered to permit operators to survive. Of the fifty-five men dropped, approximately twenty-two returned to the British lines over the days following the operation. The remainder — thirty-three operators, including the operators of three of the five sticks — were killed in the drop, killed on the desert in the days following the drop, or captured by the German and Italian forces that had been alerted to the operation by the storm-scattered survivors of the failed insertion. Stirling himself returned. Lewes returned. Mayne returned. The unit's first operation, by every operational measure, had eliminated more than half its operational strength in a single night and had not destroyed a single German aircraft.[^ch3-39]

In the days following the failed insertion of Operation Crusader, Stirling — whom the survivors had collected at a rendezvous point inside the British lines and who had immediately driven, on his own initiative, to Bagnold's LRDG forward base at Siwa Oasis — proposed to the LRDG commander, Major Guy Prendergast, an institutional arrangement that would, in the next eighteen months, reconfigure the operational character of the SAS more fundamentally than any other single decision of the unit's history. The proposal was that the LRDG should, beginning immediately, provide ground transport for the SAS's future operations. The LRDG's modified Chevrolet 30-cwt trucks — vehicles Bagnold had personally engineered for sand-dune operation across two decades of inter-war private exploration — could carry SAS operators across the deep desert, deposit them within walking distance of their targets, wait for them at agreed extraction points, and return them across the open desert to the British lines. Parachute insertion, on the operational evidence the failed Crusader drop had produced, was unreliable in the desert weather conditions and operationally expensive in trained personnel. Ground insertion through the deep desert, using the LRDG's existing operational architecture, would eliminate both problems at once. Prendergast agreed. From December 1941 through the spring of 1942, the SAS operated as, in effect, the offensive raiding component of a combined SAS-LRDG operational system in which the LRDG supplied the navigation, transport, and extraction infrastructure and the SAS supplied the assault element at the target. The arrangement was the operational pivot on which the British SAS's eventual reputation rested.[^ch3-40]

The technical complement to the SAS-LRDG operational arrangement was the Lewes bomb. Jock Lewes — who had survived the Crusader disaster and who had assumed, in its aftermath, the institutional role of L Detachment's principal training and demolitions officer — designed in late November and December 1941 a custom incendiary device specifically engineered for the SAS's airfield raiding mission. The device combined a small charge of plastic explosive, a quantity of thermite, and a measured pour of motor oil, in a configuration that could be sealed in a small fabric pouch and carried in numbers across the desert in operator backpacks. A single Lewes bomb, placed in the engine compartment of a parked aircraft and detonated by a time pencil, would destroy the aircraft's engine and ignite the fuel system in a fire that the aircraft's onboard fire-suppression systems could not extinguish. The Lewes bomb was, on the operational record of the SAS's airfield raids of 1942, the principal instrument by which the unit produced its operational effects. Lewes himself was killed in late December 1941, in an aerial attack on the LRDG convoy returning from one of the early SAS raids. He had been in operational command of the SAS at the moment of his death. Stirling, who had been operating with a separate party at the time, learned of Lewes's death on his return to the base camp. The bomb that bore Lewes's name survived its inventor by, in some operational reckonings, a margin of decades.[^ch3-41]

Between December 1941 and June 1942, the SAS-LRDG system produced an operational record that would, in the institutional history of the unit, become canonical.
