SAS raids destroyed approximately ninety German and Italian aircraft on the ground at the Luftwaffe airfields at Tamet (December 1941), Sirte (December 1941, with Mayne in personal command), Wadi Tamet (December 1941, second raid), Agedabia (December 1941), Marble Arch (December 1941, in which Lewes was killed), Bouerat (January 1942), and a succession of secondary targets through the spring. The operational concept was repetitive and successful. The SAS would be inserted by LRDG ground transport at a deep desert lying-up point. The raiders would walk in, on foot, to the target airfield's perimeter over a period of one to three nights. They would penetrate the perimeter on the night of the attack, place Lewes bombs on as many parked aircraft as could be reached in the available window, withdraw to the lying-up point, and be extracted by the LRDG within twenty-four to forty-eight hours of the attack. German and Italian airfield security, in the desert conditions of the western theater, was not engineered against the operational threat the SAS posed. The raids depended on the assumption that the Axis security perimeters would not, in the deep-desert installations where most of the principal aircraft were dispersed, anticipate a ground-based assault delivered through the empty quarter rather than from the British lines to the east.[^ch3-42]

In the summer of 1942, the SAS acquired the operational instrument that would, for the closing year of its desert career, allow the unit to operate independently of the LRDG. The instrument was the American-built Willys jeep — a four-wheel-drive utility vehicle that the United States Army had begun supplying to British forces under the Lend-Lease program in the spring of 1942. Stirling and Mayne, recognizing immediately the operational potential of a small, fast, four-wheel-drive vehicle that could traverse the desert at speeds far in excess of the LRDG's Chevrolet trucks, ordered the conversion of a first batch of fifteen jeeps for armed reconnaissance and assault. The conversion was extensive. Each jeep was fitted with twin Vickers K aerial machine guns — drum-fed 0.303-inch weapons originally designed for installation on RAF biplane gunners' rear cockpits, deemed obsolete by the Air Ministry and released to Stirling on his personal request to Tedder. The Vickers K's rate of fire — approximately 950 rounds per minute, on each gun — produced, with the twin installation, a combined volume of fire that approximated the firepower of a small infantry company concentrated on a single rapidly moving platform. Each jeep mounted two such installations — one forward by the front passenger, one aft by the rear seat. The configuration converted each jeep, in effect, into a heavily armed mobile assault platform whose firepower exceeded by a substantial margin the firepower of the Italian and German security installations the SAS was attacking. The new SAS, fully motorized and heavily armed, could operate independently of LRDG support and could engage Axis security installations directly rather than evading them.[^ch3-43]

The operational climax of the SAS's pre-Stirling-capture period was the airfield raid on Sidi Haneish, conducted on the night of the twenty-sixth to twenty-seventh of July 1942. Sidi Haneish was a forward Luftwaffe airfield located approximately forty miles inland from the Mediterranean coast, on the rail line between Mersa Matruh and El Daba, in the area in which the German and Italian air forces had concentrated the Junkers Ju 52 transport aircraft that supplied the front-line Axis units during the operational pause that followed the First Battle of El Alamein on the first of July. Stirling led the raid personally in command of a column of eighteen jeeps. The column approached the airfield overnight from the south through the open desert. On the airfield perimeter, on Stirling's hand signal, the eighteen jeeps formed up into two parallel lines — nine vehicles in each line, the lines separated by approximately one hundred feet, the formation oriented along the airfield's principal aircraft dispersal area. Stirling's signal opened fire. The thirty-six Vickers K guns of the column — eighteen jeeps, two guns per jeep, fore and aft — produced a combined volume of fire of approximately 34,000 rounds per minute. The column drove the length of the airfield twice, with the formation reversing its orientation on the second pass to engage aircraft on the opposite side of the dispersal area. The action took approximately fifteen minutes. Forty German aircraft — predominantly Junkers Ju 52 transports and Messerschmitt Bf 109 fighters — were destroyed or damaged beyond repair. SAS losses were two killed and three wounded. The Sidi Haneish raid was, by any measure that the operational analysis of the desert war can produce, one of the most cost-effective small-unit operations of the campaign. It was also, by the institutional measure that this book is constructing, the operational moment at which the British SOF tradition that Clarke had theorized in June 1940 had become the operational reality that the post-war national SOF traditions would draw on as the founding template.[^ch3-44]

Stirling was captured on the night of the twenty-fourth to twenty-fifth of January 1943. He had been operating with a small SAS party in the area between Gabes and Tripoli — in the closing weeks of the Tunisian campaign, with the Eighth Army advancing from the east and the First Army from the west — when his party was tracked by a German specialist unit that had been raised in the autumn of 1942 specifically for the purpose of countering British long-range raiding. Stirling and his driver were apprehended at first light in a wadi south of the coastal road. Stirling escaped from his initial place of detention within hours; he was recaptured within two days; he attempted a second escape within a week; he was recaptured within three days. After the fourth recapture, the German command transferred Stirling to Colditz Castle — the Wehrmacht's high-security prisoner-of-war facility for repeated escapers — where he spent the remainder of the war. Mayne assumed command of the SAS on Stirling's capture. By the spring of 1943, under Mayne's command, the SAS had been expanded from L Detachment's original sixty men into a two-regiment formation: 1 SAS Regiment under Mayne's command, 2 SAS Regiment under the command of Stirling's brother Bill — the same Bill Stirling whom the previous chapter has identified, briefly, as the SOE officer who had been one of David's closest pre-war operational interlocutors. The unit would operate, in its two-regiment configuration, through the closing campaigns of the Tunisian, Italian, French, and German fronts. It would be dissolved, in October 1945, in the institutional reflex that the next section of this chapter will reconstruct as the recurring fate of British SOF formations at the conclusion of major wars.[^ch3-45]

The Yishuv consequences of the SAS's emergence in 1941–1943 were, in operational terms during the war itself, modest. Through the SOE Cairo station, Captain Herbert Cecil Buck — a German-speaking British officer of the Punjabi Regiment who had escaped from German captivity in 1941 by walking out of a prisoner-of-war camp in his captured German uniform and walking, in German, through the German rear areas to British-controlled territory — assembled in early 1942 the Special Interrogation Group, a small unit of German-speaking Jewish volunteers drawn from the German Platoon of the Palmach and from the German-Jewish refugees of the Auxiliary Military Pioneer Corps. The SIG operated in collaboration with the SAS on several operations of 1942, including the joint raid on the Luftwaffe airfields at Martuba and Derna in June 1942 in which the SIG operator who had been the operation's principal cover element — later identified by the German cover name Brueckner — betrayed the operation to the German garrison at the cost of multiple SAS and SIG casualties. The Martuba operation is reconstructed in §3.6 of this chapter. What concerns the present section is the institutional transmission. Through the operational collaboration with the SIG, and through the parallel SOE Syrian Scheme operations that drew Palmach operators directly into British irregular operations in 1941 and 1942, the Palmach — the Yishuv's strike force that Sadeh had constituted in May 1941 and that Allon would inherit in 1945 — acquired direct operational knowledge of the SAS doctrinal package. The long-range desert insertion. The airfield raid template. The Lewes bomb. The jeep-mounted heavy-weapons platform. The cellular small-team organization. The radical decentralization of operational decision authority to the team leader on the ground. The institutional pattern by which a small permanent special operations unit could be administratively absorbed within a deception cover that supplied it with the prefabricated institutional reality the conventional bureaucracy had not authorized.[^ch3-46]

The institutional history of the Palmach's drawing on the SAS doctrinal package was, in the post-war decades, partly concealed and partly forgotten. It was concealed, in the first instance, by the political imperatives of the late 1940s — when the Palmach's institutional self-presentation, in the months leading up to the British departure from Palestine and in the founding war of the Israeli state in 1948, did not benefit from public acknowledgment of the unit's wartime collaboration with the British Mandate authority's clandestine arms. It was forgotten, in the second instance, by the institutional reflex of the post-1948 IDF — which dissolved the Palmach in November 1948 and which absorbed the Palmach's surviving veterans into the new army's conventional formations in a process whose institutional logic actively suppressed the unit's distinctive operational doctrine. The doctrinal package the Palmach had absorbed from the SAS, in 1941 and 1942, did not, in the institutional sense, pass directly into the new Israeli military. It passed into private memory — into the operational experience of the few Palmach veterans who would, in the middle and late 1950s, supply the personnel and the doctrinal substance for the next Israeli round of special operations innovation. The transmission belt, in the institutional history of the post-1948 Israeli SOF tradition, was a generation of Palmach veterans who carried the SAS template in their personal operational memory through the dispersal years and who, when the institutional opportunity emerged in 1957, reassembled it. The fuller story of that reassembly belongs to Chapter 5. The end of the British SOF tradition's wartime arc, and the post-war institutional dissolutions through which the British template passed into the keeping of the few officers and operators who would carry it into the next round of wars, belongs to §3.7 and §3.8 of the present chapter. The §3.6 that immediately follows turns first to the Yishuv side of the wartime collaboration — to the Auxiliary Military Pioneer Corps, the Palestine Regiment, the SOE Syrian Scheme, the German Platoon and the Mistarvim, the parachutist mission of 1944, and Buck's Special Interrogation Group — and to the specific operational and personnel channels through which the British SOF doctrine reached the Palmach.[^ch3-47]

## 3.6 The Yishuv as Junior Partner, June 1941 – June 1942

On the morning of the eighth of June 1941, a twenty-six-year-old Haganah officer named Moshe Dayan led a small reconnaissance party from a forming-up position in the Galilee panhandle, across the international frontier into Vichy-controlled Lebanon, and toward a French police post at a site that British military maps recorded as Khirbet Iskandaroun, a few kilometers north of the Litani River. The party numbered, by the standard reconstructions, thirty-one men — twenty-one Australians of the 7th Division's 2/16th Battalion, eight Palmach operators drawn from the Yishuv volunteers who had been trained over the preceding three months by the Special Operations Executive's Syrian Scheme team at Mishmar Ha-Yam on the Carmel coast, and two officers of the Special Operations Executive's Cairo station who were operating in the field as liaison and operational supervision. Dayan was the senior officer of the Palmach element. The party's mission was a forward seizure of the police post and the road bridges to the north of it, ahead of the Australian 7th Division's main advance across the same terrain, which would begin at dawn on the same day as the opening phase of Operation Exporter — the Allied invasion of Vichy Syria and Lebanon that the British, Australian, Indian, and Free French commands had been planning, in coordination with the SOE Cairo station and the Haganah liaison apparatus, since the early weeks of 1941. The bridge was seized within the first hour. The police post was taken with light French resistance. Approximately ten in the morning, while Dayan was on the roof of the captured police post observing the next French defensive line through a pair of British military binoculars, a Vichy French rifle round struck the binoculars at a near-perpendicular angle. The lenses shattered. Glass and metal fragments drove inward into Dayan's left eye socket. The eye was destroyed. Dayan was evacuated to a field hospital on the British side of the frontier within four hours and to the hospital at Haifa within twenty-four. He would, for the remainder of his life, wear the black eye patch that would, in the decades after the founding of the Israeli state, become one of the most recognized visual signatures of any military and political figure in the modern history of the country.[48]

The Iskandaroun action of the eighth of June 1941 was, in the operational record of the British–Yishuv collaboration of the war's middle years, one of the early and most consequential field demonstrations that the Haganah's operators could be inserted into the SOE Cairo station's clandestine apparatus as functional equals rather than as auxiliary labor. The institutional architecture that had made the action possible had been assembled in stages across the preceding eighteen months. In the autumn of 1940, the SOE's Cairo station, operating under cover of the Inter-Services Liaison Department designation, had opened a quiet channel of operational coordination with the Haganah's intelligence apparatus in Jerusalem, mediated by David Hacohen — the Haganah's senior contact within the Solel Boneh construction company, whose Mandate-licensed engineering contracts had supplied a cover under which Haganah personnel and matériel could be moved across the eastern Mediterranean — and Reuven Zaslani, the Haganah Intelligence Service officer who would, after the founding of the Israeli state seven years later, change his surname to Shiloah and become the institutional architect of the Mossad. In the early months of 1941, with the Vichy French position in Syria and Lebanon becoming a strategic problem for the British Middle East Command's planning, the SOE Cairo station had been authorized to expand the Mishmar Ha-Yam training facility into a formal SOE field station and to begin training Yishuv operators for clandestine insertion into Vichy territory. Maurice Oldfield — the same Oldfield who would, in the post-war decades, become the chief of the Secret Intelligence Service — was the station's principal officer on the SOE side. Tony Simonds was the principal British training officer. The Yishuv side of the arrangement, conducted on Sadeh's authority after his appointment as Palmach commander in May 1941 and with the explicit approval of the Haganah's command apparatus in Jerusalem, was managed in the field by Yigal Allon and by Yitzhak Sadeh's principal training officer for irregular operations, Yitzhak Hochman.[^ch3-49]

The Yishuv operators trained at Mishmar Ha-Yam in the spring of 1941 — Dayan and his Iskandaroun party were the first cohort to be inserted operationally — were organized within the SOE's clandestine apparatus as the German Platoon (Plugat HaGermanim) and the Mistarvim (HaMistarvim; literally "those who become like Arabs"). The two platoons differed in their operational mission. The German Platoon was the platoon of German-speaking operators, drawn principally from the German-Jewish immigrants of the late 1930s who had reached Palestine on illegal-immigration ships from Trieste and Marseille between 1937 and 1939, and was trained for clandestine insertion into German and Italian rear areas under German uniform and German linguistic cover. The Mistarvim was the platoon of Arabic-speaking operators, drawn principally from the Mizrahi and Sephardi Jewish communities of Palestine — Yemenite, Iraqi, Syrian, and Maghrebi Jews who had grown up in Arabic-language households and who could pass, in the appropriate dress and with the appropriate linguistic cover, as Palestinian Arabs or as Lebanese, Syrian, or Iraqi Arabs — and was trained for clandestine insertion into Arab-majority areas of the Levant in indigenous cover. Both platoons drew, doctrinally, on the operational template that the Brandenburger establishment had pioneered under Theodor von Hippel four years earlier in Germany. Both platoons drew, institutionally, on the British SOE infrastructure — the training facility, the SOE-supplied uniforms and matériel, the SOE-coordinated insertion and extraction. Both platoons would, by the spring of 1942, be operating in the field in coordination with the corresponding British units. The German Platoon supplied the principal operator pool for Captain Herbert Cecil Buck's Special Interrogation Group, which the SOE Cairo station authorized in January 1942. The Mistarvim supplied the principal operator pool for the SOE Syrian Scheme's continuing clandestine operations in Vichy Syria, in Lebanon after the September 1941 Allied occupation, and in the Iraqi and Persian operations that the SOE conducted in support of the British suppression of the pro-Axis Rashid Ali coup in Baghdad in May 1941 and the subsequent British–Soviet occupation of Iran in August.[^ch3-50]

The most operationally consequential collaboration between the Yishuv's clandestine units and the British SOF establishment of 1942 was the Special Interrogation Group. Buck had assembled the SIG at Mersa Matruh in February 1942, on the authority of the SOE Cairo station and with the operational support of the SAS that David Stirling had, by that date, established at Kabrit. The unit's initial strength was approximately forty operators. Roughly thirty were German-Jewish refugees drawn from the Auxiliary Military Pioneer Corps and from the German Platoon's Mishmar Ha-Yam cohort. The remainder were British officers and specialist personnel who supplied the operational planning and the field coordination with the SAS and the LRDG. Training at Mersa Matruh through February and March 1942 was conducted to a level of operational realism that exceeded, in its insistence on linguistic and cultural cover, anything the British SOE establishment had previously attempted. Operators were required to speak German exclusively for periods of weeks at a time. They were required to maintain German military identities — name, rank, unit, hometown, regimental detail — under interrogation pressure that simulated, as closely as British training methods of the period could simulate, the conditions of German rear-area arrest. They wore German uniforms — the Afrika Korps tropical pattern, sourced from the captured stocks that the British had seized in O'Connor's December 1940 offensive and that the SOE Cairo station had reserved for clandestine use. They carried German small arms, German rations, German personal effects. They were inserted, in operational deployments, in German military vehicles — captured Volkswagen Kübelwagen utility cars and Mercedes-Benz staff cars, repainted in Afrika Korps markings — which the SIG operators had been trained to drive and to service in the German manner. The unit's first operational deployments, in March and April 1942, were small-scale reconnaissance and intelligence-collection operations against German rear-area positions in eastern Cyrenaica. The operations were successful. The operational technique appeared to be viable.[^ch3-51]

The Martuba and Derna airfield raid of the night of the thirteenth to fourteenth of June 1942 was the SIG's first major operational deployment in collaboration with the SAS, and was, in the operational record of the British–Yishuv SOF collaboration of the war's middle years, the unit's institutional catastrophe. The operation had been planned by Stirling and Buck in coordination, with SOE Cairo station authorization, as a coordinated assault on the four principal Luftwaffe airfields in the Martuba and Derna area — installations from which the German close air support assets for Rommel's June 1942 advance on Tobruk were being staged. The operational concept depended on the SIG's identity-deception cover. A SIG party — German-uniformed, German-speaking, mounted in repainted German vehicles — would, at the planned hour of the operation, drive openly through the perimeter security of the airfield's outer cordon, present authentic-looking German movement orders to the perimeter guards, and reach the airfield's principal aircraft dispersal areas before the German garrison had time to identify them as hostile. Once inside the perimeter, the SIG operators would silence the immediate German security with suppressed weapons. A larger SAS raiding party, following the SIG penetration on foot from a lying-up point outside the perimeter, would then enter the airfield's interior and place Lewes bombs on the parked aircraft in the manner established in the earlier SAS airfield raids. The planning was sound. The operational rehearsals were thorough. The SIG cover party that drove to the Martuba perimeter on the night of the thirteenth was led by a SIG operator whose German cover name was Brueckner and whose actual identity — the subject of considerable post-war reconstruction — was that of a German-Jewish refugee who had reached Palestine in 1939, had volunteered for the AMPC in 1940, had been recruited into the German Platoon's Mishmar Ha-Yam cohort in 1941, and had been transferred to Buck's SIG in February 1942.[^ch3-52]

What occurred at the Martuba perimeter shortly before midnight on the thirteenth of June 1942 has been reconstructed, in the post-war literature, from the testimony of the few SIG and SAS operators who survived the operation and from the German operational records of the Luftwaffe security units that detected and responded to the British penetration. The reconstructions diverge on the question of agency. The standard British version, drawing on the post-war debriefing of the surviving SAS officer Lieutenant David Russell, holds that the SIG operator Brueckner, immediately on arriving at the Martuba perimeter, broke from the cover party, walked openly toward the German guard post, and informed the German sentry — in fluent German, without coercion — of the operation's composition, the planned penetration point, and the location of the SAS lying-up area. The German garrison, alerted to the raid before the SAS party had reached the perimeter, mounted an ambush at the lying-up area as the SAS party was forming up for the perimeter assault. The ambush killed approximately fourteen SAS operators outright. Six SIG operators who had been with the cover party at the perimeter were captured and were, within a small number of days, executed under Hitler's Kommandobefehl — the Commando Order of the eighteenth of October 1942 that would, in its formal promulgation four months after the Martuba operation, codify the German military's practice of executing all Allied special operations personnel on capture without regard for the conventional protections of the laws of armed conflict, but that had already been informally in effect against SIG operators since the Brandenburger establishment's identification of the SIG as an operational mirror-image of their own identity-deception units. Two SAS officers — Captain Augustin Jordan and Lieutenant Russell — escaped the ambush. They reached the British lines, on foot, across one hundred and forty miles of German-controlled desert, eight days after the operation. The SIG cover party did not survive. Buck himself, who had not been with the field party on the night of the operation, withdrew the remaining SIG personnel to the SOE Cairo station compound within seventy-two hours of the operational confirmation of the failure. The SIG was institutionally suspended within a week. It was formally disestablished by the SOE Cairo station in October 1942, four months after the Martuba operation, and its surviving operators were dispersed back to the AMPC, the Palestine Regiment, the Palmach, or — in a small number of cases — to other SOE clandestine operations in the Mediterranean theater.[53]

The Martuba disaster ended the SIG. It did not end the operational collaboration between the British SOF establishment and the Yishuv's clandestine units. Through the second half of 1942 and into 1943, the SOE Syrian Scheme's continuing operations in the Levant — directed against the residual Vichy French intelligence apparatus in Lebanon and Syria after the September 1941 Allied occupation, against the Italian and German covert agent networks that the SIME had identified as operating in Syria and Iraq, and against the Axis-aligned Iraqi political elements that had survived the British suppression of the Rashid Ali coup of May 1941 — continued to draw on the Mistarvim operator pool. The German Platoon's surviving operators were absorbed, in the institutional reorganization of the Palmach that Sadeh authorized in the autumn of 1942, into the Palmach's emerging Seventh Company — the company-sized formation that would, by 1944, consolidate the Palmach's specialized intelligence, reconnaissance, and clandestine-operations cadres into a single institutional vehicle and would, in the operational and personnel history that Chapter 4 will reconstruct, supply the principal Yishuv-period precedent for the IDF's post-1948 special-reconnaissance establishment. The institutional architecture of the British–Yishuv SOF collaboration, in other words, survived the Martuba disaster. The specific operational vehicle — Buck's SIG — did not. The operational pattern the SIG had pioneered — German-speaking Jewish operators in German uniform conducting identity-deception operations against German rear-area positions — would not be reattempted, at unit scale, in the remaining years of the war.[^ch3-54]

The wider institutional consequence of the SIG's brief operational career, for the Yishuv side of the wartime collaboration, was the institutional confirmation that the British SOE establishment was willing to absorb the Yishuv's existing clandestine apparatus on terms of effective operational equality. The Mishmar Ha-Yam training facility was, by the autumn of 1942, the central institutional node through which the Haganah's intelligence and clandestine-operations cadres were being trained to the operational standard the British SOF establishment had developed across 1940 and 1941. The German Platoon and the Mistarvim were, by the same date, institutionally absorbed within the SOE's regional operations apparatus on terms that gave the Haganah operational and personnel control over the deployment of its own people. The institutional precedent the collaboration established — that the Yishuv's clandestine apparatus could be operated within a larger Allied SOF establishment as a junior but functionally equal partner, with operational control retained at the Yishuv level — would survive the war, would survive the post-war dissolution of the British SOF establishments that this chapter is about to take up, and would supply the institutional template under which, in the founding war of the Israeli state of 1948, the same Mistarvim platoons and the same German Platoon veterans would be deployed against the Arab and the British forces in operations that the previous generation's British trainers had not anticipated.[^ch3-55]

## 3.7 The Closing Wartime Arc, October 1942 – August 1945

The institutional turning point of the entire British wartime SOF establishment, as of the Yishuv's wartime relationship with the British apparatus, was the Second Battle of El Alamein. The battle opened on the night of the twenty-third of October 1942, in the operational sector approximately sixty miles west of Alexandria where Field Marshal Bernard Montgomery — appointed to the Eighth Army command in August 1942 in the institutional shake-up that had also brought General Sir Harold Alexander to the Cairo theater command — had concentrated, across the preceding nine weeks, an Allied force of approximately 195,000 men, 1,029 tanks, 908 artillery pieces, and 530 operational aircraft. The German–Italian Panzer Army Africa under Rommel, depleted by the Allied air interdiction of Axis logistics across the Mediterranean through the summer and by Rommel's own decision to commit his last strategic reserves in the failed Battle of Alam Halfa in early September, fielded approximately 116,000 men, 547 tanks, 552 artillery pieces, and 350 operational aircraft against Montgomery's deliberately constructed defensive operation. The battle lasted thirteen days. Montgomery's combination of conventional armored breakthrough, infantry consolidation, and persistent air pressure broke the Panzer Army Africa's operational coherence on the third of November and produced, on the fourth, Rommel's first major operational retreat of the war. By the eleventh of November 1942, the Eighth Army had pursued the Axis remnants three hundred miles west to Mersa Matruh. By the twenty-third of November, the British had reentered Tobruk, retaken in five weeks the ground it had taken Rommel eighteen months to conquer. By the early weeks of January 1943, the Eighth Army was approaching the Tunisian frontier, in operational coordination with the United States First Army's Torch landings in Algeria and Morocco of November 1942. The North African campaign would conclude with the surrender of Army Group Africa at Tunis on the thirteenth of May 1943. The strategic position of the British Middle East Command, and of the SOF establishment the command had built around itself, was transformed.[^ch3-56]

The transformation, for the SOF establishment, was double-edged. The institutional space that the conventional staff had conceded to the unconventional units during the operational crisis of 1940 and 1941 was, by the spring of 1943, beginning to contract. The SAS, expanded under Mayne's command into two regiments and operating from the spring of 1943 in the Italian theater rather than the Western Desert, was now operating in a strategic environment in which the operational rationale for small-unit airfield raiding was, for the first time since the unit's establishment, less compelling than the conventional alternative of Allied air superiority. The LRDG, whose deep-desert operational specialism had been the indispensable institutional asset of the British operations in 1941 and 1942, was operationally unemployed in the Mediterranean theater after the Tunisian campaign's conclusion. The SBS, which had operated successfully alongside the Greek and Italian resistance through 1943 and 1944, was institutionally over-extended by the end of the war. The Commando establishment, which had been used at scale in the Normandy landings of June 1944 and in the subsequent campaign in northern France and the Low Countries, had completed by the spring of 1945 the operational function the conventional army staff regarded as the unit type's principal institutional justification. By the early months of 1945, the conventional army establishment was beginning, in the institutional language of the period, to "regularize" the SOF formations — to absorb them back into the conventional order of battle, to subject them to the standard establishment table, to limit their operational autonomy, and, in the cases the conventional staff regarded as the most institutionally aberrant, to dissolve them outright.[^ch3-57]

The Yishuv's institutional position, across the same closing arc of the war, ran in the opposite direction. The Palmach, which Sadeh had constituted in May 1941 with three companies of approximately three hundred operators, had grown by the middle of 1944 to approximately one thousand operators distributed across six companies, two of which — the Sixth and the Seventh — were specialized formations rather than conventional infantry. The growth had been achieved through an institutional arrangement that Sadeh and his successor as Palmach commander, Yigal Allon — who had taken command on the fifteenth of October 1945, six months after the European armistice and one month before the end of the chapter's wartime arc — had negotiated with the kibbutz movement. Under the arrangement, Palmach operators would, after their initial training, be permanently stationed at member kibbutzim of the Kibbutz Movement's three principal federations. Each operator would spend approximately fourteen days per month on operational training and operational deployment, and approximately sixteen days per month working as agricultural labor in the host kibbutz's fields, dairy operations, and construction projects. The arrangement solved, in a single institutional move, two operational problems the Palmach had faced from its founding. It solved the funding problem — the Palmach had no independent income, and the British Mandate authorities had withdrawn the operational subsidy they had extended through 1941 and 1942 once the immediate Axis threat to the Mandate had receded after El Alamein. It solved the personnel problem — by tying Palmach service to host kibbutzim, the arrangement created a permanent operator pool whose members could be mobilized rapidly without the institutional friction of conventional army recruitment and dispersal. It produced, as an institutional side-effect, a Palmach culture that would, in the post-war decades, become indistinguishable in important respects from the kibbutz movement's broader political and ideological culture. The institutional pattern would have profound consequences for the post-1948 IDF's relationship with the Palmach's institutional inheritance, consequences the next chapter will take up at length.[^ch3-58]

The Yishuv's broader contribution to the British wartime SOF establishment, in the closing two years of the war, expanded through two channels the operational rationale this chapter has not yet traced. The first channel was the Yishuv Parachutist Mission to occupied Europe, conducted jointly by the SOE Cairo station and the Haganah's intelligence apparatus between February 1943 and the European armistice of May 1945. The mission inserted, by parachute and by clandestine ground infiltration from neutral and partisan-controlled territory, approximately thirty-seven Palestinian Jewish operators into Yugoslavia, Hungary, Slovakia, Bulgaria, Romania, and Italy. The operators' mission was double — they were to coordinate with the local Allied intelligence and resistance apparatus in the territories of their insertion, and they were to make contact, where contact was possible, with the surviving Jewish communities of the occupied territories to facilitate clandestine rescue and emigration to the Yishuv. The operational record was mixed. Twelve of the thirty-seven operators were captured. Seven were executed by the German or the collaborationist authorities of their territories of operation, including the parachutist operator Hannah Szenes, who was captured shortly after her insertion into Hungary in June 1944 and was executed in Budapest in November 1944, and the parachutist operator Enzo Sereni, who was inserted into northern Italy in May 1944, was captured within forty-eight hours, was transferred to Dachau concentration camp in late 1944, and was executed there in November 1944. The institutional importance of the mission, in the operational and doctrinal arc this chapter is reconstructing, was not the operational success of the insertions — the operational record was, in narrow military terms, modest — but the institutional confirmation that the Yishuv's clandestine apparatus could conduct strategic-depth insertions into European territory in coordination with the SOE and the relevant national resistance movements. The institutional template would, in the post-war decades, become an essential element of the Israeli intelligence apparatus's strategic operational doctrine.[^ch3-59]

The second channel was the Jewish Brigade Group. Authorized by the British War Cabinet on the twentieth of September 1944, after five years of Yishuv lobbying that had been resisted by the British Mandate authorities and by the Foreign Office on the political grounds that an organized Jewish military formation would, after the war, prefigure the founding of a Jewish state that the Mandatory power did not wish to authorize, the Brigade was formally constituted in November 1944 from the three Palestine Regiment battalions that had been operating in the Mandate and the Middle East theater since 1942. The Brigade's authorized strength was approximately five thousand men. Its commander was Brigadier Ernest Benjamin, a Canadian-born British officer whose appointment had been negotiated specifically to provide the Brigade with a commanding officer who was both technically British and culturally sympathetic to the Yishuv's political aspirations. The Brigade was deployed to Italy in February 1945, was committed to operations on the Senio River front in March, participated in the Eighth Army's spring 1945 offensive across the Po Valley, and was holding a sector of the Allied line at the moment of the German surrender in Italy on the twenty-ninth of April 1945. After the European armistice the Brigade was redeployed to the Belgium–Netherlands border, where its institutional position became, in the post-war reckoning, more consequential than its operational role had been during the war. From the Brigade's positions on the German frontier through the second half of 1945 and into 1946, the Brigade's personnel — operating in coordination with the Haganah's emerging Mossad le-Aliyah Bet (the Haganah's clandestine immigration apparatus) — would organize the European illegal immigration networks that brought tens of thousands of Holocaust survivors to the Yishuv through the British Mandate's anti-immigration blockade. The institutional architecture of the post-war illegal immigration operations was, in important measure, the institutional residue of the Jewish Brigade Group's wartime authorization.[^ch3-60]

The third Yishuv institutional development of the closing wartime arc was the formal separation, on the seventeenth of April 1945, of the Palmach Naval Company — the Palyam — from the Palmach's conventional infantry organization. The Palyam had originated, in 1943, as a small naval-operations cadre within the Palmach's Sixth Company. It had been operating, under SOE coordination, against the Italian and German shipping in the eastern Mediterranean and along the Lebanese and Syrian coasts. After the April 1945 separation, the Palyam was reorganized as an independent Palmach sub-unit under the command of Yochai Bin-Nun, with a strength of approximately one hundred operators trained in maritime sabotage, underwater demolition, small-boat reconnaissance, and the coastal infiltration operations that the unit would, in the post-war period of British blockade of illegal immigration to Palestine, conduct against the Royal Navy's blockade vessels in the Mediterranean. The Palyam's institutional inheritance — the maritime SOF tradition that the unit would carry into the post-1948 IDF naval establishment — would supply the doctrinal and personnel foundation of the Israeli naval special operations apparatus that the post-war decades would build into a strategic capability of national consequence.[^ch3-61]

By the European armistice of the eighth of May 1945, the Yishuv's military establishment had reached an institutional configuration that the British Mandate authorities of 1939 had not anticipated and that the post-war British policy in Palestine would, across the following three years, attempt unsuccessfully to dismantle. The Haganah numbered, in active and reserve combatants, approximately forty thousand. The Palmach numbered, in standing operators, approximately one thousand. The Jewish Brigade Group numbered, at its formal strength on the day of the armistice, approximately five thousand. The Palestine Regiment's residual battalions and the Yishuv volunteer presence in other British army formations added a further several thousand trained personnel. The Mistarvim and the German Platoon, dispersed institutionally after the SIG's Martuba disaster of June 1942, had been absorbed into the Palmach's Seventh Company by the closing months of the war and were operating as the Yishuv's specialized clandestine-operations unit under the Palmach's direct institutional control. The institutional precedent the Mishmar Ha-Yam training facility had established, in the period of the SOE Syrian Scheme's operational collaboration of 1941 and 1942, had been generalized across the Haganah's wider intelligence and operational apparatus. The Yishuv had become, in institutional terms, a small national military establishment that operated at the operational standards of a major Allied power — for the immediate reason that the wartime collaboration with the British SOF establishment had taught it to operate at those standards, and for the longer reason that the institutional architecture the Haganah and the Palmach had developed across the war years had been engineered to absorb and to internalize the operational doctrine the British collaborators had transmitted.[^ch3-62]

## 3.8 The Dissolutions of October 1945

The institutional reflex that the British Army staff carried into the post-war period was, by the late summer of 1945, already in motion against the SOF establishment that the wartime emergency had created. The first formal dissolution came on the first of October 1945, when the War Office issued the order that disbanded both regiments of the Special Air Service. The order had been drafted, in the War Office's establishments branch, on the standard institutional grounds that the SOF formations had been raised for the specific operational requirements of the wartime emergency and that the conclusion of the war removed the operational rationale for the formations' continuing existence. Mayne, by then a lieutenant-colonel and the senior surviving SAS officer of the wartime period, accepted the dissolution without formal protest. The institutional space within which Mayne might have contested the dissolution had been closed off by the broader political pressure on the British army establishment to demobilize at scale. The SAS, an institutionally aberrant formation that had been politically protected through the war by Churchill and operationally protected by Wavell and Alexander, had no comparable patron in the post-war Labour government that had taken power in July 1945 on the platform of post-war demobilization and the institutional reconstruction of the welfare state. Mayne returned to his pre-war legal practice in Newtownards, Northern Ireland. He would, across the next decade, conduct one more substantial operational deployment — the Falklands Islands Dependencies Survey expedition of 1945–1946, in which he served as the survey's commander of land operations on the Antarctic Peninsula — and would die in a road traffic accident outside Newtownards in December 1955, at the age of forty.[^ch3-63]

The dissolutions cascaded. The Long Range Desert Group was disbanded on the first of August 1945, two months earlier than the SAS, in an institutional sequence the War Office's establishments branch did not separately justify. The Special Boat Service — the wartime SBS, which had operated through the Mediterranean and the Aegean as a small permanent unit of approximately one hundred operators since 1942 — was disbanded in October 1945. The Commando establishment was dissolved in November 1945, with the exception of the three Royal Marines Commandos, which were retained in the Royal Marines' permanent establishment and would, after the institutional reconstruction of 1946, supply the post-war British amphibious special operations capability that the Korean War and the Suez Crisis would call back into action. The Special Operations Executive was the institutional last to be dissolved. SOE was formally wound up by an order of the fifteenth of January 1946, with its files transferred to the Foreign Office and the Secret Intelligence Service, its operational personnel demobilized or absorbed into the SIS or the SIS's clandestine successor organizations, and its institutional memory dispersed across a series of post-war debriefing volumes and official histories that would, in the case of the official history that William Mackenzie completed in 1948, be held under classification for fifty-five years before being released in 2000.[^ch3-64]

The institutional inheritance the dissolutions did and did not transmit divided, in the post-war reckoning, along three lines. The first line was the institutional persistence within the British army of a small number of officers who had served in the wartime SOF formations and who would, in the operational and political opening of the late 1940s, push for the reconstitution of the units. David Stirling himself was central. Stirling had been released from German captivity in May 1945 at the end of the European war. He had returned to Britain, had been demobilized, and had moved, in 1946, to Southern Rhodesia, where he had attempted across the late 1940s to build a private commercial empire that would underwrite his subsequent political activities in Africa and the Middle East. From his Rhodesian base, Stirling had remained in contact with the dispersed network of wartime SAS officers — Brian Franks, John Woodhouse, the brothers Stirling collectively — who would, in the operational opening that the Malayan Emergency of 1948 would create, push the War Office to reconstitute a Special Air Service formation for the operational requirements of the colonial counter-insurgency campaign in the Malayan jungle. The reconstitution was authorized in 1950. The Malayan Scouts (SAS) of 1950, redesignated 22 SAS Regiment in 1952 and consolidated within the regular British army establishment in 1959, would supply the institutional continuity through which the wartime SAS doctrinal package would survive the post-war dissolutions and would be carried into the operational opening of the Cold War and the post-colonial conflicts of the 1950s, 1960s, and 1970s. The institutional path was indirect and was operated by a small group of officers whose personal commitment to the wartime template was the principal institutional resource that the reconstitution depended on.[^ch3-65]

The second line of inheritance was the institutional persistence within the Yishuv of the Palmach as a standing strike force, in which the wartime operational collaboration with the British SOF establishment had produced a doctrinal package that the Palmach's institutional architecture had been engineered to absorb. The Palmach itself would, in the institutional convulsion of November 1948, be dissolved by Ben-Gurion in the same War of Independence-period decision that integrated the Haganah's military formations into the institutional structure of the new Israel Defense Forces. The dissolution would scatter the Palmach's personnel across the conventional infantry, armored, paratrooper, and naval establishments of the new IDF, and would actively suppress, in its institutional execution, the distinct operational doctrine that the Palmach's wartime training and operational experience had developed. The doctrinal package the Palmach had absorbed from the British SOF establishment of 1940 to 1945 — the SAS template that the SIG operational collaboration had transmitted, the SOE clandestine operational technique that Mishmar Ha-Yam had institutionalized, the LRDG deep-reconnaissance pattern that Bagnold's wartime operations had supplied, the Brandenburger identity-deception model that Mistarvim and German Platoon had operated against — would pass, in the post-1948 dispersal, into the private operational memory of the dispersed Palmach veterans. The next chapter takes up the personnel and institutional trajectories through which that private memory was carried into the IDF's first decade. Chapter 5 takes up the institutional reassembly of the doctrinal package, in the spring of 1957, at the institutional opening that the Sinai Campaign of 1956 and the establishment of the Northern Command's first reconnaissance unit in the summer of that year would together create.[^ch3-66]

The third line of inheritance was the doctrinal one that operated independently of either of the institutional vehicles. The British SOF tradition of 1940 to 1945 had produced, in the operational record of its principal units and in the published memoirs and operational histories of its principal commanders, a body of doctrinal material that would, across the following four decades, become canonical reading for the founders and the commanders of the post-war national SOF establishments of the major and minor powers. The Cowles biography of Stirling, published in 1958 and rapidly translated into the principal European languages and into Hebrew, supplied the founding scene that the SAS-derived units of the post-war period would invoke in their own institutional founding documents. The Foot official history of SOE, although held under classification until 1999, circulated within the British intelligence and special operations community across the late 1940s and the 1950s in officer-only versions that influenced the doctrinal development of the post-war British clandestine apparatus. The Lloyd-Owen memoir of the LRDG, published in 1980, would supply the founding institutional memory for the deep-reconnaissance and long-range patrol doctrine that the post-war American, Australian, and New Zealand SOF establishments would build their own deep-reconnaissance units around. The German operational analyses of the Brandenburger establishment, available in fragmented form in the post-war German military literature and in the captured German documents that the United States and British intelligence services had inventoried in 1945 and 1946, would supply the doctrinal substrate for the identity-deception operational pattern that the Yishuv's Mistarvim of the late 1940s, the IDF's reconstituted Mistarvim of the 1950s and 1960s, and the post-1980 Israeli special-reconnaissance establishment would adapt for the operational requirements of the Israeli–Arab conflict. The doctrinal inheritance, in other words, operated as the institutional substrate of the post-war national SOF traditions even where the wartime institutional vehicles had been formally dissolved.[^ch3-67]

The chapter closes, then, with an institutional irony. The British SOF establishment of 1940 to 1945 had been built, on the operational evidence of its origin, on the proposition that the conventional military bureaucracies of the major powers could not, by themselves, produce the unconventional operational instruments that the German doctrinal challenge of the late 1930s and early 1940s had created the operational requirement for. The establishment had been built, between June 1940 and July 1942, by a small number of unconventional officers operating in institutional positions of political protection — Churchill in London, Wavell in Cairo, Dill at the War Office, Alexander at Cairo after Wavell, Ritchie at the Eighth Army's deputy chief of staff's office in the moment of Stirling's July 1941 visit — and against the institutional preferences of the conventional army staff. The establishment had produced, across five years of operational deployment in the principal theaters of the war, the institutional and the doctrinal inheritance that the post-war national SOF traditions would build on. And then, with the war's conclusion, the same conventional army staff that had been institutionally reluctant about the SOF formations across the war had dissolved them, at administrative speed, in the autumn of 1945. The institutional vehicles that the wartime emergency had produced had not survived the wartime emergency. The doctrinal inheritance had survived, in the personal operational memory of the dispersed officers and operators who had served in the wartime formations and who would, in the next round of wars, supply the institutional resources for the reassembly of the operational tradition. The Yishuv's institutional position, on either side of the chapter's bracketing dates, had been the unusual position of a small national community whose own military establishment had been engineered, by deliberate institutional design across the period of the British collaboration, to absorb the doctrinal inheritance the wartime collaboration was transmitting and to preserve it through the post-war institutional dissolutions on the British side. The next chapter takes up the period — from the November 1947 United Nations partition vote through the 1948 founding war, the IDF's institutional consolidation of 1949 to 1953, and the operational and institutional opening that the 1956 Sinai Campaign would produce in 1957 — in which the doctrinal inheritance the present chapter has reconstructed would, on the Yishuv-and-then-Israeli side, be reassembled into the operational instrument that the rest of the book is about.[^ch3-68]

# Chapter 4 — Old New Threats (1948–1956)

*The Marginalization of Special Operations and the Doctrinal Vacuum, 1948–1953*

## 4.1 The Sinking of the King Farouk, October 22, 1948

The afternoon of the twenty-second of October 1948 found Yochai Bin-Nun aboard the Israeli Navy patrol vessel Ma'oz, off the coast of Gaza, approximately twelve kilometers north of the small port of el-Bureij. The thirty-four-year-old former Palyam officer had assumed command, six weeks earlier, of the small unit the Naval Service of the new Israel Defense Forces had constituted by merging the Palyam's explosive-boat squadron — which Bin-Nun himself had commanded since the autumn of 1947 — with the smaller and operationally less spectacular underwater-sabotage cadre that Yosef Dror had built in the closing months of the same year. The new formation, designated under the cover name Shayetet 13 (Flotilla 13), had been institutionally constituted in late August 1948 in the small Mediterranean port of Atlit, on the Carmel coast south of Haifa. By the late afternoon of the twenty-second of October it had not yet conducted an operation of its own. The Egyptian fleet, in the closing hours of Operation Yoav — the IDF's offensive against the Egyptian forces in the Negev, that had begun on the fifteenth and was scheduled to end with the United Nations–brokered ceasefire that would take effect at midnight — had provided the new flotilla with the operational opportunity its institutional founders had been waiting for.[1]

The Egyptian flagship Emir Farouk — a twenty-year-old destroyer of the type the Royal Navy had built in the closing years of the First World War and had sold to the Egyptian Navy in 1928 — had been spotted by Israeli aerial reconnaissance at first light on the twenty-second, escorted by a small minesweeper of the BYMS class, transiting north toward the Egyptian coast after delivering ammunition to the Egyptian land forces still holding positions in the southern Gaza pocket. By midday the two vessels had been brought, by the Israeli Navy's main surface combatant Ma'oz, into operational range of the four explosive boats — Italian-built motor torpedo boats of the type the Decima Flottiglia MAS had used during the Second World War — that Bin-Nun's Shayetet 13 had spent the preceding ten months learning to operate. At nine minutes past nine on the evening of the twenty-second, in the calm sea and the moonless dark of the new lunar month, the Ma'oz released the four explosive boats and the small extraction launch that would, if the operation succeeded, retrieve the four operators who would have ejected from their boats in the moments before impact. The two boats designated for the Emir Farouk both struck the destroyer's hull amidships. The third boat, originally targeted for the minesweeper, was redirected by Bin-Nun himself on his initiative as commander of the operation when he calculated that the minesweeper might survive the first attack and escape. Bin-Nun's boat struck the minesweeper. The ejection mechanism of his own boat failed. Bin-Nun jumped clear of the vessel at a distance of approximately fifty meters from the point of impact — less than half the minimum safe distance the Italian operational manual prescribed — and reached the surface, lightly burned but uninjured, in the moments before the boat detonated. The Emir Farouk sank within fifteen minutes. The minesweeper sank shortly afterward. The fourth boat picked up the three other operators and Bin-Nun. By the time the Egyptian and the British naval response had arrived on the scene, Shayetet 13's first operational deployment had concluded with the destruction of the principal warship of the Egyptian Mediterranean fleet.[^ch4-2]

The institutional consequences of the sinking of the Emir Farouk, for the Yishuv-to-Israel transition this chapter is reconstructing, were of two kinds. The immediate political consequence was the operational confirmation, on the eve of the United Nations–imposed ceasefire that would end the active phase of the 1948 war, that the Israeli Navy possessed the technical capability to inflict strategically significant damage on the principal warships of the Arab navies — a consequence Ben-Gurion himself, in a Knesset speech of November 1948 that would become canonical in the institutional histories of Shayetet 13, characterized as "the straw that broke the camel's back" in the Egyptian decision to accept the Rhodes armistice negotiations of February 1949.[^ch4-3] The longer institutional consequence, more important for the argument this chapter is constructing, was the operational confirmation — at the level of cabinet and senior military discussion in the autumn of 1948 — that the Palmach's wartime doctrinal absorption of the British and Italian special operations templates had produced, in the unit cohort that Bin-Nun commanded, operational capabilities the new Israeli state could not afford to dismantle without significant operational cost. The political logic that would shortly produce Ben-Gurion's order of the seventh of November — the order to dismantle the Palmach as an independent institutional formation and to absorb its personnel into the conventional formations of the new IDF — operated, in the autumn of 1948, against the operational evidence the Bin-Nun action had just supplied.[4]

The political logic prevailed. Sixteen days after the sinking of the Emir Farouk, on the seventh of November 1948, Ben-Gurion signed the order that dismantled the Palmach. The order's institutional consequences are the subject of the next section of this chapter. Its operational consequences — the dispersal of the Palmach's specialized doctrinal package across the conventional formations of the new IDF, the suppression of the unit's distinctive culture, and the absence of any institutional vehicle that could carry the special-operations inheritance the wartime collaboration with the British SOF establishment had transmitted to the Yishuv — would define the operational landscape of the new Israeli military for the next nine years, until the spring of 1957, when, as Chapter 5 will reconstruct, Avraham Arnan would propose to the General Staff the establishment of a small permanent reconnaissance unit modeled on the British SAS template that the Palmach's wartime training had absorbed. The institutional logic of the post-1948 Israeli military, in the period this chapter is about, ran in the opposite direction from the institutional logic the Palmach veterans of 1948 had expected it to run in.[^ch4-5]

## 4.2 The Palmach Dismantling Order, November 7, 1948

The order Ben-Gurion signed on the seventh of November 1948 was, in its bureaucratic language, an administrative instrument of three operative paragraphs. It announced the dissolution of the institutional headquarters of the Palmach — the command staff Sadeh had founded in May 1941 at the Mishmar Ha-Emek dining hall and that Yigal Allon, since his October 1945 succession to Sadeh, had commanded for three years. It ordered the absorption of the Palmach's six wartime brigades — the three infantry brigades (Yiftach, Negev, Harel), the Eighth Armored Brigade Sadeh had constituted in the spring of 1948, the Palyam (whose institutional separation from the conventional Palmach the previous chapter has reconstructed), and the Seventh Company that had consolidated the Palmach's intelligence and reconnaissance cadres — into the conventional command structure of the IDF General Staff. It dispersed the Palmach's central institutional functions — operational planning, doctrine development, training — across the regional commands and the General Staff branches of the new army. The order did not, in its administrative language, abolish the Palmach. It did not declare the unit dissolved. It did not, on the surface of the text Ben-Gurion signed, do anything more than reorganize the institutional position of an existing formation within a larger institutional structure that the new state's army had constructed in the months since the May 1948 declaration of independence.[^ch4-6]

What the order did, in the institutional reality of the months that followed, was end the Palmach as a distinct institutional formation. Allon, who had been the Palmach's commander since October 1945 and had led the unit through the entire 1948 war, recognized the administrative language of the order as the institutional vehicle for the unit's effective dissolution. He resigned within ten days. The Palmach's senior officer corps, in the institutional reorganization of the IDF General Staff that the Allon resignation triggered, found itself dispersed across the new army's conventional brigades and General Staff positions in arrangements that — in the post-war analysis of the institutional sociology of the Palmach diaspora — would be read as the deliberate political dilution of the unit's cohesive institutional culture. Yitzhak Sadeh, the Palmach's founder and the doctrinal architect of the wartime absorption of the British SOF template that the previous chapter has reconstructed, was reassigned in the institutional shuffle of the winter of 1948–1949 from his summer 1948 command of the Eighth Armored Brigade to the ambiguous and politically subordinate position the IDF General Staff designated, in the language of the period's institutional documentation, as "advisor to the Chief of Staff." The position carried no operational authority. Sadeh would hold it through 1949 and into 1950, would write the two Maarachot articles on commando doctrine the next section of this chapter will take up, and would, in the institutional rearrangement that followed Yadin's December 1952 resignation, find himself effectively retired from active military service. He would die in August 1952 at the age of sixty-two, an institutional figure the new IDF's leadership had largely ceased to consult.[^ch4-7]

The political motivations for the seventh-of-November order have been the subject of a substantial post-war scholarly literature. The literature divides, in its institutional reconstruction of Ben-Gurion's decision, into three principal interpretive schools. The first school — represented in its mature form by Uri Ben-Eliezer's Emergence of Israeli Militarism of 1995 — locates Ben-Gurion's motivation in the doctrine of mamlachtiyut (sovereignty, or "statehood") that Ben-Gurion himself, in the political writings of the 1940s and early 1950s, had elaborated as the foundational principle of the new state's institutional architecture. The principle's operational consequence for the new state's military was that a sovereign state, in Ben-Gurion's reading, could not tolerate the existence of politically affiliated armed formations within its sovereign territory. The Palmach's institutional bond with the United Kibbutz Movement — the political-economic federation of kibbutzim that, in the early 1950s, would become the institutional core of the left-wing party Mapam — was, in Ben-Gurion's mamlachtiyut reading, the institutional condition under which the Palmach had to be dismantled. The second school — represented in Dov Tamari's Armed Nation of 2012 — locates the motivation in the more immediately political fact that Ben-Gurion's own party, Mapai, was in the autumn of 1948 in an institutional rivalry with the United Kibbutz Movement, and that the Palmach's institutional sympathies for the kibbutz movement made it, in Ben-Gurion's calculation, an unreliable instrument of Mapai's political program. The third school — represented in Yoav Gelber's Why Was the Palmach Disbanded? of 1986 — locates the motivation in Ben-Gurion's strategic judgment that the Palmach's specifically counterinsurgency-oriented operational doctrine, however effective it had been against the Arab partisan formations of the 1947–1948 inter-communal phase of the conflict, was inadequate for the conventional inter-state war that the Arab regular armies' invasion of May 1948 had transformed the operational character of the campaign into. The three interpretations are not mutually exclusive. In the institutional account this chapter is constructing, all three motivations are taken to have operated, in varying weights at different stages of the autumn of 1948, on Ben-Gurion's decision.[^ch4-8]

What concerns the argument of the present chapter, more than the question of which of the three motivations weighed most heavily on Ben-Gurion in the autumn of 1948, is the institutional question of what the order's execution did to the doctrinal package the Palmach had carried out of its wartime collaboration with the British SOF establishment. The institutional answer, on the operational evidence of the years 1948 to 1953 that the rest of this chapter is reconstructing, was that the order's execution scattered the doctrinal package without preserving it. The Palmach's veteran officers and operators were dispersed across the new IDF's conventional formations in arrangements that did not permit the unit's distinctive doctrine to be transmitted at the institutional level. The Mistarvim platoons, the German Platoon, the Seventh Company's specialized intelligence and reconnaissance cadres — the institutional vehicles through which, in the wartime years 1941 to 1945, the Palmach had absorbed the SAS, the SOE Syrian Scheme, and the LRDG operational templates — were broken up in the institutional dispersal of 1948 and 1949. Their personnel went, in the institutional disposition of the new IDF, to conventional infantry battalions where the specialized doctrine they carried did not survive the institutional pressures of conventional regimental life. The new Israeli army would, in the closing years of the 1940s and the early 1950s, operate as a conventionally organized institutional formation in which the doctrinal inheritance the Palmach had carried out of the war existed only in the private operational memories of dispersed individuals.[^ch4-9]

This institutional outcome, the chapter argues, was the most consequential operational fact of Ben-Gurion's seventh-of-November order. Yaakov Markovitzki, in his 1989 institutional history Palmach's Special Ground Units, makes the argument with characteristic analytical precision. The Palmach, Markovitzki writes, "was not a special operations force." It had not been founded as one. It had not, in its institutional self-understanding through the 1940s, identified itself as one. But the wartime operational collaboration with the British SOF establishment had produced, in the unit, an institutional body of knowledge that, by the closing years of the Mandate period, had no operational equivalent anywhere else in the Yishuv's military apparatus. The knowledge — irregular warfare and night combat and demolition; intimate familiarity with the terrain of Palestine and the surrounding Levant; identity-deception capabilities developed in the German Platoon and the Mistarvim under the SOE's clandestine direction — had been absorbed across five years of operational deployment. It would, after the dispersal of November 1948, take more than a decade to reconstitute. The institutional vehicle through which the reconstitution would, eventually, occur — Sayeret Matkal under Avraham Arnan, established in late 1957 — would, in its institutional founding, draw not on a continuous institutional inheritance from the Palmach but on the private operational memories of a few dispersed Palmach veterans who had been carrying the doctrinal package, in their own individual ways, across the institutional dispersal years.[^ch4-10]

Ben-Gurion's seventh-of-November order, in other words, did not extinguish the Yishuv's wartime SOF inheritance. It privatized it. The doctrinal package the Palmach had absorbed across the war years became, on the eighth of November 1948, the property of the dispersed individuals who had served in the Palmach's specialized cadres. The institutional vehicle that had carried the doctrinal package — that had carried it institutionally, doctrinally, in the form of standing units and training programs and operational practices that could be reproduced and extended — was gone. The reconstitution of the institutional vehicle would have to wait, in the operational history that the rest of the chapter and the next chapter reconstruct, until the spring of 1957.[^ch4-11]

## 4.3 The Founding Doctrine of the IDF, 1949–1953

The institutional architecture of the new IDF was constructed, in the years between the end of the active phase of the 1948 war and the spring of 1957, in three principal documents that successive Chiefs of Staff and Ministry of Defense Directors-General signed into operational force. The first was Ben-Gurion's own national security doctrine, formulated in the long memoranda the prime minister and minister of defense drafted across 1949 and 1950 and published in the consolidated form of the operational papers known, in the institutional documentation of the period, as the "Five Pillars of Israeli National Security." The five pillars — deterrence against escalation through the projection of disproportionate response; the construction of a sophisticated strategic intelligence apparatus that would provide Israel with advance notice of Arab military planning; a multilayered defensive system along the new state's borders; the formation of a small first-rate standing conscript army backed by a large reserve mobilization apparatus; and an offensive war doctrine that would, on the outbreak of war, take the fighting across the enemy's territory and use overwhelming concentrated force to reach a rapid and decisive conclusion — became, across the 1950s and into the 1960s, the institutional framework within which the IDF's branch-level doctrines were elaborated.[^ch4-12]

The second document was Yigael Yadin's reserve-army architecture, formulated by the second Chief of Staff during his three-year tenure of January 1949 to December 1952. Yadin, who had served as the Haganah's chief of operations in the 1948 war and who had been promoted to the chief-of-staff position on the recommendation of Ben-Gurion himself, brought to the institutional reconstruction of the new army a strategic insight that the political conditions of the new state had made operationally unavoidable. The state, in the years 1949 to 1952, could not afford a large standing army. The economic burden of the absorption of approximately seven hundred thousand Jewish immigrants between 1948 and 1951 — most of them indigent refugees from the displaced-persons camps of Europe or from the Arab countries that had withdrawn their citizenship after the founding of the Jewish state — had stretched the new state's institutional capacity to its operational limits. The state could not afford, simultaneously, to fund a large standing military, an immigrant-absorption apparatus, and the basic institutional infrastructure of a sovereign state. Yadin's solution, formalized in the Hok Sherut Bitachon (Defense Service Law) of 1949 and in the institutional reorganization of the IDF that followed, was the small standing army backed by a large reserve mobilization apparatus that the fourth pillar of Ben-Gurion's national security doctrine had specified. Conscripts would serve, on the Yadin model, for three years (men) or two years (women) in the standing army's combat units. After the conclusion of their conscription service, they would remain liable to annual reserve duty until the age of fifty-five for combat soldiers and longer for specialist personnel. The reserve obligation produced, on the operational paper of the period's military demographics, an army of approximately 250,000 mobilizable personnel against a standing force of approximately 70,000. The reserve architecture was Yadin's principal institutional contribution to the new state's military. It would survive, with adaptations, into the twenty-first century.[^ch4-13]

The third document — and the one that mattered most for the operational landscape this chapter is reconstructing — was the doctrinal restructuring that Yadin's successor, Mordechai Maklef, signed into operational effect during the brief eleven months of his chief-of-staff tenure between December 1952 and December 1953. Maklef's appointment had been, by the standards of the institutional succession of the new state's military, politically charged. Yadin had resigned on the seventh of December 1952 over a budget dispute with the Mapai-led cabinet — the cabinet, citing the state's fiscal emergency in the closing months of the immigration absorption crisis, had ordered the IDF to reduce its standing budget by approximately twenty-five percent at a moment when the chief of staff considered the standing army to be already under-equipped and under-trained for the operational requirements of the post-armistice period. Yadin, in his resignation letter to Ben-Gurion, identified the cabinet's budget decision as institutionally incompatible with the operational responsibilities the chief of staff had been given to discharge. He left the army. Ben-Gurion appointed Maklef — a Haganah veteran, a British army veteran of the Second World War, and, perhaps as importantly, a member of Ben-Gurion's own Mapai party — to succeed him.[^ch4-14]

Maklef's institutional consequence, in the operational history this chapter is constructing, was less the brevity of his tenure than the doctrinal framework his eleven months in office produced. In the closing months of 1952 and the opening months of 1953, Maklef convened a series of institutional discussions of what the new army's branch-level priorities should be. The discussions — reconstructed in Amiram Oren's 2002 archival study of the IDF's Order-of-Battle Assessment documents and in Noam Tibon's Maarachot article of 2011 — produced, by the spring of 1953, the doctrinal document that would become known, in the institutional usage of the period, as the "Four Strike Forces" assessment. The document identified four branch-level forces as the IDF's operational priorities for the second half of the 1950s. The first was a strategic-intelligence apparatus that could provide the political and military leadership with advance notice of Arab military planning at the operational scale. The second was an air force capable of delivering decisive strikes against the air and ground forces of the surrounding Arab states. The third was an armored corps capable of conducting offensive armored operations against the conventional formations of the Arab armies. The fourth — and the operational element that mattered most for this chapter's argument — was a paratrooper force dedicated to special operations behind enemy lines.[^ch4-15]

The fourth strike force was, in the doctrinal logic of the Maklef document of 1953, the IDF's institutional answer to the operational requirement for special operations capability. The institutional logic the document operated on was straightforward. The new Israeli army required, in the operational scenarios its strategic-intelligence apparatus would identify, an institutional vehicle for operations behind enemy lines — airfield raids, communication-infrastructure sabotage, deep-reconnaissance and intelligence-collection missions of the kind the British SOF establishment of 1940 to 1945 had pioneered and that the IDF's potential adversaries in the surrounding Arab states would themselves, by the early 1960s, begin to develop dedicated commando capabilities to conduct. The institutional vehicle the document specified for the role was the paratrooper force. The paratroopers, in the Maklef doctrine, would be airborne-inserted behind enemy lines for the duration of the operational period. They would conduct the kind of operations the British SAS had conducted in the western desert in 1941 and 1942. They would, on the Maklef model, be the IDF's special-operations force.[^ch4-16]

The Maklef doctrine had three institutional consequences that defined the operational landscape of the IDF for the rest of the 1950s. The first was the institutional confirmation that the IDF would not, in its founding doctrine, possess a dedicated SOF formation of the British SAS model that the Palmach's wartime training had absorbed. The doctrinal package the Palmach had carried out of its 1941–1942 collaboration with the SAS, the SOE, and the LRDG would not, in the Maklef institutional disposition, be reconstituted at the unit level. Instead, the operational responsibilities the British dedicated SOF units had performed in the Second World War would, on the Israeli side, be assigned to the paratrooper force — a force structured, in the institutional sociology of the period, as an elite infantry formation operating at battalion scale rather than as a small permanent special-operations cadre operating at company or sub-company scale. The institutional difference was substantial. The British SAS that the Palmach had collaborated with in 1942 had operated, at its institutional peak, with two regiments of approximately three hundred operators each. The IDF paratrooper force that the Maklef doctrine designated as the Israeli SOF equivalent would, by the mid-1950s, operate at brigade strength — three battalions of approximately five hundred operators each. The institutional scale was different. The institutional logic was different. The operational character of the force that would result was different.[^ch4-17]

The second consequence was the institutional positioning of the infantry branch — the conventional ground-force backbone of the IDF in the late 1940s — as a secondary rather than a primary operational vehicle.
