The four surviving operators of the team broke under interrogation in the days following Ilan's suicide. The Aman signals-intelligence apparatus along the Syrian front was operationally compromised. The institutional fallout — the cabinet investigation Prime Minister Moshe Sharett initiated in the closing days of December 1954, the institutional indictment Sharett directed against Gibli for criminal negligence in the operation's planning, the institutional rupture that the Sharett indictment produced between the political and military leaderships — would persist as an institutional fault line through 1955 and into the institutional rearrangement that Ben-Gurion's return to the prime ministership in November 1955 would produce.[^ch4-62]

The institutional consequences of the Lavon Affair and the Uri Ilan suicide, taken together, were the institutional consequences of the operational and institutional immaturity of the IDF's clandestine and signals-intelligence apparatus by the closing months of 1955. The institutional vehicles the Maklef 1953 doctrinal framework had designated for the strategic-intelligence and special-operations function — the Aman directorate in its post-December 1953 institutional configuration, the paratrooper-as-SOF concept that Sharon's 890th Battalion was operationally executing, the regional preventive units that Yarkoni's Sayeret Shaked exemplified — had each, in their distinctive institutional ways, demonstrated through the operational record of 1954 and 1955 the operational limits the institutional framework was operating under. The strategic-intelligence apparatus could not, on the Operation Susannah and Operation Cricket evidence, conduct sustained clandestine operations against the surrounding Arab states without producing operational disasters of institutional consequence. The paratrooper-as-SOF apparatus could conduct sustained reprisal operations against limited tactical targets but could not, on the institutional evidence the 890th Battalion's operational record was producing, perform the strategic-depth special-operations function that the Maklef framework had assigned to it. The regional preventive units could perform their narrow operational mission within their designated geographical sectors but could not, on the institutional evidence the institutional sociology of the period was producing, substitute for the dedicated SOF formation the institutional framework continued to lack. The institutional vacuum the November 1948 dismantling had produced was, by the closing months of 1955, becoming visible — at the institutional level of the IDF's senior officer corps and at the political level of the cabinet's defense decisions — as an operational vacuum that the existing institutional vehicles could not, on the evidence the operational record was producing, fill.[^ch4-63]

4.[^ch4-insert-7] From Commando to Sayeret

In 1950, Ma'arachot, the journal of the General Staff, published an article by Moshe Dayan.[^ch4-insert-1] The title announced its subject: "The Commando Battalion Raids Lod." The author was the army's rising star. The battalion was his own 89th, whose war Chapter 3 followed. The article walked its readers back through the raid that had carried the battalion into Lod in the summer of 1948. Dayan needed no Hebrew word for what his raiders had been. He wrote the loanword as if it had always been Hebrew, in the army's house organ, under his own name. Within seven years, the same army would field its most secret unit under a different kind of name. It named that unit not for what it did, but for what it answered to. How the army traveled from the first name to the second is the story of this section.

The word was not a passing loan. Ma'arachot had introduced the type in September 1942, in a study of the British commandos titled "Strike Companies."[^ch4-insert-2] The editors treated the commando as a model worth studying, and from that issue on the word belonged to Hebrew military writing. The war of 1948 spread it across the order of battle. Dayan's 89th carried it as a formal designation, and a commando platoon fought in the 12th Battalion. One southern formation, the Beasts of the Negev, carried the double title of a reconnaissance and commando force: the two words side by side, not yet rivals.[^ch4-insert-3] A young army that wanted to praise its raiders praised them in commando's name.

The word also outlived the war. In the early 1950s, the army argued over its failing raids, and the argument ran through the same vocabulary. Yitzhak Sadeh took to print in favor of commando forces, and Dayan did the same.[^ch4-insert-4] Sadeh had built the Palmach, and the word his old movement had sanctified would defeat the one he now championed. The reprisal record that opened this chapter gave their case its urgency. The remedy on the table bore a name, and the name was commando. Nothing in the military Hebrew of 1953 pointed anywhere else.

Why, then, did the word not stick to the units the army built next? Part of the answer lies a decade earlier, and I flag it as my hypothesis rather than my finding. The Palmach had loaded a different term with prestige: siyur, reconnaissance, the scout's craft of moving, seeing, and returning unseen. In the Haganah and the Palmach, siyur became a synonym for sabotage operations behind enemy lines.[^ch4-insert-5] A siyur in that world meant more than looking: it meant arriving unseen, striking, and walking home before light. The company that raided the British coast-guard station at Givat Olga in November 1945 drew what the Palmach considered the best of its scouts.[^ch4-insert-6] The word for scouting came to cover the act of raiding, and the habit fit the movement's cult of navigation and knowledge of the land. No document in my sources ties that habit to the army's later choice of names. I read the prestige of siyur as the permissive condition: the soil in which a strange naming could later look natural.

A sayeret (plural sayarot) is a reconnaissance unit, the noun Hebrew builds from siyur. On the eve of the change, the name promised nothing. Golani formed a Sayeret Golani in 1950, and the unit did routine security work, not elite raiding.[^ch4-insert-7] One account counts three command-level sayarot in the same year; the trail is thin, and I flag it rather than build on it. Competing traditions crown one formation or another of those years as the first sayeret; I treat that contest as folklore, not as evidence. The army's most famous raiders, meanwhile, carried no such name at all. Unit 101, whose short life this chapter has traced, went by the plainest label the army had: a unit. In 1953, then, the ledger of names was clear: commando named the raiding tradition, sayeret named the scouts and the border watchers. The paratroopers were about to cross the two.

The crossing began with a platoon. The previous section left Meir Har Zion at the head of Company A. In those same years, Battalion 890 raised a reconnaissance platoon around Har Zion, and a standing company followed. Micha Ben-Ari, known as Kapusta, recalled the founding decision without ornament. "Har Zion and I decided that we had to establish the sayeret," he testified. "The role was mainly commando, and less intelligence-gathering."[^ch4-insert-8] The testimony survives in the brigade's heritage material, and I use it for the actors' language rather than for dates. The founders knew what they were building: a raiding force under a scout's name. Reconnaissance, by the founder's own account, was the smaller share of the work.

The same heritage record preserves the moment of conversion in one sentence. A veteran commander recalled the decision "this time to establish a reconnaissance company (a palsar) for special missions in the paratroopers' brigade, in short, a brigade sayeret of the paratroopers."[^ch4-insert-9] A palsar, from plugat siyur, is a reconnaissance company on a brigade's establishment. The sentence deserves a second look. A slot named for reconnaissance received the mission of special operations, and the long designation collapsed, in the telling, into one word: the abbreviation was the baptism. The record resists a firm date. The platoon belongs to 1954; the heritage accounts place the standing company in 1955; the commander who recalled its founding spoke of 1956. Where the testimonies split, I decline to invent a year. They agree on the substance: between 1954 and 1956, the paratroopers turned a reconnaissance slot into a raiding unit and called it a sayeret.

Moshe Dayan, by then chief of staff, made the local choice general. He determined that the new elite units would stand as brigade reconnaissance units. No one above him needed persuading; he was the persuader. One retired general later judged that this decision and its execution "constituted the concept of the sayarot that endures in the IDF to this day, even though the unit's purpose and missions bear no connection to reconnaissance."[^ch4-insert-10] On that reading, Dayan knew that the word and the work did not match. He chose the modest label with open eyes and wrapped a raiding force in the gray name of a support function. The choice, on this account, was camouflage from the day of its birth.

My reading of Dayan's Lod article points another way.[^ch4-insert-11] The Dayan of 1950 drew no line between reconnaissance and commando. In his prose, the man who finds the enemy and the man who strikes him are one man. On that reading, the name hid nothing, because in the namer's mind there was nothing to hide. The two readings assign different minds to the same act. Under the first, the name is a strategy; under the second, a soldier's indifference to categories. An order in the archives could settle the matter, and none has surfaced. So I let the readings face each other and hold on to what they share. Under either one, the army acquired an elite unit that wore a workaday name.

Whichever reading holds, the label did institutional work. A reconnaissance company was a legitimate line on any brigade's establishment. Doctrine required it, staffs understood it, and budgets carried it without debate. An officer who asked a small conscript army for commandos invited a fight over roles and privilege. An officer who filled a reconnaissance slot invited no fight at all. The slot supplied manpower, equipment, and a mission vague enough to cover almost anything. Secrecy gained as well: a unit listed as reconnaissance drew none of the questions a unit listed as commando would have drawn. The modest name gave an immodest unit a place to live. This is the survival wrapper, and the chapters ahead will meet it again.

Other armies knew the politics of unit names. The SAS took its name from a unit that never existed, a fictitious parachute brigade that the deception officer Dudley Clarke invented to mislead Axis intelligence.[^ch4-insert-12] When the British command folded its Commandos into "Special Service Battalions," the units fought for the old word and kept it.[^ch4-insert-13] Britain's Long Range Desert Group and the American long-range reconnaissance patrols in Vietnam were raiders under reconnaissance labels.[^ch4-insert-14] In each case the modest name described a real share of the work and never spread beyond the unit that bore it. The British units kept their name by fighting for it; the Israeli units never had to fight, because the name they wore asked for nothing. Only in Israel did the label become the name of the genre. Commando, whose Boer birth the Introduction traced, had reached Hebrew first. The word that stayed was sayeret.

I read this history of two words as the book's argument in miniature. No formal naming decision has surfaced in the record I have assembled, and I treat the absence itself as the finding. Armies write down what they decide; they do not write down what they assume. A permissive legacy prepared the ground: the Palmach's word outlived the Palmach, and the tradition Ben-Gurion had dissolved won the naming war against the British template he preferred. A cluster of decisions between 1954 and 1956 fixed the form. A wrapper that worked proved too useful to discard. What no one decided, no one could later repeal. Commando survived as the name of a skill, not of units: the course the previous section described taught commando fighting to men who would serve in sayarot. This is the pattern.

The label also multiplied. Once the paratroopers had a sayeret, every brigade and command could ask for one. The next section follows one of the first, Sayeret Shaked, into the Negev. Then the label stretched until it thinned. By 1998, the army's own dictionary offered "a sayeret in an infantry brigade" as its example of a crack unit that is not a special force.[^ch4-insert-15] The word that had cloaked the army's raiders now covered any good infantry. The units that stayed special had to reach for other markers.

Two dates close the arc. In 1957, the army founded the unit this section's opening promised. It named that unit, once more, not for its missions but for the body it answered to; Chapter 5 tells the story. In 2015, the army reached past the sayarot for the older word. It raised a Commando Brigade and gave the formation the number 89, in memory of Dayan's battalion.[^ch4-insert-16] The circle that opened in Ma'arachot in 1942 closed there.

## 4.8 The Sinai Campaign and the Institutional Opening, October 1956 – Spring 1957

The institutional decision the IDF General Staff authorized in the summer of 1956 to constitute, within the Paratroopers Brigade's institutional structure, a small specialized reconnaissance unit operationally distinct from the conventional paratrooper battalions was the institutional decision that produced Sayeret 5173 — the brigade-level reconnaissance unit that would, in the operational reality of the Sinai Campaign of October–November 1956 and in the institutional history of the post-Sinai Israeli special-operations apparatus, become the operational and personnel precursor to the institutional vehicles the post-1957 reckoning would produce. The decision's institutional context was the operational record of the 890th Battalion's reprisal operations through 1954 and 1955. Sharon, in his institutional position as the brigade's senior officer and in the institutional autonomy his operational reputation had earned him, had been advocating since the closing months of 1955 for the institutional constitution of a small reconnaissance unit that could conduct, at the brigade-internal level, the deep-reconnaissance and target-identification operations the 890th Battalion's reprisal operations had been depending on. The institutional decision the General Staff authorized in the summer of 1956 — the institutional decision that took the form of Sharon's personal request to two of his Unit 101 cadre veterans, Meir Har-Zion and Micha Ben-Ari (whose nom-de-guerre was Kapusta, "Cabbage"), to constitute the brigade reconnaissance unit at the Camp Sataf base that had served, in 1953, as Unit 101's founding facility — was the institutional consolidation of the operational practice the Unit 101 cadre had been developing under different institutional designations for three years.[^ch4-64]

Sayeret 5173 was, in the institutional intent Sharon and Har-Zion articulated in the institutional discussions of the unit's founding period, an SAS-style formation. The institutional model Sharon and Har-Zion explicitly invoked, in the documentation Micha Ben-Ari (Kapusta) would subsequently include in his memoir Not Every Bullet Kills, was the British Special Air Service in its post-war institutional configuration. The unit's operational mandate was the conduct of strategic-depth reconnaissance, target-identification, and direct-action raids in support of the Paratroopers Brigade's operational deployments. The unit's institutional structure — three platoons of approximately fifteen operators each under the platoon commands of Efraim Bar, Tzviki Nur, and Dov Tamari — was institutionally distinct from the conventional battalion organization the rest of the brigade operated under. The unit's training program was institutionally heterodox in the manner the Unit 101 Sataf training cycles had pioneered. The institutional location of the unit's facility at Camp Sataf — physically remote from the Paratroopers Brigade's main base at Tel Nof — was deliberately chosen, in the institutional intent of the founding period, to maintain operational and institutional independence from the conventional discipline of the regular paratrooper service. The institutional pattern Unit 101 had established in August 1953 was, in the institutional configuration Sayeret 5173 was given in the summer of 1956, formally institutionalized at the brigade level.[^ch4-65]

The institutional distinction Sharon and Har-Zion drew, in the institutional documentation of Sayeret 5173's founding period, between the unit's operational mandate and the operational mandate of the dedicated intelligence-collection SOF that the IDF would, in the spring of 1957, authorize Avraham Arnan to constitute, was an institutional distinction of considerable consequence for the institutional history this book is reconstructing. Sharon's institutional vision for Sayeret 5173 was the institutional vision of an SAS-style raid unit — a formation oriented toward direct-action operations, oriented toward operational engagement with the enemy at the target's physical location, oriented institutionally toward the operational culture that the Unit 101 cadre had developed through the reprisal years. The institutional vision that Arnan would, in the post-Sinai reckoning of the spring and summer of 1957, propose for the unit that would shortly be designated Sayeret Matkal — a clandestine intelligence-collection formation oriented toward operations whose operational success depended on remaining undetected, oriented institutionally toward the operational culture that Arnan himself had absorbed through his Mossad LeAliyah Bet service in the early 1950s and his Aman Unit 154 service in the Safed northern branch through 1953 and 1954 — would be a substantially different institutional vision. The institutional distinction between the two visions — between the SAS-style raid-and-direct-action unit and the SAS-style deep-reconnaissance-and-clandestine-intelligence unit — would persist, across the institutional history of the post-1957 Israeli special-operations apparatus, as one of the principal axes along which the IDF's elite-unit ecosystem would organize itself.[^ch4-66]

The Sinai Campaign of 29 October to 8 November 1956 was, in its institutional and operational consequences for the IDF's special-operations apparatus, the operational test of the Maklef 1953 doctrinal framework that had designated the paratroopers as the IDF's principal special-operations force. The opening operational maneuver of the campaign — the parachute jump of the 890th Battalion at the Mitla Pass on the afternoon of the twenty-ninth of October — was the institutional showcase of the paratrooper-as-SOF concept. At 15:00 on the afternoon of the twenty-ninth, sixteen Douglas DC-3 transport aircraft of the Israeli Air Force took off from the Tel Nof airbase, each aircraft carrying approximately twenty-four operators of the 890th Battalion under the operational command of Lieutenant Colonel Rafael "Raful" Eitan. The aircraft maintained low-altitude flight along the Negev's southern approaches to evade Egyptian radar detection. At approximately 17:00, the aircraft reached the operational drop zone — the Parker Memorial site at the eastern entrance of the Mitla Pass, approximately two hundred kilometers behind the Egyptian forward lines in the central Sinai Peninsula. The 395 operators of the 890th Battalion jumped into the desert sky. The institutional intent of the operation, in the operational planning the Paratroopers Brigade staff had conducted in the closing weeks of October, was to seize the operational chokepoint that the Mitla Pass represented along the principal east–west axis of the central Sinai and to force the Egyptian forces in the eastern Sinai into a simultaneous engagement on both their front line in the east and their rear in the central Sinai. The operational logic the institutional planning had operated under was the operational logic the Maklef 1953 doctrine had assigned to the paratrooper force — strategic-depth airborne insertion behind the enemy's main operational lines, in support of the conventional ground forces' main operational thrust.[^ch4-67]

What the operational reality at the Mitla Pass in the closing days of October and the opening days of November 1956 demonstrated, in the institutional reckoning the post-campaign analysis would produce, was that the operational logic the Maklef 1953 doctrine had assigned to the paratrooper force was operationally inadequate to the requirements of the wartime deployment. The 890th Battalion's airborne insertion on the afternoon of the twenty-ninth succeeded operationally — the unit reached the operational drop zone, established perimeter security, and held the Parker Memorial site through the night of the twenty-ninth into the morning of the thirtieth. The conventional armored thrust the airborne insertion was institutionally synchronized to support — the advance of the Paratroopers Brigade's overland column under Sharon's direct command from the eastern Sinai frontier at Kuntilla toward the Mitla Pass — encountered significant Egyptian resistance and was institutionally delayed beyond the operational planning the brigade staff had constructed the campaign timeline around. By the late afternoon of the thirtieth, with the overland column still distant from the Mitla Pass and with the operational situation at the Pass institutionally uncertain, Sharon authorized — without explicit authorization from the brigade or General Staff command — an exploratory infantry advance into the Mitla Pass itself. The advance was institutionally controversial at the time and would remain institutionally controversial in the post-campaign institutional analysis the IDF General Staff would conduct in the closing months of 1956 and through 1957. The exploratory force — approximately two reinforced companies of the 890th Battalion under the operational command of Major Mordechai "Motta" Gur — entered the Mitla Pass at approximately 12:30 on the afternoon of the thirty-first. They were ambushed by Egyptian forces in dug-in positions on the Pass's elevated southern wall. The engagement that followed — the Battle of the Mitla, in the institutional designation the IDF would assign to it — produced the highest single-engagement Israeli casualty figures of the Sinai Campaign. Thirty-eight operators of the 890th Battalion were killed in the engagement. More than one hundred and twenty were wounded. The Egyptian forces' positions on the Pass's southern wall were eventually destroyed by close-air-support strikes and by the institutional repositioning of the 890th's operational forces, but the institutional cost — to the brigade's institutional cohesion, to the operational reputation Sharon had constructed through the reprisal years, and to the institutional credibility of the paratrooper-as-SOF concept the Maklef 1953 doctrine had institutionalized — was substantial.[^ch4-68]

The institutional consequences of the Mitla engagement, in the post-campaign institutional reckoning the IDF General Staff conducted across November and December 1956 and through the closing months of the Sinai withdrawal of March 1957, were the institutional consequences of an operational failure that compelled the institutional reconsideration of the doctrinal framework the engagement had been conducted under. The institutional conclusions the General Staff drew, in the institutional documentation of the post-campaign analysis, were specific. The paratrooper force, in the institutional configuration the Maklef 1953 doctrine had constructed, was not — on the operational evidence of the Mitla engagement — institutionally adequate to perform the strategic-depth special-operations function the Maklef framework had assigned to it. The unit was institutionally too large, operationally too conventional in its training and doctrinal practice, and institutionally too vulnerable to the operational and command pressures of a wartime deployment to perform the operational function that a small permanent dedicated SOF formation could perform on the institutional model the British Special Air Service of the Second World War period had institutionalized. The institutional conclusion the General Staff drew — in the institutional documentation of the closing months of 1956 and the early months of 1957 — was that the IDF required, as a complement rather than as a replacement to the paratrooper force, a small permanent dedicated SOF formation oriented toward the strategic-depth operations the paratrooper force could not effectively conduct. The institutional vehicle the General Staff authorized for the constitution of the new formation, in the institutional discussions of the spring and summer of 1957, was the Aman directorate's collection branch — the institutional vehicle Avraham Arnan would, in the institutional decision the chief of Aman Yehoshafat Harkabi authorized in the closing months of 1957, exploit to constitute the small permanent dedicated formation that would shortly be designated Sayeret Matkal.[^ch4-69]

The chapter closes, then, on the institutional opening the Sinai Campaign's operational reckoning produced. The doctrinal vacuum that Ben-Gurion's seventh-of-November order had created in 1948 had persisted, through the institutional and operational history this chapter has reconstructed, across the nine years that separated the Palmach's dismantling from the post-Sinai institutional reckoning of 1957. The institutional vehicles the IDF had constituted in the interim — the Frontier Corps of September 1949, Dayan's Unit 30 of August 1951, Sharon's Unit 101 of August 1953 and its successor formation in the 890th Paratroopers Battalion from January 1954, Yarkoni's Sayeret Shaked of May 1955, Sayeret 5173 of the summer of 1956 — had each, in their distinctive institutional ways, performed institutional functions the doctrinal vacuum had created the operational requirement for. None of them had constituted the institutional vehicle the Sadeh 1950 Maarachot essays had proposed and that the institutional history of the British SAS the Palmach's wartime training had absorbed had institutionalized as the institutional pattern for dedicated SOF. The institutional vehicle the post-Sinai institutional reckoning would authorize — the institutional vehicle Arnan would, in the spring and summer of 1957, exploit the institutional opening the Mitla Pass operational failure had produced to constitute — would be that institutional vehicle. The institutional history of its founding, of its institutional and operational development across the late 1950s and the 1960s, and of the institutional and personnel paths through which the doctrinal package the Palmach's wartime training had absorbed would, by the institutional initiative of a small number of dispersed Palmach veterans and Aman officers who had been carrying the doctrinal package in their individual operational memories, be reconstituted at the institutional level the Israeli state's military had not, in the nine years since the November 1948 dismantling, succeeded in constituting — is the subject of the chapter that follows.[^ch4-70]

# Chapter 5 — The Second Entrepreneur

*Avraham Arnan, Sayeret Matkal, and the Birth of Israeli Special Reconnaissance, 1953–1973*

## Prologue: Givat Brenner, August 1952

On Wednesday, 20 August 1952, shortly after 9 p.m., Major General (ret.) Yitzhak Sadeh died of cancer at Ha-Sharon Hospital in Petah Tikva. He was sixty-two. The news caught many by surprise. Only his close friends had known he was ill. Sadeh — ha-Zaken, the Old Man — had not been in the public spotlight for years. Politicians, senior military officers, artists, and bohemians made their way through the night to the hospital. A small group of officers, most of them Sadeh's protégés from the Palmach years, formed an honor guard at the entrance and stood there until morning.[fn-prologue-1]

At 9:30 the next morning a curious group of men carried the coffin out of the hospital on their shoulders. Among them were Lieutenant General (ret.) Yaakov Dori, the first Chief of Staff of the Israel Defense Forces; the poet Nathan Alterman; the Knesset member Aharon Zisling; and a small contingent of Palmach veterans of the strike force Sadeh had founded eleven years earlier at the Mishmar HaEmek kibbutz dining hall. They placed the casket in a car that carried it the few miles to the Histadrut headquarters in Tel Aviv. The morning was hot and humid in the way that late August in Tel Aviv has always been. Twenty thousand Israelis stood outside the building, waiting their turn to file past the coffin and pay last respects.[^ch5-fn-prologue-2]

Shortly after 3 p.m., former Palmach officers carried their commander to a car that proceeded slowly down Allenby Street. Veterans of the unit, members of Mapam — the United Workers Party, in which the Palmach political tradition by then resided — and representatives of the Hapoel sports federation walked alongside the vehicle. Before it turned right onto King George Street the procession halted for a minute in front of the apartment building where the novelist Yosef Haim Brenner had lived; the lives of the two men had been woven together in the cultural geography of pre-state Jewish Palestine in ways the procession's pause acknowledged without explaining.

When the car reached Beit HaBima — the home of Israel's national theater — Major General Moshe Dayan and Major General (ret.) Yigal Allon stepped forward. Aided by four other senior officers, Dayan and Allon carried the man who had shaped both their lives to a military truck. This was the beginning of the formal military part of the funeral. At 4:30 p.m. the motorcade embarked on the last leg of Sadeh's journey — to the cemetery at Kibbutz Givat Brenner, twenty-five miles south of Tel Aviv. The convoy moved slowly enough for the mourners along the roads to salute the Palmach commander one last time. Yisrael Galili, the former Chief of Staff of the Haganah, Sadeh's commanding officer and close friend, told a journalist on the convoy: "The people love their heroes." The crowds, he said, reminded him of the funerals of Joseph Trumpeldor in 1920 and of Eliyahu Golomb in 1945 — the two foundational deaths of the pre-state Jewish military tradition that Sadeh had inherited from one mentor and the other.[^ch5-fn-prologue-3]

The funeral service at Givat Brenner began at 6:30 p.m. Sadeh, by then, was no longer at the center of Israel's security establishment. The entire state leadership nonetheless attended. Even Prime Minister David Ben-Gurion — Sadeh's political rival, the man who had ordered the dissolution of Sadeh's Palmach four years earlier, who had reassigned Sadeh in the institutional shuffle that followed to the ambiguous and politically subordinate position of "advisor to the Chief of Staff," and who in Sadeh's own private account of the period had effectively pushed him out of the army — stood in the front rank of mourners.

In his impassioned eulogy, Galili wove together the qualities that had made Sadeh the foundational figure of the Jewish armed forces of the inter-war and 1948 period. Sadeh had taught the youth, Galili said, the value of comradeship and had made them fall in love with the landscape of the country. He had taught them that danger could be kept at bay only by approaching it face to face. He had introduced the future commanders of the IDF to the principles of military reconnaissance, cultivated their shooting skills, and taught them how to lay ambushes, outflank a position, and storm an objective. For this, Galili continued, the nation owed Sadeh — for unveiling the virtues of its youth. As for his close friends, Galili concluded, they owed him for the human values he had instilled in them: for teaching them how to fight while hating war, for his firm stance against terror, for his friendship, for his love of life. A passionate, kind, noble, brotherly, and fatherly figure.[^ch5-fn-prologue-4]

Galili did not exaggerate. An innovative tactician, a charismatic leader, and a pragmatist who consistently prioritized collective goals over his individual ambitions, Yitzhak Sadeh had shaped the Haganah from its early days. The tactics he developed — first during the Great Arab Revolt of 1936–1939, then as the commander of the Palmach from 1941 to 1947 — outlived him and shaped the trajectory of the IDF for the half-century that followed his death.

I open this chapter with Sadeh's funeral because the moment is the institutional hinge on which the chapter's argument turns. The first entrepreneur of the Israeli special operations tradition died at Givat Brenner in the late summer of 1952, surrounded by the men whose lives he had shaped and by the prime minister who had pushed him out of the army that had grown from his work. The second entrepreneur — Avraham Arnan, then a twenty-one-year-old junior officer of Aman, still nine months away from his appointment as commander of Unit 154's northern base in Safed — was not at the funeral. There is no documentary evidence that Arnan and Sadeh had ever met. The institutional thread between the two men was carried, through the intervening years, by David Elazar, who had served under Sadeh in the Palmach's Harel Brigade and would, within a decade, become Arnan's institutional protector in the General Staff that resisted the founding of Sayeret Matkal.

What follows is the institutional history of how that thread was carried, from the funeral at Givat Brenner in August 1952, through the years in Safed, through the institutional shock of February 1960, through the founding of the unit Arnan would build, and on to the operational moment fifteen years later — the assassination raid in West Beirut on the night of 9 April 1973 — at which the unit Arnan had founded had drifted so far from its founding mission that, six months later, when the Yom Kippur War broke out, the State of Israel could no longer draw on the specific capability for which Arnan had built it.

## 5.1 A Book on a Desk in Safed

The book was the Hebrew translation of The Phantom Major: The Story of David Stirling and His Desert Command, by the American journalist Virginia Cowles. It had been published in English in 1958. It had been translated into Hebrew shortly afterward by the IDF's Maarachot publishing house. By the early 1960s it sat on the desks of officers across the Israeli military, and by the late 1960s it would be distributed by the founding commander of the Sayeret Matkal to every operator who completed the unit's selection course, a tradition that would persist into the 1990s. But on a particular morning in the summer of 1959, in the small intelligence office of the northern base of Aman's Unit 154 in Safed, the book was, for the first time, being read carefully by a twenty-eight-year-old captain named Avraham Arnan, who was about to do something with what he was reading that no one else in the Israel Defense Forces had thought to do.[1]

Arnan was at that point the commander of Unit 154's northern collection branch. Unit 154 was Aman's classical human-intelligence service, the IDF's principal apparatus for running agents in Syria, Lebanon, and Jordan. Arnan's branch ran the agent network across the northern frontier. The work was conducted out of an unmarked apartment building on a side street in Safed, two miles from the Lebanese border, and it consisted, in the main, of the routine of any HUMINT station: meeting handlers, processing reports, evaluating new recruits, occasionally crossing the border with one of the operators to verify the existence of a piece of physical infrastructure that an agent had described.

It was not, in Arnan's increasingly impatient view, very useful work. The agents Unit 154 ran in Syria and Lebanon, by his assessment, supplied intelligence that ranged from the trivial to the actively misleading. The reports that came back from the field described border crossings that had not happened, troop movements that were ordinary garrison rotations, and military installations whose existence the agent had inferred from public sources. The product was thin. The cost — in money, in handler time, in the constant risk that any agent in any moment might prove to be a Syrian double — was high. And it had recently become catastrophic.[^ch5-2]

In December 1954, four years before Arnan arrived at the Safed station, an attempt by Unit 154 to renew a wiretap on a Syrian communications line — a routine maintenance mission that the unit's military arm carried out periodically — had ended in disaster. The five-man team, four paratroopers and a Golani soldier named Uri Ilan, had been captured by a Syrian patrol that had stumbled on them en route to the line. They had been interrogated under torture in a Damascus prison. Uri Ilan had hanged himself in his cell, leaving behind a Hebrew note that the Syrians had not found and that the bereaved Israeli intelligence community would discover only after the bodies were returned: lo bagadeti — I did not betray. The note had become one of the foundational documents of the moral self-image of the Israeli intelligence community. The capture itself had become the foundational disaster of Israeli technical signals collection. From the day the Ilan team was lost, the IDF had ceased to send soldiers into hostile territory to maintain the wiretap network. The network had decayed. The Syrian end had begun to feed false traffic into the lines the Israelis were still able to read. By the time Arnan was reading Cowles in Safed in the summer of 1959 — six years after he had taken command of Unit 154's northern base in the autumn of 1953 — Israeli SIGINT against Syria was, in the assessment of the people doing the work, a wreckage.[^ch5-3]

The wreckage was not, however, what kept Arnan reading Cowles past midnight. What kept him reading was the operational architecture Cowles described — the strategic-depth reconnaissance teams that David Stirling had built in the Western Desert in 1941, the small teams of trained soldiers, never agents, never paid informants, but military operators in the literal sense, who infiltrated into the enemy's rear, lingered there for days or weeks, observed, recorded, sometimes sabotaged, and returned. The British had built such a force in 1941. The British had, by 1959, already disbanded it, then reconstituted it, then sent it through Malaya. The Australians and the New Zealanders had copied the model. The Americans were thinking about it. The Israelis, who needed the capability more urgently than any of them, had no such force at all.

What kept Arnan reading was the gap. The gap between what David Stirling's small force was designed to do — to bring back, by direct observation, the strategic intelligence that no agent could be trusted to bring back — and what the Israeli intelligence community of 1959 was, in the wake of the Uri Ilan disaster, no longer doing.

Sometime in the autumn of 1959, in conversation with a small circle of officers that included his old Palmach commander David Elazar — then a colonel commanding an armored brigade, later the IDF's chief of staff during the Yom Kippur War — and his predecessor at Unit 154's military arm, Avraham Dar, Arnan began to describe what he had read. The British had built a small unit. It had worked. The Israelis could build a small unit. It could work.

What he was proposing — over coffee, in a Tel Aviv kitchen, without authorization, without a budget, without a position on any IDF table of organization — was the founding of Sayeret Matkal. It would take him another two years to argue the proposal through every echelon of the General Staff. He would be told no, and he would be laughed at, by every senior officer who had not served under his predecessor in the Palmach. The unit, when it eventually came into existence, would be conducting its first selection course in a borrowed barracks at Camp Sirkin by the end of 1961. The first operational deployment would not come for another two years after that.

The chapter that follows is the story of how Avraham Arnan, with a copy of an English-language journalist's book on his desk and no other obvious institutional resource, built the most consequential elite military unit in the second half of the twentieth century history of the State of Israel. It is also the story of how that unit, by the spring of 1973 — fourteen years after the book had first been read in Safed — had drifted so far from what Arnan had built it to do that, when the Yom Kippur War broke out six months later, the very capability the unit had been founded to provide was the one capability the State of Israel could not draw on.

The chapter begins with the institutional wreckage out of which Arnan built. It ends with Spring of Youth, the operation that crowned the institutional drift.

## 5.2 The Pre-Arnan Wreckage, 1948–1956

The State of Israel had attempted to build special operations units before Arnan, and had failed. The eight years between the conclusion of the 1948 war and the Sinai campaign of 1956 are remembered, in the conventional Israeli military narrative, as the period in which Ariel Sharon's Unit 101 and its successor Battalion 890 of the Paratroopers conducted the cross-border reprisals that established the doctrine of Israeli deterrence. They were also, less remembered, the period in which the IDF stood up four discrete attempts to build an Israeli equivalent of the SAS and watched all four of them collapse.

The first attempt was Unit 30, established in August 1951 under the personal sponsorship of Moshe Dayan, then the commanding general of the IDF's Southern Command. Unit 30 was designed as a small force of selected paratroopers who would conduct reprisal raids across the southern border into the Egyptian-administered Gaza Strip in response to the cross-border infiltration that, by 1951, had become the principal security problem of the new state. The unit conducted, by the limited records that survived, perhaps four or five small operations over the course of its short institutional life. It was dissolved in August 1952, a year after its founding. The reasons for the dissolution are documented poorly. Dayan himself, in his memoir, devoted no more than a single sentence to the unit. What is clear is that Unit 30 had been a personal project of a single senior officer, that the project had not been institutionalized inside the IDF's order of battle, and that when Dayan moved out of the Southern Command in the summer of 1952 the unit had no institutional sponsor and therefore ceased to exist.[4]

The second attempt, two years later, was Unit 101 under Ariel Sharon. The story of Unit 101 has been told many times. It is the founding myth of the Israeli paratroop tradition, and within it the story of the Qibya raid of October 1953 — which produced sixty-nine Palestinian civilian deaths and an international scandal that shaped Israeli reprisal policy for the next decade — is the foundational ethical reckoning of the IDF's relationship to non-combatant casualties. Unit 101 lasted less than seven months as an independent formation. In January 1954 it was merged into the existing 890th Paratroop Battalion to form what would, under Sharon's continued command, become the Israeli paratroop tradition. The doctrine of small-unit cross-border reprisal that had defined Unit 101 was absorbed into the paratroopers. The institutional category of a small, separate, mission-specific elite force was not.[^ch5-5]

The third attempt was the small, secret offensive sabotage organization that Aman's Major General Benjamin Gibli established within Unit 131 between 1953 and 1954. Gibli's concept was modeled, more or less directly, on the British SOE of the Second World War — a clandestine cell network in Egypt, recruited from Egyptian Jews who had not yet emigrated to Israel, capable of conducting sabotage operations against Western interests in Egypt in a manner that would discredit the new Egyptian regime of Gamal Abdel Nasser in the eyes of the Western powers. The operation, executed in the summer of 1954 under the name Operation Susannah, was a disaster of nearly every kind. The Egyptian network was rolled up within forty-eight hours of its first attempt. Two of the operatives were hanged. The rest were imprisoned for years. The Israeli political establishment fractured over the question of who had given the order to activate the network, and the resulting Lavon Affair — named for Pinhas Lavon, the Israeli defense minister of the period, who was forced to resign — became the constitutional crisis of the first decade of the state. What is less remembered is that Operation Susannah was an attempted Israeli imitation of the British SOE doctrine of sabotage networks behind enemy lines, and that the imitation had failed comprehensively.[^ch5-6]

The fourth attempt was Sayeret Shaked, the southern-command reconnaissance unit that began as a small platoon under the 890th Paratroop Battalion in 1955 and grew, through a process of operational expansion under a succession of capable commanders, into the Israeli army's first sustainably institutionalized small-unit elite formation. Shaked, alone among the four pre-Arnan attempts, would survive. It would not, however, be the kind of unit Arnan had in mind. Shaked was a frontier-defense and counter-infiltration force, fighting at the southern border at battalion strength, operating in its own assigned sector, with no mission profile for deep reconnaissance into the Egyptian strategic depth. What David Stirling and the SAS had built — and what Arnan in his book on his desk was reading about — was something else entirely.[^ch5-7]

The fifth and sixth elements of the pre-Arnan landscape were the Sayeret Tzanchanim, the Paratroopers' brigade reconnaissance company, which by 1956 had become Sharon's principal cross-border instrument; and the post-1956 reorganization of the IDF that absorbed the lessons of the Sinai campaign and rebuilt the paratroop tradition around the campaign's most successful elements. By the time the dust settled in the late winter of 1956–1957, the IDF had three small-unit assets: the Paratroopers' brigade reconnaissance company (Sayeret Tzanchanim); the southern command's frontier-defense reconnaissance (Sayeret Shaked); and the small naval-commando unit that would, in 1960, be redesignated Shayetet 13. None of the three was designed to conduct strategic-depth reconnaissance against Syria. None of the three was designed to provide the specific kind of intelligence that the Uri Ilan disaster had taken away from the Israeli intelligence community. None of the three, in Arnan's developing view in Safed, was an answer to the problem he was watching unfold in his own daily work.

## 5.3 The 1954 Catastrophe and Its Long Echo

The Uri Ilan disaster was not, strictly speaking, the operational disaster Arnan inherited; it had taken place nearly five years before he reached Safed. It was, instead, the institutional disaster he inherited. What had happened in December 1954 had changed the IDF's posture toward technical signals collection in a way that, by the time Arnan was reading Cowles, had become a structural feature of Israeli intelligence rather than an event in its history.

The operational details of Tzartzar — the codename of the December 1954 mission — are themselves worth recovering, because they explain exactly what kind of capability the IDF had lost. The team that was sent across the Syrian border had consisted of four paratroopers and Uri Ilan, attached from Golani. The mission was technical: the existing wiretap installed on a Syrian military communications line required maintenance. The wiretap had been installed on a previous mission, undetected, several months earlier; it had been producing intelligence of high value on Syrian military deployments in the upper Galilee and on Syrian negotiations with Egypt regarding joint operations against Israel; and the wiretap's batteries had been calculated to last approximately six months. The maintenance mission was a routine extension of an ongoing operation. The team had been assigned because the IDF lacked any other formation capable of conducting such a mission.

The team had been compromised within hours of crossing the border. The Syrian forces had been waiting. There is, to this day, no consensus on the source of the compromise. Some sources have attributed the disaster to a leak in the Israeli operational planning chain. Others have attributed it to a chance encounter with a Syrian patrol that had been deployed for a different purpose. What is established beyond dispute is that the team had been captured, taken to Damascus, interrogated under torture, and four of the five had survived. Uri Ilan had not. Ilan had been the youngest of the five, eighteen years old at the time of the operation, and the only one who had not been able to bear the prospect of revealing operational information to his interrogators. The note he left behind — lo bagadeti, I did not betray — would be the title of three books over the next forty years.[^ch5-8]

The institutional response of the IDF was clear and consequential. The General Staff concluded — in a series of decisions taken between January and April 1955 — that the IDF would no longer send soldiers into hostile territory to maintain technical signals installations. The maintenance of existing installations would be left in place; the technical equipment would be allowed to degrade where it could not be replaced; the future of Israeli technical SIGINT against the principal Arab adversaries was, by the spring of 1955, a question with no obvious answer. The intelligence loss was substantial. Israeli SIGINT against Syria, the country's most active adversary in the immediate post-1948 period, declined sharply through 1955, 1956, and 1957. The 1956 Sinai campaign was conducted with substantially less intelligence on Syrian and Jordanian military movements than the IDF had possessed three years earlier.[^ch5-9]

The institutional response was, from a particular angle, rational. The IDF had attempted, with Tzartzar, to use a small ad-hoc team of conventional infantrymen — paratroopers and a Golani soldier, with no specialized training in the specific skills required for the mission — to perform an operation that, in any military with mature small-unit traditions, would have been performed by purpose-built operators. The team had not been the problem. The institutional category had been the problem. The IDF in late 1954 had not had operators of the kind the mission required. It had sent the closest substitute it possessed. The substitute had been inadequate.

What Arnan, reading Cowles in Safed in 1959, was beginning to formulate was not a return to the Tzartzar concept. It was a structural reform. What the IDF needed, in his developing view, was not another ad-hoc team. It was a permanent, institutionalized, purpose-built unit of operators trained from selection to specialize in exactly the kind of operation the IDF had stopped attempting. The wiretap maintenance of December 1954 was the mission. The David Stirling Long Range Desert Group of 1941 was the model. The combination of the two was the unit Arnan was about to argue into existence.

## 5.4 The Helicopter Window, 1956–1957

The third element of the pre-founding landscape was, of all things, a piece of equipment. Between 1956 and 1958, the Israeli Air Force took delivery of its first transport helicopters: a small fleet of Sikorsky S-58s of the type the United States Marine Corps had been flying for half a decade. The helicopters arrived at the IAF's Squadron 124, the IAF's first rotary-wing formation, under the command of a young captain named Uri Yarom whom the IAF's senior leadership regarded, in their own internal correspondence of the period, as a problem case. Yarom had been the IAF's most aggressive advocate, since the early 1950s, for an Israeli rotary-wing capability. He had been ignored, blocked, and finally — when the S-58s became available through American military aid in the wake of the 1956 Sinai campaign — grudgingly allowed to build the squadron he had been pushing for. Squadron 124 stood up in late 1956. Its early life was not a happy one. The IAF's fixed-wing leadership regarded the squadron as a stepchild. The aircraft were given limited maintenance priority. The pilots were assigned, when they were assigned anything, to missions that the fixed-wing squadrons had declined. Yarom, in his own later account, spent the first year of the squadron's existence looking for a customer.[10]

He found one. The customer, by the spring of 1958, was an emerging proposition from a junior intelligence officer in Safed. What Arnan had been arguing — in conversations with David Elazar, with Avraham Dar, with the small circle of officers willing to listen — was that the David Stirling model of strategic-depth reconnaissance required a method of insertion that the IDF did not currently possess. Stirling's force had used, in the Western Desert, lightly armored trucks across hundreds of kilometers of open desert that no Arab opponent had been able to police. The Israeli operational environment, by 1958, was different. The borders of the State of Israel were policed. The terrain between Israel and the Syrian and Lebanese strategic interior was traversable on foot but slowly, and at every kilometer the risk of detection rose. What the David Stirling model needed, to be transposed to the Israeli case, was an insertion method that could deliver operators at depth, at night, in a single sortie, into terrain the operators could then traverse on foot.

The helicopter, Arnan and Yarom concluded in late 1958, was that insertion method. The S-58 of Squadron 124 had the range to insert a four-man team thirty to forty kilometers across the Syrian border under cover of night. It had the lift to recover the team several days later from a designated extraction point. It had the speed to do both at altitudes that the Syrian air-defense network of 1958 could not reliably engage. What it required — in order to be useful for the kind of mission Arnan was proposing — was a small ground unit of operators whose selection, training, and operational planning were tailored to insert from a single helicopter at night, conduct a forty-eight to seventy-two-hour reconnaissance mission, and recover from a different helicopter at a different point.

The unit did not yet exist. The argument for it, however, had its first institutional ally. Yarom and Arnan, both junior officers, neither holding any institutional authority that would allow them to compel the IDF to build what they were proposing, became — over the course of 1959 and 1960 — the central pair of a small coalition of officers across the IAF, Aman, and the operational branches who began, quietly, to argue inside the General Staff that the IDF needed something it did not have.[^ch5-11]

What they were arguing was that the IDF needed Sayeret Matkal.

## 5.5 The Man

Avraham Arnan had been born Avraham Herling in Jerusalem on 29 December 1930, the youngest of eight siblings of Nechama and Eliezer-Dov Herling, in a religious family that was third generation in the Land of Israel. His grandfather Yaakov Yosef Herling had been one of the leaders of Agudat Yisrael in Jerusalem; the family owned the Varshavsky Hotel in Zion Square. He had been educated at the Mizrahi movement school and at the Bagrut school of Jerusalem, had spent two years at the Hebrew University, and had grown up moving through the institutions of religious Jerusalem in a way that none of his future Palmach comrades — kibbutzniks and labor-movement secularists almost to a man — had ever known. He was a member and instructor in the Scouts movement, Tnu'at HaTzofim, and had gone for agricultural training at a kibbutz before the institutions of religious Jerusalem could finish claiming him. His main hobby, by the family's own later recollection, was sayarut — reconnaissance.[12]

He had joined the Haganah at sixteen, in 1946. With the outbreak of the events in Jerusalem in 1948, he had completed an instructor's course and had been posted to the Moriah Battalion of the Etzion Brigade of the Haganah's field force — the Hish. He had fought in most of the sectors of the battle for Jerusalem: Atarot, Neve Yaakov, Sheikh Jarrah, Yemin Moshe. He had been lightly wounded in an attempt to break into the Old City through Jaffa Gate. His brother Yaakov had been killed in the attack on the Convoy of Ten on the road to Gush Etzion. It was only during the siege of Jerusalem, after his brothers Yehuda and Moshe had joined the Palmach, that Avraham followed them — and was posted to the Portzim Battalion of the Harel Brigade under Motke Ben Porat. He had been wounded a second time in the battle for the capture of Mount Zion. After he recovered he returned to the battalion, fought in the Ten Days Battles, and was wounded a third time near Har-Tuv. He commanded the Gachal — the foreign recruits — in his unit, by virtue of his Yiddish. In Operation Horev at the war's end, he was a platoon commander. He had been, by the war's end, a junior officer in his late teens whose military reputation rested on a single trait that everyone who had served with him in those years remarked upon: he was a dreamer.[12]

The dreamer characterization, in the Hebrew of the period, was not necessarily a compliment. Uri Milstein, recording the testimony of Sami Nachmias — the man who would, fifteen years later, become Sayeret Matkal's first operations officer and who had served alongside Arnan in the Harel Brigade in 1948 — would write that Arnan was "of fertile imagination but limited operational capacity, who would catch fire, and whose fantasies would begin to work overtime." The phrase is double-edged. The Israeli military culture of the 1940s and 1950s rewarded what its officers called practi — the practical, the executable, the achievable in the time allotted with the resources at hand. The Palmach veterans who had become, by the early 1950s, the senior officers of the new IDF tended to be — or at least to perform — that kind of soldier. Arnan was something else. He read books. He talked in concepts. He proposed ideas that were not, in any obvious institutional sense, possible. He was respected for his service in 1948 and tolerated, by his fellow Palmach veterans, for what they regarded as a charming peculiarity of imagination, but he was not, in the consensus of the senior officers who had to assign him work, a man on whom to base a battalion.[^ch5-13]

What he was, however, was Dado's friend. David Elazar, who would in 1972 become the chief of the general staff of the IDF and would in the autumn of 1973 carry the institutional weight of the Yom Kippur War to its conclusion, had served alongside Arnan in the Harel Brigade. The friendship had been forged in the brutal months of the Jerusalem siege — Bab al-Wad, Latrun, the breaking of the road — and it had survived everything that came after. By the time Arnan was at Safed in the summer of 1959, Elazar was a colonel commanding the armor school. By the time Arnan would be proposing the founding of Sayeret Matkal to a skeptical General Staff, Elazar would be the head of the operations branch. The structural fact that explains why Arnan's proposition was not laughed out of the General Staff entirely is not Arnan's eloquence, which everyone respected, or the analytical power of his proposal, which was real, but the fact that the second-highest operations officer in the IDF was prepared to defend the proposition in every meeting in which Arnan himself could not. Ehud Barak, who would join the unit a few years later and would eventually command it, would describe Arnan in his autobiography as "the heart and soul of Sayeret Matkal," with "a face made more arresting by eyes of different colors, one brown and the other a piercing green," and a "playful, almost bohemian relation to the constraints, structures, rules and regulations of the armed forces." That was the Arnan everyone who served under him remembered. The Arnan the General Staff dealt with, however, was the Arnan who, but for Elazar, would have been ignored.[^ch5-14]

Between his Palmach service and his arrival at Unit 154, Arnan had spent the year between November 1949 and January 1951 in the Mossad le-Aliya Bet, the clandestine organization that the Yishuv had built to bring Jewish refugees to Palestine in defiance of the British White Paper and that, after 1948, continued to operate the routes by which Jewish refugees from the Arab countries reached the State of Israel. After completing infantry officers' and reconnaissance courses in November 1949, Arnan was dispatched on an underground mission to bring up the Jewish community of Iraq through Iran. That experience — running operations across closed borders, building networks under conditions of constant surveillance, moving people across hostile terrain — was the substantive education in clandestine work that the IDF had not, in 1948 and 1949, been able to give him. He returned to Israel in January 1951, settled briefly at Kibbutz Kabri, and in 1953 was recalled to regular service and appointed commander of the northern base of Unit 154. The Mossad le-Aliya Bet network would, over the following decade, become the recruiting pool for the Mossad proper. Arnan, for reasons that the documentary record does not fully clarify, was directed instead to military intelligence. The transfer was, in retrospect, the institutional accident that produced Sayeret Matkal.[^ch5-15]

## 5.6 The Conversation with Dar, 1957

The man who, more than any other single individual outside the General Staff, was responsible for the institutional spark that produced Sayeret Matkal was not Arnan. It was Avraham Dar.

Dar was, in 1957, in his late thirties, a small and quiet man with a long and complicated history. He had served, like Arnan, in the Palmach. He had been seconded, after the War of Independence, to the small Aman cell that ran the Egyptian-Jewish sabotage network that would, in the summer of 1954, produce the Operation Susannah disaster I described in §5.2. He had been, until that moment, the operational handler of the network. He had, in the months after the disaster, been quietly recalled from his foreign posting. By 1957 he had been reassigned, in the small and tight world of Israeli clandestine personnel, to Unit 154's military arm — to the small element inside Aman's HUMINT directorate that was responsible for the soldier-deployed wiretap installation and maintenance operations that the Tzartzar disaster had, two years earlier, brought to a halt.[^ch5-16]

The institutional pressure on Dar in the spring of 1957 was substantial. Moshe Dayan, who had become the IDF's chief of the general staff in December 1953 and who had returned to the position in the wake of the 1956 Sinai campaign, regarded the post-Tzartzar suspension of soldier-deployed wiretap operations as a strategic disaster that had to be reversed. The Israeli SIGINT picture against Syria was, in Dayan's assessment by 1957, intolerably bad. The Egyptian deployments along the Sinai frontier were, in Dayan's assessment, increasingly threatening. The intelligence community needed, in Dayan's view, to find some way to put soldiers back behind enemy lines for technical-emplacement purposes. The task of finding that way had fallen, by the early months of 1957, to Avraham Dar.

Dar's proposition, when he came to Arnan at Safed in the spring of 1957, was not the proposition that Arnan would eventually adopt. Dar did not propose a small unit of trained military operators on the David Stirling model. Dar proposed something quite different: a small mista'arvim cell — operatives disguised as Arabs, drawn from the Mizrahi Jewish communities that had recently arrived in Israel from Iraq, Syria, and Lebanon, fluent in colloquial Arabic and physically indistinguishable from the populations on the other side of the border — who would, in the manner of the Egyptian-Jewish network that Dar himself had run before 1954, cross into Syria and Lebanon disguised as locals, conduct wiretap-maintenance and intelligence-collection missions over weeks or months, and return. The proposition married Dar's own pre-Susannah operational experience to the post-Tzartzar institutional vacuum. It was, in 1957, the only proposal anyone had made.[^ch5-17]

Arnan, in the assessment of the Nachmias testimony that Milstein recorded a generation later, accepted Dar's proposition in despair. The mista'arvim concept was not the unit Arnan had been imagining — he had not yet read Cowles, in the spring of 1957, and the Stirling reference point had not yet entered his thinking — but it was, in the moment, the only institutional opening any senior officer was prepared to provide him. By the second half of 1957, Dar and Arnan had begun, in informal communication between Dar's office in Jerusalem and Arnan's apartment in Nahalal where he was now living with his wife, to recruit the first operators. The early recruits were drawn, in the manner of every Israeli unit of the period, from the personal networks of the founders. The founding nucleus, by the end of 1957, was a small cluster of men recruited individually and outside any formal selection process: Yitzhak Shoshen, Yair Harari, Eli Gil — who operated under the cover name Daoud — Charles Levy (cover name Salem), Rami Saer, Moshe Levin (known throughout his service in the unit by his Palmach nickname Kokla), Yitzhak Gibli (known as Ha-Katan, "the small one"), and Yechiel Amsalem, who would become the first team commander of the unit and who would be killed in action on operational service some years later. Meir Har-Zion — the Unit 101 and 890 Paratroop Battalion reconnaissance-company veteran whose institutional reputation in the small SOF community of the period was unmatched — was associated with the nucleus from its earliest months in a senior operational-advisory capacity, even as his formal service remained in the paratroopers. The total nucleus, by the end of 1957, numbered fewer than ten men. The unit had no name, no table of organization, no budget, and no formal position in the IDF order of battle. It existed because Dar and Arnan had, on the personal authority of Dar's office, decided that it existed.[^ch5-18]

Inside Unit 154, the nucleus was barely tolerated. Arnan's direct commander — Rehavia Vardi, the head of Unit 154's northern collection branch in those years — regarded the project as a distraction from the unit's primary HUMINT mission and as a probable embarrassment to the institutional reputation of the unit. Vardi did not move to shut the project down. He did decline, repeatedly, to provide it any resources beyond the bare minimum. The nucleus operated, through 1958 and into the early months of 1959, in the institutional shadows of Unit 154 in Safed. It conducted its own selection, on its own time, in the open countryside around the Galilee. It conducted its own training, often with equipment borrowed from regular infantry units, in the wadis east of the Sea of Galilee. It planned operations that, for lack of authorization, it could not execute. Across the IDF, in the rare cases where its existence was known at all, it was regarded — in Nachmias's later recollection — as "a joke."[^ch5-19]

## 5.7 The Mista'arvim That Failed and the Stirling Model That Replaced It

What happened over the next two years, between the spring of 1957 and the summer of 1959, was that the mista'arvim concept on which Arnan had founded the nucleus failed.

The failure had two dimensions. The first was operational. The few cross-border missions that the early nucleus attempted in 1958 — most of them small reconnaissance excursions into the Syrian or Lebanese border zones, conducted on the assumption that operators in Arab dress could pass briefly through villages without arousing notice — produced a sequence of disappointments. The operators were spotted. The villages were not, in the Israel-Syria border environment of 1958, the anonymous and porous spaces that the Egyptian urban environment of 1954 had been. The local populations on both sides of the border knew one another by face. A stranger in Arab dress on the streets of a Syrian Druze village in the upper Hermon foothills was not a stranger merely from the next village; he was a stranger from outside the entire local kinship network, and his presence was reported, within hours, to the Syrian gendarmerie. The mista'arvim model, which had worked — for a time — in the Egyptian urban environment in which Dar had operated it before 1954, did not work in the rural border zones of 1958 Syria.[^ch5-20]

The second dimension of the failure was conceptual. The mista'arvim model was designed to put operatives into the enemy population. The intelligence problem that the IDF needed solved was not, primarily, intelligence on the enemy population. It was intelligence on the enemy military — on the deployment of Syrian armored brigades along the Damascus-Quneitra corridor, on the construction of Syrian air defense installations along the Hermon ridge, on the radio traffic moving through the Syrian regional military communications grid. None of those things was visible from inside a Druze village. None of those things was, in any case, something that an Arabic-speaking operator on foot could meaningfully collect.

It was, in the developing assessment of Arnan over the course of 1958 and into early 1959, the wrong unit for the right problem.

What Arnan needed — and what he was, by the summer of 1959, in the small Safed apartment with Virginia Cowles's book on his desk, beginning to articulate — was an entirely different unit. He needed soldiers, not agents. He needed men in uniform under fatigues, not men in Arab dress. He needed teams of four or five, inserted deep into the enemy military rear by means an Arab informant could not interdict, conducting reconnaissance against military installations rather than civilian populations, returning under cover of darkness to a recovery point that the operators themselves had selected and the IAF could reliably reach. He needed the Long Range Desert Group. He needed the Special Air Service. He needed, in the institutional language of the IDF of 1959, something that did not yet exist.

The reorientation, when it came, was gradual rather than dramatic. There was no single meeting at which Arnan declared the mista'arvim model dead and the Stirling model adopted in its place. There was, instead, a slow shift through the second half of 1958 and the first half of 1959 in the kind of operator the nucleus was recruiting (away from Arabic-speakers, toward men with military reconnaissance backgrounds in the regular IDF), in the kind of training the nucleus was conducting (away from civilian-passing drills, toward small-team navigation and observation in open terrain), and in the kind of insertion method the unit was beginning to imagine (away from on-foot border crossing in disguise, toward helicopter insertion at night). By the autumn of 1959, the unit that Arnan and Dar had founded as a mista'arvim cell in 1957 had quietly become, in operational profile and in self-understanding, a Stirling-model deep-reconnaissance unit. Dar himself, by mid-1959, had moved on to other assignments. Arnan was running the project, by then, more or less alone — alone except for Sami Nachmias, who had joined as operations officer in 1958, and for Elazar in Tel Aviv, and for the small circle of officers in the IAF rotary-wing community that, by late 1959, included Uri Yarom.[21]

The reorientation produced, in late 1959 and through 1960, a unit that was operationally coherent in a way the 1957 nucleus had not been. It also produced, however, a unit that no senior officer in the IDF outside Arnan's immediate circle understood, regarded as legitimate, or was prepared to fund at the level its proposed operations required. The unit, by the end of 1959, was — operationally — the thing Arnan had been arguing it should be. It was — institutionally — still a joke.

The thing that made the unit no longer a joke was not anything Arnan or Yarom or Elazar or Nachmias did. It was the catastrophic failure of Israeli intelligence in the third week of February 1960.

## 5.8 Rotem, February 1960

In the second week of February 1960, the Egyptian army began to move three infantry divisions from the Suez Canal zone toward the Sinai frontier with Israel. The move was carried out at night, under strict communications discipline, and across the Egyptian desert under conditions of intentional concealment. The Egyptian intent — which would not become fully clear to the Israeli intelligence community until weeks later — was a deterrent demonstration in support of Syria, with which Egypt had, the previous year, formed the United Arab Republic, and which had been the subject, in the assessment of the Egyptian general staff, of an Israeli military buildup in the Galilee that might develop into a Syrian-front campaign. The move, in other words, was a piece of strategic signaling. It was not, on the best post hoc reconstruction of Egyptian intentions, the prelude to an attack.

The IDF did not know any of this at the time. The IDF, in fact, did not know about the Egyptian deployment at all. The first significant Israeli detection of the deployed Egyptian forces occurred on 22 February 1960, when a Mossad agent in Egypt — operating outside the channels of military intelligence — reported the movement of armor in the Sinai. By the time the report reached the IDF General Staff, the Egyptian formations were already deployed in their forward positions in the western Sinai, within striking distance of the Israeli border. The detection had occurred not days but weeks after the deployment had begun.[^ch5-22]

The Israeli response, when it came, was a hurried partial mobilization carried out under the codename Rotem — the Hebrew word for the desert broom shrub. The mobilization was conducted under conditions of considerable confusion. The Israeli intelligence picture of what the Egyptian forces in Sinai were actually doing remained, throughout the crisis, fragmentary. The IDF General Staff was unable to determine, in any meaningful sense, whether the Egyptian deployment was a feint, a positioning for negotiation, or the prelude to an attack. The crisis was de-escalated, over the following weeks, by diplomatic means. No combat took place. The Egyptian forces eventually withdrew. The Israeli forces eventually demobilized. The bill that came due, however, was institutional. The IDF had been caught, in the contemporary phrase of Yitzhak Rabin — who had been chief of the operations branch during the crisis and would, three years later, become the IDF's chief of the general staff — with its pants down.

The post-mortem on Rotem produced, in the spring and early summer of 1960, the most important institutional shift in the prehistory of Sayeret Matkal. What the General Staff concluded — in a series of internal reviews that have only partly been declassified — was that the failure of detection in February 1960 had been a failure of method as much as it had been a failure of any individual collection element. The Israeli intelligence community had been relying, in February 1960, on HUMINT, on aerial photography (which was limited by weather conditions in the relevant weeks), and on SIGINT (which had been depleted, as I argued in §5.3, since the Tzartzar disaster of 1954). The community had not been relying on, because the community had not possessed, any capability for direct ground reconnaissance against the strategic deployments of the country's principal adversaries. The Rotem post-mortem was, more than anything else, an institutional argument that the community needed such a capability.[^ch5-23]

The argument fell, by the late spring of 1960, on Arnan's desk. Or rather, by then, on Arnan's small Tel Aviv office — by 1960 he had moved his project from Safed to the IDF's central headquarters compound at HaKirya in Tel Aviv. The unit that the General Staff had laughed at for two years had become, in the wake of Rotem, the only proposal on the table that addressed the gap the post-mortem had identified. Arnan was given, in a sequence of decisions during the second half of 1960, what he had been asking for since the 1957 conversation with Dar. He was given a position on the IDF table of organization — Sayeret HaMatkal, the Reconnaissance Unit of the General Staff, reporting directly to Aman. He was given a budget, modest but real. He was given access to the IAF's Squadron 124 for training and for eventual operational use. He was given authorization to conduct a formal selection course, drawing candidates from across the IDF rather than from his own personal networks, in the spring of 1961.[^ch5-24]

The unit moved its operational base, in stages over the course of 1960 and 1961, from Safed to a small site at the IDF's training base at Kfar Sirkin east of Tel Aviv. By the end of 1961, Sayeret Matkal — the name the unit would carry, with one brief variation, for the rest of the twentieth century — was conducting its first formal selection course at Kfar Sirkin. By the spring of 1962, the unit was conducting its first authorized operational deployments — the first of the deep-reconnaissance missions that, over the following decade, would establish the unit's reputation. The unit that had been a joke in 1959 had become, by 1962, an institutional reality.

What had changed, between 1959 and 1960, was not Arnan and not Yarom and not Elazar. What had changed was the General Staff's assessment of what the IDF needed. The Rotem failure had produced — in the precise mechanism of the entrepreneur-at-critical-juncture framework that runs through this book — the moment at which the bureaucracy concluded it had no other answer. Arnan and Yarom and Dar and Elazar had spent three years building, in the institutional shadows, the only proposal that the General Staff, on the morning after the Rotem failure, could reach for. The proposal had been waiting. The shock had now produced the demand. The unit, by the autumn of 1960, was Sayeret Matkal.

## 5.9 The Tamari Succession, 1964

The unit Arnan had built between 1957 and 1963 was a strategic-reconnaissance unit. The unit that Dov Tamari took over in 1964 would, within eighteen months, be something different.

The succession itself was administrative. Arnan had already, in September 1960, departed for a year of studies at the IDF's Command and Staff College, and the unit's command had been temporarily handed to Yosef Kastel for the duration of his absence. Arnan had returned in 1961 and resumed command, but the institutional point had been made: the unit could function without its founder. By 1964, after his own continued tenure had become impossible to justify under the IDF's career-rotation rules, Arnan handed off command formally to his deputy.
