He moved into a staff role at Aman, then to the head of the Technological Unit (Unit 432) in 1966, and would over the next decade become — formally, informally, and against his own wishes — the patron figure of the unit rather than its commander. The man who took the long-term command in 1964 was Dov Tamari, who would later become the IDF's first Chief Intelligence Officer and the holder of the Oz decoration and two Chief of Staff citations, and who had served as Arnan's deputy. Tamari was, however, not Arnan's choice of successor. He was the General Staff's choice. And Tamari's institutional formation — by background and temperament — was in the paratroop tradition that I described in §5.2 as the principal alternative to Arnan's own strategic-reconnaissance model.[25]

The appointment was a quiet repudiation of what Arnan had built. Tamari was not, by background or temperament, a strategic-reconnaissance officer. He was a reprisal-raid officer. His career had been built in the paratroop battalions whose institutional purpose, through the second half of the 1950s, had been the cross-border punishment operations that I described in §5.2 as the principal alternative tradition to Arnan's own. Tamari's appointment to Sayeret Matkal meant, in institutional terms, that the unit was being reassigned — gradually, never explicitly — from the strategic-reconnaissance mission Arnan had built it around to the reprisal-raid mission that the paratroop tradition had been carrying.[^ch5-26]

The reorientation became unmistakable on the night of 4 September 1965. On that night, Tamari personally led a Sayeret Matkal force across the Jordanian border in a punitive operation against a Fatah training facility in the West Bank. The operation was a tactical success. The unit's operators conducted it in the precise small-team idiom that Arnan had built them to execute. The objective, however — the destruction of a paramilitary training camp by a cross-border raiding force — was an objective indistinguishable from what the 890th Paratroop Battalion had been doing under Sharon a decade earlier. It was the kind of operation Arnan had founded his unit specifically not to do. The 4 September raid was, in Nachmias's later assessment, the moment at which Sayeret Matkal entered the reprisal-operation circle of the IDF and joined the institutional company of every other small elite formation in the country.[27]

I have, earlier in this book and again in the chapter on Sadeh, made the argument that the institutional entrepreneur founds the institution but does not get to choose what it becomes. The Tamari succession is the cleanest illustration of that pattern in the unit's history. Arnan founded the unit on a specific operational concept, in a specific institutional vacuum, on the basis of a specific theoretical model. Within six years of his handing off command, the unit had been reassigned to a different operational concept under a different commander whose institutional formation was in a different tradition. Arnan, by 1965, was no longer in a position to defend the original vision. The unit was now Tamari's, and Tamari, with the institutional support of the General Staff Operations Branch under Bar-Lev and the implicit endorsement of the political leadership in Dayan's defense ministry, would for the next two years use Sayeret Matkal as a reprisal-raid instrument.

What this meant for the operational story of the unit between 1964 and 1967 was not, as it would have been in another military, the collapse of the strategic-reconnaissance mission. It meant the coexistence, inside one unit, of two missions: the strategic-reconnaissance work that Arnan had built and that Aman continued to need, and the cross-border reprisal raid work that Tamari preferred and that the operations branch continued to demand. The unit was now executing both — and, with the institutional pressures of the period mounting from every direction, beginning to execute neither as well as it had once executed only one. The institutional drift had begun.

## 5.10 The Technological Unit and the Bird Operations, 1962–1967

The drift was, however, masked for several years by the spectacular operational success of the unit's strategic-reconnaissance side. Between 1962 and 1967, Sayeret Matkal — alongside a sister formation that I have not yet introduced, and that the chapter requires me to introduce — became the executor of the most consequential strategic-intelligence operations the State of Israel had ever attempted against its principal adversaries.

The sister formation was Aman's Technological Unit, designated Unit 432, and its founding in the spring of 1962 was a piece of institutional architecture that ran in parallel to the Sayeret Matkal story and that is impossible to separate from it. Unit 432's purpose was technical: to design, build, and emplace the specialized signals-collection devices — wiretap kits, radio repeaters, line taps, antenna arrays — that Arnan's reconstituted strategic-reconnaissance mission required. The unit's founding commander was Uri Goren, a young engineering officer in his late twenties who had been recruited into Aman by his old officer-school classmate — Avraham Arnan.[^ch5-28]

The recruitment chain that produced Unit 432 is itself a vignette of the entrepreneurial-coalition mechanism that runs through this book. Meir Amit, who had become the head of Aman in early 1962, had concluded — on the basis of his own analysis of the post-Rotem intelligence requirements — that Israel needed an organic technical-emplacement capability that the IDF's existing electronics infrastructure could not provide. Amit assigned the recruitment task to Arnan. Arnan reached out to Goren, his old officer-school classmate then in the IDF's electronics corps. Goren agreed in principle but required institutional sponsorship from the operations branch of the General Staff for the inevitable resource fights that would follow. Arnan supplied that sponsorship by recruiting David Elazar — who had by 1962 risen to the head of the operations branch and who had been Arnan's commanding officer in the Harel Brigade fifteen years earlier — into the project. The four-man chain of Amit, Arnan, Goren, and Elazar — three of whom had served together at some point in the Palmach, two of whom had been classmates, all four of whom were prepared to defend the project against the regular electronics corps's institutional objections — produced, in the second half of 1962, the founding of Aman's Technological Unit.[^ch5-29]

What Unit 432 produced over the following five years was the technical infrastructure for what the Israeli intelligence community would, in its internal correspondence of the period, call ha-emtza'im ha-meyuhadim — the special means. The phrase was deliberately vague. It covered an entire generation of signals-collection devices designed to be emplaced, by Sayeret Matkal operators or in a few cases by Mossad or Shin Bet operatives, inside the strategic infrastructure of Syria, Egypt, Jordan, and Lebanon: wiretaps on military communications lines, repeater nodes on military command networks, line-of-sight relay devices in elevated terrain. The operations were conducted under the codename Bird Operations — Mivtza'ei Tziporim — a Hebrew nickname whose origin no one I have been able to consult can now reconstruct with certainty.[^ch5-30]

Between 1962 and 1967, Sayeret Matkal conducted, by the consolidated estimate of the published Hebrew-language sources, somewhere between thirty and fifty Bird Operations against Syrian, Egyptian, Jordanian, and Lebanese military infrastructure. The exact number is not known outside the closed corridors of Aman, where the records remain classified. What can be said with confidence is that the Bird Operations were the operational fulfillment of the original Arnan vision — the David Stirling Long Range Desert Group model, transposed to the Israeli operational environment, executed by helicopter-inserted small teams of trained military operators against military rather than civilian targets, returning under cover of darkness with strategic intelligence that no agent could supply. The Bird Operations were the reason Sayeret Matkal had been founded.[^ch5-31]

The published Hebrew accounts permit, however, a reconstruction of the operational sequence in considerably greater detail than the general estimate allows, and the sequence is worth setting out because it traces the institutional pattern by which the Arnan concept moved from theoretical proposal in 1959, through pilot test in the summer of 1963, through first operational emplacement on the Golan Heights in the autumn of the same year, through the first Egyptian emplacement in the early months of 1964, and on into a four-year campaign whose intelligence product would, by the spring of 1967, become the operational foundation of the Israeli Air Force's opening strike of the Six-Day War. The reconstruction below follows the chronology established in Eli Shur's biography of Arnan, in Asher Margalit's institutional history, in Efraim Lapid's overview of the Israeli intelligence community, in Moshe Zonder's history of Sayeret Matkal, in Amos Gilboa's biography of Meir Amit, in Uri Bar-Joseph's academic monograph Recovery (Hit'oshrut), in Nehemia Dagan's pilot memoir Flying Low to See Far, in the Notion-archived institutional timeline of the Bird Operations database that Ami Pedahzur has compiled, and — for the first-person operational dialogue and the named-operator detail — in Anshel Pfeffer's Haaretz magazine reconstruction of April 2018 and in Ehud Barak's autobiography My Country, My Life, published in the same year, both of which Barak corroborated through his direct cooperation with Pfeffer's reporting.[31a]

The institutional precondition for the campaign was the cooperation that Avraham Arnan, in the second half of 1962, negotiated with Uri Yarom, the commander of Israel's single helicopter squadron of the period. Yarom had just received the IAF's first operational consignment of Sikorsky S-58 (CH-34) Choctaw helicopters and was, in Yarom's own institutional self-description, "eager to put the new aircraft to operational use." The Arnan–Yarom relationship was the third leg of the institutional tripod the Amit–Arnan–Goren–Elazar chain had built in the spring of 1962. Without Yarom's willingness to commit his squadron to the multi-hour cross-border insertion-and-extraction profile the Arnan concept required — and without his readiness, in the months that followed, to spend his squadron's training resources on the night-flying, low-altitude, terrain-following, multi-sector navigation skills the Bird Operations would demand — the helicopter-borne SIGINT emplacement concept would have remained, in 1963 as it had been in 1960, an idea on a sheet of paper inside an Aman briefing folder.[31a-bis]

Operation Halutz — Pioneer — was the pilot test. On the night of 10–11 August 1963, a Sayeret Matkal force inserted by Yarom's helicopters into a deserted area inside the Sinai Peninsula completed a model penetration whose specific purpose was to test the feasibility of the helicopter-borne SIGINT-emplacement concept in actual Egyptian terrain. The operation carried no live intelligence payload. Its purpose was to establish that the helicopter could cross the frontier undetected, that the Sayeret Matkal team could move with the heavy emplacement equipment, and that the helicopter could return at the agreed pickup time without alerting Egyptian air defense. The team completed the operation without incident. The Sayeret Matkal operators on the pilot test had been training for two years, by Barak's autobiographical recollection, in night navigation by compass and stars alone, repeatedly evading the IDF's own desert-tracker units in the Negev rehearsals — until their commanders judged them ready. The institutional decision to proceed to the first operational emplacement followed within weeks.[^ch5-31b]

The first real Bird Operation was not in Egypt. It was in Syria. The operational record requires the correction because the institutional narrative the campaign would generate has, in much of the subsequent Israeli defense journalism, telescoped the first Egyptian emplacement (Operation Shrakrak / Bee-eater, February 1964) and the first Syrian emplacement (late September 1963) into a single founding event. They were two distinct operations, separated by approximately five months.

The first emplacement was conducted on the night of late September 1963 on the Syrian-held Golan Heights, against a Syrian Army telephone trunk line. The force commander was Ehud Barak — at that point still using his birth name Brog, a 21-year-old Sayeret Matkal lieutenant — leading a team of five operators: Avi Mukhtar, of Iraqi background; Kuti Sharabi, Yemeni; Moshe Elimelech, a kibbutznik whom Barak would later describe as "strong, flexible, fearless"; Barak himself; and one further operator. Each man carried an Uzi submachine gun and two hand grenades, plus the SIGINT-emplacement payload divided across the team's load-carriage. Chief of the General Staff Zvi Tzur personally received Barak's pre-operation briefing — a procedure that, beginning with this operation, would become the standard pre-mission protocol for every Sayeret Matkal cross-border emplacement. Meir Har-Zion, the legendary Unit 101 and paratroop Company-A operator who had retired from active service three years earlier but who remained, in the small SOF community of the period, the senior operational adviser on this class of operation — and who had himself led the only previous successful Israeli SIGINT emplacement on the Golan, the 1954 operation that had ended in the institutional trauma of the failed battery-replacement return mission — was present at the final pre-operation exercise and signed off.[^ch5-31c]

The operation went badly enough, in its tactical details, that the institutional learning that came out of it would shape the conduct of every subsequent Bird Operation. The team crossed the frontier after dark north of Kibbutz Dan. The Banias River, which the route required them to cross, was still in flood from recent rains; the team had not trained for the crossing and had no specialized equipment for it, and they spent additional time at the river that the operational plan had not allocated. While moving toward the target they nearly walked into a sleeping Syrian three-man ambush position; only the discipline of the team's night-movement training prevented detection. The recall order from the command post arrived at 1:15 a.m. — well before the team had reached the target — and Barak made the decision to disregard it by ordering his radio operator to switch off the unit's transceiver, on the calculation that aborting the mission within sight of the objective would forfeit the entire institutional investment of the previous four years. The team reached the Syrian telephone trunk pole at 2:30 a.m. and completed the SIGINT emplacement in fifteen minutes. They were back across the frontier at first light, three hours behind the planned schedule. At the border the AMAN Director, Meir Amit, was waiting for them in person.[31c-bis]

The institutional aftermath of the first emplacement was the founding myth of the Bird Operations campaign. Chief of the General Staff Tzur sent the Sayeret Matkal base a case of French champagne with his personal congratulations. Two bottles had been removed from the case before delivery, with a note from Tzur reading approximately: "to teach a lesson to Ehud Brog about not switching off his radio in the field." The deputy COGS Avraham Yofe demanded, separately, that Barak be placed under arrest for the recall-order violation; the demand was overruled at the General Staff level. The intelligence yield from the emplaced device on the Syrian Army's command communications would, within the year, become a principal input to the IDF's understanding of the Syrian deployment posture along the post-1957 frontier. The same device, or its successors, would still be functioning four years later when the IDF captured the Golan Heights in thirty-six hours in June 1967.[31c-ter]

Operation Shrakrak — Bee-eater, the name from which the broader codename Mivtza'ei Tziporim would be derived — was the first Egyptian Bird Operation. It was conducted in February 1964, approximately five months after the Syrian first emplacement. The mission's operational complexity exceeded the Syrian operation's by an order of magnitude. The Egyptian target — the Sinai telephone trunk lines serving the Egyptian Air Force base assessed in the open literature to have been al-Arish, approximately seventy kilometers inside Egyptian territory — was nearly an order of magnitude deeper than the Syrian operation's. The SIGINT-emplacement device required for the Egyptian target — a long-range relay system whose battery weight alone, by Bar-Joseph's reconstruction, ran to several hundred kilograms — could not be carried on the operators' backs across the distance from the helicopter landing zone to the target.

The institutional invention that made the Egyptian operation possible was a small four-wheeled cart of chromium-alloy tubing, with telescoping axles so that the cart could be loaded into the CH-34 fuselage through the helicopter's side door, and with front wheels borrowed from the IAF's jet trainer aircraft. The cart was the second prototype produced by Unit 432's design team after the first prototype — a two-man rickshaw — had failed in Negev rehearsal trials by leaving distinctive zigzag tracks in the sand that would, in Sinai, have compromised the operation's deniability. The institutional invention that produced the second prototype came from a colonel on Meir Amit's personnel staff, who attended one of Amit's monthly progress visits to the Sayeret Matkal training base and proposed the four-wheel rickshaw concept after listening to Barak describe the weight problem. Within days the design team had produced a working prototype. Among the smaller items of operational equipment the team deployed on the mission, by Barak's later recollection, was material acquired by Unit 432 from a hobby shop in Pennsylvania.[^ch5-31d]

The force commander on the Egyptian mission was again Barak. The operators were Oded, Nissim, Kobi, Ahiud, and Barak — five men in total. The helicopter navigator was Savron. The training cycle for the mission ran nearly nine months and included the recruitment of geologists to identify Negev terrain that matched the specific surface texture and dune geometry of the planned Sinai target area, the development of techniques to defeat the Israeli desert-tracker rehearsal teams that had, in earlier rehearsals, repeatedly detected the Sayeret Matkal force, and the iterative refinement of the cart's mechanical performance in sand conditions. The command post for the operation was established in a wooden structure on Mount Keren in the central Negev, equipped to receive the SIGINT feed in real time once the device on the Sinai trunk line was activated. Among those present at the command post were Amit; Arnan; and the new Chief of the General Staff Yitzhak Rabin, who had succeeded Tzur the previous month and whose decision to authorize the operation in his first weeks as COGS would, in the years that followed, become one of his earliest institutional commitments to the entire Bird Operations campaign.[31d-bis]

The helicopter crossed the frontier at 18:52 on the operation's evening and set the team down approximately thirty minutes later at the planned landing zone, roughly ten kilometers from the target. The team began the foot movement toward the target with the cart and the emplacement payload. The Sinai conditions diverged from the Negev rehearsals in ways the planning team had not anticipated — the surface, in particular, behaved differently under the cart's wheels — and the team fell progressively behind schedule. Barak made the decision to commit all five operators to the emplacement work rather than maintaining outer-perimeter watch. The principal emplacement was completed approximately three hours behind the planned schedule. The supplementary emplacement that the operational plan had also called for was abandoned. During the team's movement back toward the pickup zone, a heavy fog — code-named "milk" in the operation's lexicon — developed over the area, and Barak broke the operation's strict radio silence to call in the fog warning to the command post on Mount Keren. The helicopter's run-in to the alternate pickup zone was, by Pfeffer's reconstruction from Barak and from the IAF pilot's memoir, a near-disaster: the navigator, recognizing that the helicopter was drifting toward the cart and the ground team, broke the operation's strict navigation-lights blackout to flash the landing lights as a warning to the pilot, who pulled the helicopter's nose up at the last instant and set down within approximately six meters of the team rather than on top of them. The team boarded the helicopter, secured the cart, and was back across the frontier within forty minutes. First daylight arrived as the helicopter cleared Israeli airspace. The first intelligence began to flow from the emplaced device several hours after the team's return to base. The cooperation between Sayeret Matkal, Unit 432, and Yarom's IAF helicopter squadron — the institutional precondition the four-man Amit–Arnan–Goren–Elazar chain had constructed in the spring of 1962 — was, by the morning of the Egyptian operation in February 1964, an operational fact. Four years after the institutional shock of the Rotem affair, the State of Israel had constructed, for the first time, a technical-collection insurance policy against the recurrence of strategic surprise on both of its principal fronts.[^ch5-31e]

The institutional aftermath of the Sinai operation was at least as consequential as its operational success. Rabin presented the team with citations ten days after the operation. Arnan, at age forty-five and after seven years of continuous association with the unit, finally departed Sayeret Matkal for the staff appointment as head of Aman's Technological Unit (Unit 432) — the unit whose founding the Bird Operations campaign had institutionally required and which would, under Arnan's command from 1964 onward, become the technical-collection backbone of the IDF's strategic intelligence capability. Dov "Dubik" Tamari succeeded Arnan as commander of Sayeret Matkal, in what would become the first of the standard two-year command tenures the unit would maintain through the post-1967 period. Barak, despite his junior rank, was appointed as the unit's de facto deputy commander with responsibility for the operational supervision of the unit's missions. Within a year — by Barak's own retrospective account — he had concluded that the strategic threat environment had stabilized to the point at which his continued military service was unnecessary, and in the summer of 1965 he left the army to begin what he expected would be a civilian career. The Six-Day War of June 1967 would, of course, bring him back; but the decision he made in the summer of 1965 is itself an institutional artifact of the moment at which the Israeli SOF community's senior figures considered the strategic problem the unit had been founded to solve to have been, for practical operational purposes, solved.[31e-bis]

Between November 1964 and February 1967, at least four further named Bird Operations followed, each penetrating more deeply into Egyptian territory, several deploying multiple SIGINT emplacements in a single operational night, all carrying the ornithological codenames that gave the broader campaign its institutional nickname:

* Operation Shaldag — Kingfisher — November 1964

* Operation Kahol — Blue — December 1965

* Operation Naqar — Woodpecker — March 1966

* Operation Yargazi — Greenfinch — February 1967

Operation Kahol was the largest of the four. Three CH-34 helicopters of the IAF's helicopter squadron inserted two distinct Sayeret Matkal teams against parallel Egyptian targets in a single operational night. The intelligence yield from the operation — the specific tactical and operational picture of the Egyptian Air Force's deployment, command-and-control architecture, and standard daily operating rhythm that the emplaced devices produced in the months following — would, in the institutional retrospective assessment of Aman's senior officers after the Six-Day War, be characterized as "the seed of the air victory" that Operation Focus achieved on the morning of 5 June 1967. The Sayeret Matkal-and-IAF kill chain that the Eisenkot Commando Brigade institutionalization of 2015 and the Kochavi Ma'aseh AMAN doctrinal reform of 2011–2014 would, half a century later, codify as the contemporary IDF's standard operational architecture, was — in its first institutional form — the Sayeret Matkal-and-IAF Bird Operations cooperation of December 1965.[^ch5-31d]

Operation Naqar of March 1966 carried a specific additional institutional consequence. The Sayeret Matkal commander of the period, Lieutenant Colonel Dov "Dubik" Tamari — Arnan's General-Staff-chosen successor whom I introduced in §5.9 above — accompanied the operation in person. The Deputy Director of Aman, Major General Aharon Yariv, who had been monitoring the Bird Operations campaign from the AMAN Tel Aviv headquarters, used the operational debriefing of Naqar to press a question that had been concerning him for months: why did the IAF not have a heavier helicopter, one capable of carrying both more SIGINT equipment and more operators in a single airframe? The institutional pressure that Yariv applied across the IAF and the General Staff in the months following Naqar produced the IDF's decision to acquire the French Aérospatiale SA 321 Super Frelon — the Tzirah, "Hornet," in IDF service — a heavy-lift helicopter whose operational specifications exceeded the CH-34's in every measurable category. The Super Frelon was 56 miles per hour faster than the CH-34, its operational range was 125 nautical miles longer, its maximum payload was 6,700 pounds greater, and its fuel capacity was 1,340 gallons larger. The Super Frelon also possessed, in contrast to the CH-34, a rear-loading platform that allowed the carriage of small wheeled vehicles. The first Super Frelon was delivered to the IAF's Squadron 114 — the "Night Movers" — on 20 April 1966, approximately five months after the squadron's founding. The squadron's name, in the institutional language of the IAF's helicopter community, signaled the operational role for which Squadron 114 had been constituted.[^ch5-31z]

Operation Yargazi of February 1967 was the first Bird Operation executed with the Super Frelon. A single Super Frelon could now perform, by the empirical operational test of Yargazi, the same mission that had previously required three CH-34s. By the spring of 1967 — three months before the Six-Day War — the Israeli Air Force possessed, by the consolidated assessment of the available open-source accounts, a substantially complete intelligence picture of the Egyptian and Syrian air forces: the squadrons' deployment, the daily operational tempo, the air-defense and surface-to-air missile networks, the radar coverage, and the updated photographic and cartographic ground truth of the targets. The picture had been constructed, over the four-and-a-half years between Operation Halutz of August 1963 and Operation Yargazi of February 1967, by the institutional cooperation between Sayeret Matkal, Unit 432, and the IAF's helicopter squadrons that the Amit–Arnan–Goren–Elazar chain had founded in the spring of 1962.[^ch5-31f]

The intelligence picture had a specific operational utility that the open-source accounts of the period have only begun, in recent years, to acknowledge. The Egyptian Air Force, by the mid-1960s, was developing its own surprise-strike plan against Israel. The plan was designated Fahd — "Cheetah" — and it shared, with the IAF's Operation Focus that would eventually pre-empt it, the basic operational logic of a coordinated opening strike against the adversary's air bases. The Fahd target set, by the Israeli intelligence reconstruction subsequently published in fragmented form in the Israeli defense-history literature, included the destruction of the IAF's bases, the Israeli radar stations, the missile bases around the Tel Aviv area, and — in the operation's later phases — the bombing of the city of Eilat and its port infrastructure. The Bird Operations campaign — the SIGINT emplacements that had been collecting on Egyptian and Syrian air-force and air-base communications since the autumn of 1963 — was the institutional instrument that had allowed the Israeli intelligence community to identify, map, and continuously update its assessment of the Fahd plan's evolution.

During the IDF's tense waiting period in late May and early June 1967, in the days when the Egyptian deployment patterns into Sinai had moved seven divisions into Sinai — nearly twice the force level of the 1960 Rotem mobilization — and the Israeli political-military leadership was approaching its decision to proceed to a pre-emptive air strike, Chief of the General Staff Rabin paid a personal visit to Squadron 114's hangars. He told the assembled pilots and ground crews, in a sentence Nehemia Dagan would in his memoir describe as "the highest decoration I will ever receive," that "what you have done to this point is saving the State of Israel." On the night of 4–5 June 1967, less than thirty-six hours before Operation Focus would launch, Sayeret Matkal conducted one final Bird Operation against an Egyptian target in Sinai whose specific identification remains classified — the operation that Avner Shur, in his Arnan biography, describes simply as "an operation in Egypt a day before the war." The campaign that Operation Halutz had inaugurated in August 1963, and that the Syrian first emplacement of late September 1963 had operationally initiated, was, on the morning of 5 June 1967, complete. By every institutional account that has subsequently been published, the Israeli decision to proceed to a pre-emptive air strike on the morning of 5 June was informed not only by the conventional intelligence indicators that surrounded the Egyptian mobilization but also by the granular technical picture that the Bird Operations had constructed of the Egyptian Air Force's specific institutional readiness for Fahd.[^ch5-31g]

A second institutional development of the period requires acknowledgment before the chapter moves on, because it operates as the bridge between the Bird Operations campaign that Arnan founded and the cross-border reprisal mission that the unit's mid-1960s succession had begun to develop. On the night of 12 November 1966, a paratroop reconnaissance patrol in the south Hebron Hills struck a mine, with three Israeli soldiers killed. Within hours, Rabin authorized the largest reprisal operation the State of Israel had conducted since 1956 — Mivtsa Magreisa, Operation Crusher, against the village of Samua south of Hebron, the first Israeli daylight reprisal operation, intended to pressure King Hussein of Jordan into ordering his army to constrain Syrian-based Palestinian operations from Jordanian territory. The principal force was a paratroop brigade with armored support. Thirty Sayeret Matkal operators under Dov Tamari's personal command joined the force — and the institutional fact that the unit had been called for the operation marks the moment that this chapter has been tracking for several sections. Sayeret Matkal had been founded by Arnan in 1957 as a strategic-reconnaissance unit that would not conduct cross-border reprisal raids. Nine years later, with the founding commander now installed as head of Aman's Technological Unit and the institutional argument settled, the unit was at Samua, dropping doors and demolishing buildings alongside the paratroop battalions. The 202nd Paratroop Battalion's commander, Lieutenant Colonel Yoav Shacham, was killed in the operation. The political objective the operation had been designed to achieve — pressure on Hussein — was not achieved. What was achieved, in the institutional history this chapter is reconstructing, was Sayeret Matkal's formal entry into combat operations. Ehud Barak, by Moshe Zonder's account, was the unit's most articulate internal advocate for this transition; he argued that the combat experience the operators acquired in reprisal operations gave them, in his phrase, sheket nafshi — calm of soul — that the strategic-reconnaissance work alone could not impart and that the unit would need when the war that everyone in the senior officer corps knew was coming finally arrived.[31g-bis]

The intelligence product, by 1966 and 1967, was substantial. By the time the Six-Day War broke out on 5 June 1967, the Israeli intelligence community had — by the assessment of Aman's senior officers in their post-war debriefings — a substantially better operational picture of the Egyptian and Syrian deployments in Sinai and the Golan than it had possessed before any previous Israeli conflict. The picture was not perfect. Israeli intelligence still lacked precise data on, for example, the Egyptian air-force dispersal arrangements that Operation Focus would, on the morning of 5 June, attempt to destroy. But the gap that the Tzartzar disaster of 1954 had opened — the gap between what the IDF needed to know about its adversaries' military deployments and what it was actually able to find out — had, by the spring of 1967, been substantially closed.

What is therefore strange, from the perspective of the unit's institutional history, is that the Six-Day War itself was, for Sayeret Matkal, a frustrating spectator's war. The unit's operators were not deployed in any consequential operational role during the war's six days. They sat at their base at Kfar Sirkin, monitored the radio traffic from the front, and — as the Aman archival materials make clear — collectively chased the war that everyone else was fighting. The intelligence Sayeret Matkal had been collecting for five years had been used by the IDF's armored, paratroop, and air-force commanders to plan and execute the campaigns that produced the war's outcome. The unit itself had been left out.[^ch5-32]

The unit's response to that exclusion would shape the next six years of its institutional life — and, indirectly, the institutional disaster that would await it in the autumn of 1973.

## 5.11 From Karameh to Sabena, 1968–1972

The post-1967 period was, for Sayeret Matkal, an institutional search for a new operational identity.

Three things had happened simultaneously. The Bird Operations program had become, after the 1967 territorial expansion, partly obsolete: the Israeli strategic frontier was now the Suez Canal and the Jordan River and the Hermon ridge, and the strategic-depth reconnaissance that the unit had built itself around was — for several years until the strategic geography stabilized again — a less urgent institutional priority. The Israeli political leadership, by 1968, was facing a rising tempo of Palestinian guerrilla operations from across the Jordan River, and was looking for instruments capable of cross-border reprisal at greater operational depth than the conventional paratroop battalions could supply. And the broader international wave of aircraft-hijacking and hostage-taking operations — beginning with the July 1968 PFLP hijacking of an El Al flight to Algiers, escalating through the 1969 and 1970 wave of Mediterranean hijackings, culminating in the September 1970 Jordanian-airfield hostage crisis that produced King Hussein's expulsion of the PLO from Jordan — had begun to generate, inside the Israeli security establishment, a demand for a new operational category that no Israeli unit was institutionally positioned to provide: hostage rescue under conditions of armed terrorist control.

The unit absorbed all three demands. The reprisal mission expanded under Tamari and Tamari's successor; the unit conducted, between 1968 and 1972, perhaps a dozen cross-border operations into Jordan and Lebanon against Fatah and PFLP training and operational infrastructure. The hostage-rescue mission was added in 1968 in an ad hoc manner, then more systematically after the Sabena hijacking of May 1972, which I will describe in a moment. The strategic-reconnaissance mission continued, at reduced pace, against the new Egyptian and Syrian deployments along the post-1967 frontiers.

The most institutionally consequential event of the period — the event that produced the largest single shock to Israeli political-military thinking about elite small-unit operations — was Operation Tofet, the cross-Jordanian reprisal at Karameh on 21 March 1968. The operation, conducted by the 7th Armored Brigade under Shmuel Gorodish and the 35th Paratroop Brigade under Danny Matt, was a divisional-scale punitive raid against the Fatah training infrastructure at the abandoned Jordanian town of Karameh, five kilometers northeast of the Allenby Bridge. Sayeret Matkal's role in the operation was small — a platoon-strength force assigned to demolish five Fatah buildings south of the main objective — and was, in the broader narrative of the day's events, a footnote. What was not a footnote was the operation's institutional outcome.[^ch5-33]

Tofet was, by every operational measure, a failure. The cascade of planning and execution errors — the leaflet drop that warned the Jordanian army of the operation before the Israeli blocking force was in position, the twenty-six-minute helicopter delay that broke the surprise, Gorodish's refusal of artillery and reinforcement support, the unplanned Jordanian armored intervention from concealed positions, the forced mass commitment of the IAF to extract the engaged forces — produced an Israeli casualty bill of twenty-eight killed, three missing, and approximately ninety wounded, with the loss of four tanks and two armored personnel carriers. Most of the Fatah operatives at Karameh escaped. Yasser Arafat himself escaped. The political fallout, both internally inside the Israeli General Staff and externally in the international press, was substantial. Uri Milstein, the Israeli military historian who has written more extensively about Karameh than any other figure, has argued — and I find the argument persuasive — that the failure of Tofet produced, in the Israeli General Staff's institutional thinking, the conclusion that large-scale conventional reprisal operations against Palestinian targets in third countries were no longer worth the risk. The conclusion did not, however, mean that reprisal had been abandoned. It meant that reprisal would, from 1968 onward, be conducted by smaller, more surgical formations. The Golden Era of Israeli special operations — the four-year run of operations from 1968 to 1972 that established Sayeret Matkal's and Shayetet 13's international reputation — was, in this institutional reading, a direct consequence of the conventional failure at Karameh.[^ch5-34]

The pivot to counterterrorism was less gradual. On the morning of 8 May 1972, four operatives of Black September — the Fatah-affiliated organization that had emerged in the aftermath of the September 1970 Jordanian expulsion — hijacked a Sabena Airlines flight en route from Vienna to Tel Aviv. The aircraft landed at Lod Airport. The hijackers held one hundred passengers and crew, demanded the release of three hundred and seventeen Palestinian prisoners, and threatened to detonate explosives if the demands were not met. Over the following twenty-two hours, in a coordinated effort directed by Defense Minister Moshe Dayan and Chief of the General Staff David Elazar — Arnan's old Harel Brigade comrade, now in the highest military office in the country — a Sayeret Matkal team under the command of Ehud Barak, then a captain and the unit's deputy commander, prepared and executed what became, on the afternoon of 9 May, the first successful armed-assault hostage rescue from a hijacked civilian aircraft in the history of international aviation. Two of the hijackers were killed; two were captured. Three hostages were wounded by hijacker fire, one of whom — Meri Holtzberg-Anderson — would later die. Two of the rescuers were lightly wounded, one of whom was a young lieutenant by the name of Benjamin Netanyahu.[35]

I have described the operational architecture of Sabena — Operation Isotope, in the Hebrew operational nomenclature — at length in my earlier book on the Israeli secret services. The interested reader will find the operation reconstructed there, with the specific attention to the air-marshal program, the Shin Bet hostage-negotiation protocol, the IDF technical-deception arrangement, and the operator-level tactical execution that the present chapter does not have space for.[^ch5-36] What concerns us here is institutional. The unit that Arnan had founded in 1957 to conduct strategic reconnaissance against Syrian and Egyptian military deployments had, by 9 May 1972 — fifteen years after the Dar conversation — become the State of Israel's premier hostage-rescue formation. The operational profile that the unit had executed at Lod that afternoon was an operational profile Arnan, in his small Tel Aviv apartment in 1959, could not have imagined his unit performing. The drift that had begun under Tamari in 1964 had, by 1972, produced a unit that was — in its own self-understanding and in the institutional self-understanding of the IDF — something entirely different from what had been founded.

## 5.12 The Beirut Raid

On the night of 9 April 1973, in the Verdun Street neighborhood of West Beirut, three Palestinian leaders — Mohammed Yusuf al-Najjar, the deputy of Yasser Arafat and the operational head of Fatah; Kamal Adwan, the man Israeli intelligence had identified as the planner of the cell network responsible for the Munich Olympics massacre seven months earlier; and Kamal Nasser, the spokesman of the PLO Executive Committee and the most public face of the organization outside the Arab world — were shot dead in their apartments by Israeli operators who had reached the building from the Lebanese coast in rubber zodiacs an hour and a half before. The operation, which the IDF called Aviv Neurim — Spring of Youth — was the most ambitious raid the State of Israel had ever attempted outside its borders. It would also be, as it turned out, the last operation of its kind that the Sayeret Matkal of Avraham Arnan's design would carry out before the Yom Kippur War broke everything.[^ch5-37]

The operational details of the raid have been described elsewhere, and at length. Two of the operators on the ground that night — Ehud Barak, who entered Najjar's building dressed as a woman, and Amnon Lipkin-Shahak, who led the Nahal paratroop force on a parallel target two blocks away — went on to become Israel's chief of the general staff. A third, Yonatan Netanyahu, would die three years later commanding the rescue at Entebbe. The fourth, Muki Betser, would within fifteen months be the figure around whom the Israeli Air Force's organic ground force, Shaldag, would be built — and would, in the chapter that follows this one, become the third entrepreneur of this book. I have described the operational architecture of Spring of Youth — the Mossad's pre-positioning of the cars that carried the operators to their targets, the surveillance by Sylvia Rafael's team in the days before, the simultaneity of the four entry points, the cool of Barak's command voice on the intercepted radio traffic — in detail in The Israeli Secret Services and the Struggle Against Terrorism, and the interested reader will find the operation reconstructed there.[^ch5-38]

What concerns us in this chapter is narrower, and more institutional. Sayeret Matkal had been founded in 1957 by Avraham Arnan as a small unit of operators whose purpose was to conduct technical signals-intelligence emplacements deep inside Syria, Egypt, Jordan, and Lebanon. The unit's first decade — the years of installing what the Israelis called ha-emtza'im ha-meyuhadim, the special means, beyond enemy lines, an operational activity so secret that most of the unit's own veterans cannot speak of it even today — was an unbroken extension of Arnan's founding vision. The Tamari succession of 1964 had, as I argued in §5.9, opened the unit's mission profile to reprisal operations. The Sabena rescue of May 1972 had, as I argued in §5.11, added counterterrorism. By the spring of 1973, the unit that Arnan had founded for one specific purpose had become Israel's premier instrument for nearly every operation the General Staff thought best handled by very small, very skilled formations.

Spring of Youth was the institutional culmination of that drift. The operation was a Sayeret Matkal operation in the sense that Sayeret Matkal's commander led one of the strike teams and the operation's overall commander, Brigadier General Emmanuel Shaked, had built his career around the unit. But the operational concept — an assassination raid against named human targets in a foreign capital — was a counterterrorism mission of a kind Arnan had never imagined his unit performing. The vehicle infiltration was a Mossad concept. The targets were a Shin Bet and Mossad selection. The strategic political objective was Defense Minister Moshe Dayan's. Sayeret Matkal's specific contribution was a particular kind of operator: men who could move silently in a foreign city at night, identify a numbered apartment from a verbal description, and apply close-range fire with discrimination. The unit had become — by the spring of 1973 — the country's tactical executor for a class of operations that the country's political and intelligence leadership had decided it wanted to perform.

I make this observation neither as criticism nor as praise. It is, simply, what happened. Avraham Arnan was no longer with the unit in any operational capacity by 1973; he had handed off command in 1963 and moved through staff and consulting roles after that. The men running Sayeret Matkal in the spring of 1973 — Amiram Levin as commander, Muki Betser and Yoni Netanyahu as senior operators — had inherited an institution that had outgrown its founder's original conception, and they were using it to do what the country's leadership had concluded the country needed it to do.

What the country did not yet know, on the night of 9 April 1973, was that six months later it would need from Sayeret Matkal the exact thing the unit had been founded to provide and had quietly stopped providing: deep, technical, behind-the-lines reconnaissance on the strategic intentions of the Syrian and Egyptian armies. The institutional drift that culminated in Spring of Youth, and the institutional cost of that drift, are the subjects of the next chapter.

Arnan himself died of complications from the brain tumor he had been diagnosed with a decade earlier on 23 April 1980, at the age of forty-nine, and was buried in the military section of Har Herzl. The letter of condolence that Major General Yehoshua Sagi — then the head of Aman, the institutional descendant of the directorate within which Arnan had built his unit — sent to Dalia Arnan in the days after the funeral has, in my reading of the documentary record of Arnan's career, become the load-bearing institutional epitaph for the second entrepreneur of this book's argument. "It is difficult to find on the fingers of one hand," Sagi wrote, "the intelligence men who created yesh me'ayin — something from nothing — and substantially improved Israeli intelligence's collection capacity. In audacity, in vision, in originality of thought, in technological sophistication, and above all in endless devotion, Avraham succeeded in uprooting mountains, in bringing the enemy 'into our territory' and ourselves — into the heart of the enemy's heart. Years will pass before the archives are opened, which will allow us to tell something of Avraham Arnan's creative deeds in the service of intelligence."[^ch5-fn-sagi] The Hebrew phrase yesh me'ayin — something from nothing — is the phrase the entire entrepreneurial argument of this book has been organized around. Sagi reached for it, in 1980, to characterize a man he had known well; I have reached for it, four decades later, to characterize an institutional pattern of which Arnan was the second of four exemplars. The first, as the previous chapter described, was Yitzhak Sadeh. The third — Muki Betser, then twenty-eight years old, standing on the second-floor balcony of an apartment in West Beirut on the night of 9 April 1973, looking at the body of Kamal Adwan and not yet knowing what he would do with what he had become — was waiting his turn.

The second entrepreneur had built his unit and lost it. The chapter that follows is about the unit's golden decade as the unit drifted; the chapter after that is about the operational pattern the third entrepreneur would, in the institutional shadows of the drifting Sayeret Matkal, begin to construct.

# Chapter 6 - The Golden Era

*Sayeret Matkal, the Reconnaissance Ecosystem, and the Two Tracks of Israeli Military Power, 1965–1973*

Source base: Bar-On 2014 Moshe Dayan; Cohen & Lavi 1990 The Sky Is Not the Limit; Eilam 2009 Eilam’s Arc and Eilam’s Bow; Tamari 2012 The Armed Nation; Wald 1992 The Wald Report; Maoz 2009 Defending the Holy Land; Pollack 2002 Arabs at War; Brooks 2006 Security Studies; Asher 2009 The Egyptian Strategy for the Yom Kippur War; Adamsky 2006 Cold War History; Adamsky & Bar-Joseph 2006 Intelligence and National Security; Bar-Joseph 2005 The Watchman Fell Asleep, 2010 The Angel, 2013 MEJ and Maarachot; Spector 2008 Loud and Clear; Shur 2003 Itamar’s Squad, 2008 Border Crosser; Betser & Rosenberg 1996 Secret Soldier; Eitan 1985 Raful; Bergman & Meltzer 2003; Pedahzur 2009 The Israeli Secret Services; Zonder 2000 Sayeret Matkal; Eldar’s three Shayetet volumes; Almog 2010 Flotilla 13: Red Sea; Almog 2014 Sails of My Life.

## 6.1 The Allenby Bridge, March 21, 1968

A few minutes before five o’clock on the morning of Thursday, March 21, 1968, the first of the Israeli paratroopers and Sayeret Tzanchanim operators began their crossing of the Allenby Bridge into the Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan. They were in the lead element of what would become known, in the IDF’s institutional memory, as Operation Tofet — Inferno — and to the world’s press, simply as the Battle of Karameh.[^fn136]

The objective was the town of Karameh, ten kilometers east of the Jordan River in the Jordan Valley, which had become in the months since the Six-Day War a forward operating base of Yasser Arafat’s Fatah movement. Fatah operators had crossed back into the West Bank from Karameh through the autumn and winter of 1967–1968 and had carried out a sustained campaign of cross-border attacks against Israeli civilian buses, settlements, and military patrols. The Israeli Cabinet had authorized a punitive raid against Fatah’s principal base. The IDF — through the Central Command and the Paratroopers Brigade under Brigadier General Dan Laner — had planned a multi-axis operation involving paratroopers, armor, mechanized infantry, and air support, with a contingent of Sayeret Matkal operators assigned to a specific target deep inside Karameh itself.[^fn137]

What happened on March 21 was not what the IDF had planned. The Jordanian Arab Legion, which had been expected by Israeli intelligence to stay out of the engagement, intervened in force from the heights east of Karameh. Jordanian artillery and armor — including King Hussein’s own Centurion tanks of the 60th Armored Brigade — engaged the Israeli columns from elevated positions throughout the day. Fatah operators, instead of dispersing as IDF planners had predicted, fought from inside Karameh’s stone buildings and inflicted heavier-than-expected casualties on the paratroopers clearing the town house by house. The Israeli helicopter pickup operation, which was supposed to extract the Sayeret Matkal element after its mission inside Karameh, was delayed by Jordanian artillery fire. Three Israeli pilots flying close support over Karameh were shot down. By the time the IDF columns withdrew across the Jordan in the late afternoon, the Israeli toll was twenty-nine dead and ninety wounded, with the loss of four tanks, six half-tracks, two armored personnel carriers, and the three downed aircraft.[^fn138]

In the immediate aftermath of the operation, Arafat — who had been in Karameh on March 21 and had narrowly escaped capture by the Sayeret Matkal element — proclaimed Karameh a Palestinian victory. Karameh in Arabic means “honor” or “dignity.” The pun was unavoidable, and the political payoff to Fatah, in recruitment terms across the Arab world, was immense.[^fn139] Inside the IDF, however, the operational lessons were different. Karameh was the first major engagement of the post-1967 era in which Sayeret Matkal had operated as a publicly visible component of a brigade-level operation, and the unit’s element had — despite the broader operational disappointments of the day — performed its specific mission inside Karameh with the precision its commanders had hoped for. The young captain who had led the Sayeret Matkal element through the streets of Karameh and back to the helicopter extraction was a twenty-three-year-old paratrooper named Muki Betser, attached to Sayeret Matkal from his parent unit only a few weeks earlier. Betser was wounded twice during the engagement, evacuated, and would spend the next eight months recovering from injuries that would end his service in active reconnaissance roles for a period. He would re-enter the unit, as I described in Chapter 7, four years later under a new commander and a new institutional configuration.[^fn140]

This chapter is about the eight years that connect the funeral of Yitzhak Sadeh in 1952 — where the book began — to the morning of October 6, 1973, where Chapter 7 opens. More precisely, it is about the period from the procurement decisions of 1965–1966 that defined the IDF’s force structure for the next decade, through the Six-Day War of 1967 and its institutional aftermath, through the War of Attrition that ran from 1967 to 1970, through the operational arc of Sayeret Matkal from Karameh through the Beirut Airport raid through Sabena through Spring of Youth, to the doctrinal blindness that, in the summer of 1973, would set up the catastrophe of October 6. It is the chapter in which Avraham Arnan’s institution — the unit I described in Chapter 5 — comes of age. It is also the chapter in which the IDF’s senior officer corps becomes, through repeated operational success, too confident in its own conventional capabilities to take seriously the doctrinal threat that the Soviet-armed Arab armies were assembling on the other side of the lines.

The chapter develops two parallel tracks. The first is the conventional buildup of the IDF in the late 1960s and early 1970s: the procurement decisions, the Air Force consolidation, the Armored Corps expansion, the doctrinal evolution that would peak in the Six-Day War and that would, by 1973, ossify into the conception known to the Agranat Commission as Ha-Konseptzia — “The Conception.” The second is the operational maturation of the SOF community: Sayeret Matkal’s emergence as the IDF’s premier ground unit, Shayetet 13’s parallel emergence as the premier naval unit, the institutional and doctrinal innovations of Avraham Arnan’s Mivtsa’im Meyuhadim (MM) division within AMAN, and the counterterrorism doctrine that emerged from Karameh, the 1968 Beirut Airport raid, the Sabena rescue of May 1972, and the Spring of Youth raid of April 1973. Both tracks would, by the autumn of 1973, reach what I will argue is their peak — and both would, in October, be tested against an enemy that had been preparing for them.

The chapter ends on the eve of the Yom Kippur War. The war itself, and the entrepreneur it produced, are the subject of Chapter 7.

## 6.2 The Six-Day Triumph and the SOF Quiet

To understand why Karameh mattered — and why, in retrospect, the operational lessons of 1968 were less important to the IDF’s senior leadership than they should have been — we have to begin nine months earlier, on the morning of June 5, 1967, when the Israel Air Force opened the Six-Day War with the strike that the IDF’s official history would call simply Mivtsa Moked, “Operation Focus.”

At 7:45 in the morning of June 5, 1967, the first wave of Israel Air Force strike aircraft — a mixed force of French-built Mirage III, Super Mystère, Mystère IV, and Vautour aircraft — crossed the Mediterranean coast at low altitude in the directions of the Egyptian air bases at Cairo West, Beni Suef, Almaza, Inshas, and a dozen others. Over the next one hundred and eighty minutes, the IAF destroyed approximately four hundred and fifty-two Egyptian, Syrian, Jordanian, and Iraqi aircraft on the ground, disabled eighteen Arab airfields, and effectively eliminated Arab combat air power for the duration of the war.[^fn141] Moked is, by most assessments, the most consequential single air operation in the history of military aviation. Within six days, the IDF — using the air supremacy that Moked had won in the war’s first hours — had destroyed three Arab armies, captured the Sinai Peninsula, the Golan Heights, and the West Bank, and produced what would be remembered in Israel as the most complete military victory in the country’s history.[^fn142]

The institutional consequences of Moked and the broader Six-Day triumph were direct and lasting. The Israel Air Force, which had been a service of mixed prestige and uncertain doctrine before 1967, emerged as the unchallenged premier service of the IDF. The Armored Corps, which had carried out the breakthrough operations across the Sinai under Brigadier General Israel Tal and Brigadier General Ariel Sharon, emerged as the premier ground arm. Together, the two services consolidated what the IDF’s planning literature of the late 1960s called the Tochnit Ramatkalit — the Chief of Staff’s Plan — which was, in its essentials, an air-armor doctrine of pre-emptive offense and rapid maneuver designed to win short, decisive wars by destroying enemy forces on enemy territory.[^fn143]

For the IDF’s Special Operations Forces, the consequence of the Six-Day Triumph was, paradoxically, quiet. The war had been, in operational terms, an air-and-armor war. SOFs had played meaningful but localized roles — Sayeret Matkal had conducted a number of reconnaissance and signals-intelligence-emplacement missions in the days before the war; Shayetet 13’s frogmen had attempted to penetrate Alexandria harbor with mixed results; Sayeret Tzanchanim had operated on Mount Hermon — but none of these had been decisive at the strategic level.[^fn144] The doctrine that had emerged from the war — the doctrine that the Chief of Staff Yitzhak Rabin and his Operations Branch chief David Elazar had codified by late 1967 — was a doctrine in which the war’s decision lay with the IAF’s first hours and the Armored Corps’ first days. SOFs were retained as a strategic asset, but they were retained as a peripheral strategic asset. Most of the senior officer corps assumed, in the late 1960s, that the next major war Israel fought would resemble the Six-Day War — and that SOFs would have, in that war, the same secondary role they had had in 1967.

This was the institutional condition that made Karameh, nine months after the Six-Day War, significant in a way the senior officer corps did not fully appreciate. Karameh was the first major engagement of the post-1967 era in which the IDF found itself fighting not the war the Tochnit Ramatkalit had been designed for. It was a punitive cross-border raid against an irregular force — Fatah — operating under the protection of a state army (Jordan) that had not been expected to engage. The air-armor doctrine, when applied to this kind of operation, produced the casualties and the operational disappointments I described in §6.1. And the unit that came out of Karameh with its operational reputation enhanced — Sayeret Matkal — was a unit that the air-armor doctrine had no clear role for.

The post-Karameh period — from April 1968 through the operational climax of 1972–1973 — would be the period in which Avraham Arnan’s institution would build for itself a doctrinal role that the IDF’s senior leadership had not envisioned for it: the role of the IDF’s principal counterterrorism instrument, with a secondary doctrinal role in deep strategic reconnaissance. This was not a planned development. It was the consequence of the SOF community discovering, in the operational gaps of the post-1967 strategic environment, missions that the conventional IDF could not perform.

## 6.2½ The Reconnaissance Ecosystem and the New Border Geography, 1967–1968

Before we follow Sayeret Matkal’s emergence as the IDF’s premier ground SOF through the operations of 1968–1973, we have to dwell for a moment on the geographic and institutional environment in which that emergence took place — because Sayeret Matkal was not the only Israeli SOF that grew through the post-1967 period, and the ecosystem of reconnaissance units in which it operated is, in retrospect, as important to the chapter’s argument as the unit itself.[^fn145]

The Six-Day War’s territorial outcome transformed the border-security environment of the IDF. Before June 1967, Israel had defended approximately 612 miles of land border against the four Arab states that ringed it. After June 1967, the land borders had shrunk to approximately 404 miles — but the operational depth behind those borders had expanded enormously. The IDF was now responsible for the security of the Sinai Peninsula (twenty-three thousand square miles of desert with a single Egyptian state across the canal), the Golan Heights (five hundred square miles of basalt plateau facing Syria), the West Bank (twenty-two hundred square miles of populated Palestinian territory with Jordan beyond), and the Gaza Strip. The maritime borders, simultaneously, had expanded from approximately 158 to approximately 621 miles, with the addition of the Red Sea, the Gulf of Suez, and the eastern Mediterranean coast that the Sinai conquest had opened.[^fn146] The conventional IDF — the Armored Corps and the IAF whose doctrinal triumph I described in §6.2 — had been built to win short wars at the prewar borders. It had not been built to police the security of a state whose perimeter had just grown into a strategic depth that no single reconnaissance unit could cover.

The institutional response to this geographic asymmetry was the rapid expansion, between 1968 and 1971, of a tier of regional reconnaissance units — the Sayarot Pikudiot, the command-level reconnaissance battalions — that the IDF had previously maintained at limited strength. Sayeret Shaked (Unit 424), the reconnaissance battalion of the Southern Command founded in 1955 under Avraham Yoffe and commanded since 1956 by Major Amos Yarkoni — the legendary Bedouin tracker whose service to the IDF would, by his retirement, span three decades — was expanded after 1967 to cover the new operational depth of the Sinai. Shaked operated against Egyptian commando insertions across the canal, against Palestinian fedayeen infiltrating through the Sinai from the Gaza Strip, and against the broader pattern of low-intensity warfare that the post-1967 period had opened in the southern theater.[^fn147]

Sayeret Charuv (Unit 484), founded in 1965 under the Central Command and rapidly expanded after 1967 under the operational direction of Major (later Lieutenant Colonel) Meir Har-Zion — Sadeh’s intellectual heir, the most celebrated tracker-commando of the Paratroopers’ generation of the 1950s — took on the parallel mission in the Jordan Valley. From 1968 through the early 1970s, Charuv operators ran nighttime ambushes against Palestinian fedayeen crossing the Jordan from refugee camps in Jordan, conducted reconnaissance behind the Jordanian front during the War of Attrition’s eastern phase, and developed the small-unit tactical doctrine that would, after the Yom Kippur War, be inherited by the Paratroopers’ Reconnaissance Platoon and (by a different lineage) by what would become Sayeret Egoz.[^fn148]

Sayeret Rimon — a smaller and more clandestine unit, founded in 1970 under the Southern Command’s operational direction in the Gaza Strip and the Sinai — specialized in mistarvim operations: the disguised-as-Arab covert reconnaissance and direct-action work that, in the 1980s, would be inherited by the Duvdevan unit Chapter 8 will describe.[^fn149] Rimon operated under General Ariel Sharon’s overall southern-command direction through the early 1970s, and the unit’s institutional culture — small teams, deep cover, ambiguous attribution — would prove, in retrospect, to have been the operational seed of what the IDF would, by the late 1980s, codify as urban counterinsurgency doctrine.

The four units — Sayeret Matkal at the General Staff level, Shaked in the south, Charuv in the center, Rimon in the Gaza-Sinai theater — together formed what the IDF’s later institutional vocabulary would call the Mishpechet HaSayarot, the family of reconnaissance units. None of them were created by a single doctrinal decision. They emerged, individually, from the operational discovery that no existing unit could cover the new territorial depth that the Six-Day Triumph had opened. The senior officer corps’s doctrinal investment in the air-armor doctrine of the Tochnit Ramatkalit meant that the regional preventive-reconnaissance role was not seen as strategically central — and the Sayarot Pikudiot therefore operated, through the 1968–1973 period, with the limited institutional protection of units that were operationally useful but doctrinally peripheral. This vulnerability would have its consequences. As I described in Chapter 7 §7.7, the post-Yom Kippur dissolution of Sayeret Charuv and the original Sayeret Egoz in 1974 — and the partial dissolution of Sayeret Shaked over the following decade — followed directly from the institutional weakness of the regional reconnaissance tier in the post-1973 IDF.[^fn150]

What the regional reconnaissance ecosystem provided through the 1968–1973 period, however, was the operational backbone of Israeli border security in a strategic environment that the conventional IDF doctrine had not designed for. The reciprocal point — that the success of Sayeret Matkal’s strategic operations through this period was made possible in part by the lower-tier ecosystem that handled the routine security load — is one of the analytical points the chapter has to make. We return to Sayeret Matkal’s operational trajectory in §6.3.

## 6.3 The Procurement Revolution: Vietnam, Helicopters, and the French Embargo, 1965–1968

In the summer of 1966, a year before the Six-Day War, the IDF’s former Chief of Staff Moshe Dayan traveled to South Vietnam as a war correspondent for the Israeli newspaper Maariv and for several international syndicates.[^fn151] Dayan, who had been a defining figure in the IDF since the 1950s and who would in less than a year become Israel’s Minister of Defense on the eve of the Six-Day War, was no ordinary war correspondent. He met with William Westmoreland, the commander of the U.S. Military Assistance Command Vietnam; he flew on operational missions with the 1st Cavalry Division; he interviewed U.S. Army and Marine officers across the Vietnamese theater. The dispatches he produced — which were widely read in the IDF’s senior officer corps — emphasized two themes. The first was the centrality of the helicopter to American operational doctrine in Vietnam: the use of UH-1 “Huey” helicopters for air assault, medical evacuation, and reconnaissance, and the larger CH-47 Chinook for heavy lift, had transformed what the U.S. Army called “air mobility” into the defining feature of the war’s operational tempo. The second theme was Dayan’s skepticism that the heavy American technological dominance would, by itself, defeat the Viet Cong. The Vietnamese, he wrote, were waging a war in which the political and institutional dimensions outweighed the technical and the kinetic.[^fn152]

Dayan’s dispatches contributed to a procurement decision the IDF made in 1966 that, while small in financial scale, would have outsized consequences for the SOF community’s doctrinal development over the next decade. The Air Force decided to establish its second transport helicopter squadron and to acquire from France four heavy-lift Aérospatiale SA 321 Super Frelon helicopters at a cost of approximately twenty million U.S. dollars.[^fn153] The Super Frelon — the same airframe the French Navy used for anti-submarine warfare and the Israeli IAF would soon call the Tzir’a (Hornet) and later the Yas’ur (Petrel, after the IAF replaced the SA 321 with the larger CH-53 Sea Stallion in the early 1970s) — gave the IDF its first heavy-lift airborne insertion capability. It is the platform that would, six years later, deliver Sayeret Matkal operators to the targets of the Beirut Airport raid in December 1968 and the Spring of Youth raid in Beirut in April 1973. It is the operational predecessor of the CH-53 Yas’ur that would, in 1976, fly the Sayeret Matkal force to Entebbe; that would, in the 1980s and 1990s, become the workhorse of Shaldag’s insertion and extraction operations; and that would, on October 7, 2023, fly Unit 669’s emergency search-and-rescue teams to the Gaza envelope kibbutzim on the morning of the Hamas attack.

Two other procurement decisions of 1965–1966 deserve mention. The first was the IDF’s preliminary negotiation with the United Kingdom for the purchase of several hundred Chieftain Mk 2 main battle tanks, Britain’s most advanced contemporary tank, in exchange for partial Israeli participation in the Chieftain’s continued development.[^fn154] The Chieftain deal would, by 1969, collapse under British political pressure from Arab states — and the collapse would directly produce, in the summer of 1970, the Israeli decision to develop the indigenous Merkava tank under the project leadership of Major General Israel Tal.[^fn155] The second was the February 1966 American decision, under the Johnson administration, to authorize for the first time the sale of advanced strike aircraft to Israel: the McDonnell Douglas A-4 Skyhawk, sixty-eight of which were delivered to the IAF between 1967 and 1969.[^fn156] The Skyhawk acquisition marked, in retrospect, the beginning of the long American–Israeli defense relationship that would define Israeli strategic posture for the next half-century.

These three procurement decisions of 1965–1966 — Super Frelon helicopters, Chieftain negotiations, Skyhawk acquisition — were the proximate background of the strategic shock that the IDF would receive in June 1967 when the French government of Charles de Gaulle, in the face of the Israeli pre-emptive strike, imposed an arms embargo on all major weapons systems destined for Israel. The embargo blocked, most consequentially, the delivery of fifty Dassault Mirage 5J fighter-bombers that the IAF had ordered and paid for and that were already in production for Israeli delivery in 1968 and 1969. The Mirage 5J had been the planned successor of the Mirage III that had carried out Moked. Its blockage by de Gaulle was the moment at which the IDF understood, with absolute clarity, that the French-Israeli defense relationship that had supplied Israel’s primary combat aircraft since the mid-1950s was over.[^fn157]

The strategic response was two-fold. On the procurement side, the IDF accelerated and deepened its turn toward American suppliers. President Johnson authorized in January 1968 the sale of the McDonnell Douglas F-4 Phantom II — the IAF would call it the Kurnass, “Sledgehammer” — and the first Phantoms entered Israeli service in September 1969.[^fn158] On the industrial-policy side, the embargo catalyzed the construction of an indigenous Israeli defense industry on a scale that had not existed before. Israel Aerospace Industries (IAI) began, in 1967, a clandestine effort to reverse-engineer the Mirage 5J using technical drawings that an Israeli operative in Switzerland had obtained from a sympathetic engineer at Dassault. The result, the IAI Nesher (Eagle), made its first flight in March 1971 and entered IAF service in 1972 in time to participate in the Yom Kippur War.[^fn159] The Nesher and its development successor, the IAI Kfir, would form the institutional foundation of the Israeli aerospace industry that would, by the early 2000s, produce the Heron and Hermes long-endurance UAVs that Chapter 9 will discuss.

The Six-Day Triumph, the Karameh disappointment, the French embargo, and the American pivot — taken together, these four events of 1967 and 1968 reshaped the institutional environment of the IDF’s senior officer corps. The IAF and the Armored Corps emerged from the period more institutionally dominant than they had been in 1965; the SOF community emerged with a stronger sense of its operational independence, but with a continuing absence of doctrinal recognition by the senior staff. And both communities began, separately, to prepare for what each understood — correctly — would be a long war of attrition with the Soviet-armed Arab states along the new ceasefire lines.

## 6.4 The War of Attrition and the SAM Crisis, 1968–1970

The War of Attrition began, in the IDF’s institutional reckoning, on July 1, 1967 — three weeks after the Six-Day War’s formal end — when Egyptian artillery opened fire on Israeli positions along the eastern bank of the Suez Canal. It would continue for nearly three years, until the U.S.-brokered ceasefire of August 7, 1970, and it would, by its end, fundamentally challenge the air-armor doctrine that the Six-Day War had cemented as the operational foundation of the IDF.[^fn160]

The challenge came from the Soviet Union. After June 1967, the Soviet leadership under Leonid Brezhnev concluded — as Dima Adamsky has documented in detail — that the destruction of two Soviet-armed client militaries (Egypt and Syria) in six days could not be allowed to stand, and that the Soviet investment in those militaries had to be both recovered and dramatically expanded.[^fn161] Between 1968 and 1970, the Soviet Union deployed to Egypt and Syria what was, in scale and sophistication, the most significant Soviet expeditionary effort outside the Warsaw Pact in the Cold War. Soviet advisors entered Egyptian and Syrian air-defense units in numbers approaching ten thousand. Soviet pilots flew operational missions against Israeli aircraft in Egyptian skies. And, most consequentially for the doctrinal future of Middle Eastern warfare, the Soviets supplied the Egyptian and Syrian militaries with the new generation of integrated air-defense systems that had emerged from Soviet doctrinal evolution in response to the American air war over North Vietnam.

The Soviet-supplied Integrated Air Defense System (IADS) that the Egyptian and Syrian air-defense corps assembled across the Suez Canal and the Golan armistice lines in 1969–1970 consisted of three principal categories of weapon, deployed in overlapping engagement envelopes. The fixed long-range SA-2 Guideline and medium-range SA-3 Goa surface-to-air missile systems — semi-mobile, electronically-guided, capable of engaging Israeli aircraft at altitudes up to twenty thousand meters — provided the engagement layer that forced Israeli pilots to operate at low altitude. The mobile SA-6 Gainful surface-to-air missile system — the first generation of mobile Soviet SAMs, equipped with continuous-wave radar guidance that the IAF’s existing electronic countermeasures had no defense against — provided the low-and-medium altitude engagement layer that closed the envelope underneath the SA-2 and SA-3 systems. And the ZSU-23/4 Shilka — a radar-directed quad-mounted twenty-three-millimeter anti-aircraft gun, mounted on a tracked armored vehicle for mobility — provided the very-low-altitude engagement layer that punished aircraft attempting to dive beneath the SAM coverage.[^fn162]

The combined effect of the three-layer Soviet IADS was to deny the IAF — for the first time since the Six-Day War — the operational freedom of the airspace it had taken for granted. Through the spring and summer of 1969, the IAF carried out deep-penetration strikes against Egyptian targets in the Nile Delta and against Syrian air-defense installations in the Golan vicinity, and in those operations the IAF lost a sustained trickle of aircraft to the new Soviet systems. The losses, in absolute terms, were not large by the standards of conventional air war — over the full course of the War of Attrition, the IAF lost approximately twenty-five aircraft to enemy fire — but they were sustained, they were unprecedented, and they revealed a doctrinal problem the IDF had not previously encountered: an Arab air-defense system that could, when properly deployed, force the IAF to accept casualties that conventional Israeli strategic calculations had not anticipated.[^fn163]

The crisis came to a head in the summer of 1970. Between April and July of that year, the Soviet expeditionary effort in Egypt reached its operational peak. Soviet-piloted MiG-21s flew combat-air-patrol missions over the western bank of the Canal. Soviet-crewed SA-3 batteries engaged Israeli aircraft over the canal and the Sinai. And Soviet-operated electronic-warfare units established what the IAF’s pilots would call, in the after-action language of the period, Ha-Kayitz Ha-Elektroni — “the Electronic Summer.”[^fn164] In late June 1970, an Israeli F-4 Phantom was shot down by a Soviet-operated SA-3 over the Egyptian side of the Canal. Both crew members were killed. The IAF understood that the Soviet expeditionary force had crossed an operational threshold that, if not answered, would establish a precedent for Soviet engagement against IAF aircraft on the Sinai side of the Canal as well.

The Israeli answer was Operation Rimon 20.

## 6.5 Operation Rimon 20 and the Cost of Air Dominance, July 1970

On the morning of July 30, 1970, the IAF’s 113th Squadron (the “Hornets,” flying Mirage IIICJs) and the 119th Squadron (the “Bat,” flying F-4 Phantoms) executed what the IAF’s operational doctrine would later call Ma’arav Tilim — an aerial ambush — against the Soviet MiG-21 force that had been operating combat air patrols over the Canal zone.[^fn165] The operation, designed and approved at the chief-of-staff level under Major General Mordechai Hod (IAF commander) and Lieutenant General Haim Bar-Lev (COGS), used a deception package designed to lure the Soviet patrols into a position where Israeli interceptors held the tactical advantage.

The deception package consisted of a small flight of slow-moving A-4 Skyhawks operating at the altitude and on the flight profile that the Soviets had come to associate with Israeli reconnaissance missions. Behind the Skyhawks, screened from Soviet radar by the Sinai mountain terrain and by careful flight discipline, eight Mirage IIICJs and four F-4 Phantoms held in ambush positions. When the Soviet MiG-21s — a flight of approximately twelve aircraft, vectored by Egyptian ground control to engage what they believed was the Israeli reconnaissance flight — entered the engagement zone, the Israeli ambush sprang.
